In 1,000 simulated cohorts, a naive test called a purely composition-driven gene set significant in 82% of cohorts, whereas the proposed battery classified it as composition-independent in 5% while recovering a planted within-cell effect in 98% (moderate effect) and 50% (weak effect) of cohorts. Conclusions: The original axis associations do not establish composition-independent disease programs; their interpretation is sensitive to feature construction, scoring and adjustment for cell composition. Curated axis scores in bulk brain tissue should be reported with competitive null distributions, composition adjustment, exact small-sample inference, and endpoints and scoring fixed before analysis. We provide code for these checks.

article.title: Hepatic urea cycle suppression drives brown fat thermogenesis to counter obesity and liver disease
article.authors: Kim, L. C.; Lesner, N. P.; Cai, X.; Han, X.; Xu, J. P.; Zhao, A.; Coffey, N. J.; Zheng, D.; Keith, B.; Mesaros, C.; Arany, Z.; Simon, M. C.
article.abstract: The hepatic urea cycle is consistently suppressed in liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but whether loss of individual enzymes contributes to disease progression remains unknown. We investigated the role of urea cycle enzyme argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) in diet- and carcinogen-induced liver disease using hepatocyte-specific deletion of Ass1 in mice. Complete loss of hepatic Ass1 is lethal, but a high-fat diet extends lifespan. Unexpectedly, animals with approximately 85% loss of hepatic Ass1 are markedly protected from diet-induced obesity, liver steatosis, fibrosis, and HCC. Hyperammonemia induced by hepatic Ass1 loss activates brown adipose tissue fatty acid oxidation, driving thermogenesis and increasing energy expenditure. Importantly, targeting Ass1 after obesity onset promotes weight loss and reverses liver steatosis. These findings implicate hepatic ASS1 as a critical regulator of systemic lipid metabolism with therapeutic potential against obesity, liver disease, and HCC.

article.title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
article.authors: Russell, S.; Miller, K.; Kaplan, D.; Levin, M.; Murugan, N. J.
article.abstract: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.

article.title: Structure constrained spin responses of an FMN superoxide radical-pair model in mitochondrial complex I
article.authors: Sung, J.-Y.; Antill, L. M.; Cheong, J.-H.
article.abstract: Mitochondrial complex I produces reactive oxygen species at its flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor. We combined steric sampling of oxygen positions in human complex I with radical-pair spin simulations to examine how the FMN pocket shapes reaction-yield sensitivity, which provided singlet yields across FMN O2 centroid separations, magnetic fields and spin-dephasing conditions. A composite score combining geometric accessibility with normalised field and dephasing responses peaked near 3.3 in the reference 2.5 ~9.0 calculation. The highest-scoring 10% of accessible configurations had a mean separation of 3.28 (2.5th~97.5th percentiles, 2.77~3.64 ). The near contact score maximum persisted when the structural input, sampled distance range and recombination/dephasing rates were varied. At longer separations, the raw field response approached a broad plateau, while the composite score retained a near-contact maximum. Prescribed fluctuations in separation produced the greatest variability in calculated singlet yield within or close to this region. The analysis locates an FMN-centred range of accessible geometries where structural and spin-response effects combine in a model of radical-pair reaction branching.

article.title: Transcriptomic rejuvenation during intestinal and liver regeneration in mice
article.authors: Iqbal, S.; Gladyshev, V. N.
article.abstract: Aging and regeneration are fundamental biological processes, but the relationship between them is poorly understood. During intestinal regeneration, adult epithelial cells reactivate developmental programs that support repair. To investigate if this plasticity alters tissue biological age, we developed and validated intestinal tissue and epithelium-specific transcriptomic aging clocks. Across various regeneration models, epithelial states were predicted by these clocks to be younger than controls. Their expression changes were also negatively associated with intestinal stem-cell and progenitor aging signatures. The resulting younger state was characterized by YAP-associated regeneration and reduced mature enterocyte identity. In a separate irradiation model, the predicted epithelial age first increased, then fell at the peak of regeneration and later increased again during recovery. In a chemotherapy-induced injury model, epithelium in both young and old animals also reversibly transitioned through this younger state, returning to its preinjury state during recovery, although regenerative and fetal-like gene expression differed with host age. Further spatial transcriptomic analyses linked lower epithelial age with regeneration in selected injured and tumor-associated regions. In addition, liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy in old animals was also accompanied by decreased transcriptomic age, which persisted to the last sampled time point, and by pathway changes negatively associated with aging signatures. Overall, these findings suggest that mammalian regeneration is associated with a transient reduction in transcriptomic age, whose timing and persistence depend on tissue and the course of repair.

article.title: Polyglutamine aggregation in the C. elegans nervous system is driven by stochastic nucleation events
article.authors: van Schijndel, V.; Tiggelaar, J.; Franken, M. S. E.; Remkes, D.; Joshi, M.; Sandhu, D.; Baars, K.; de Graaf, J. D. F.; Sinnige, T.
article.abstract: Fibrillar protein aggregation is the hallmark of a wide variety of neurodegenerative diseases. It is still poorly understood how soluble proteins transition to fibrillar aggregates, in particular within the complex environment of cells and tissues. Here, we employ the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of polyglutamine aggregation in the nervous system of a multicellular animal. By using fluorescence microscopy in combination with mathematical modelling, we find that polyglutamine aggregation occurs by stochastic nucleation in individual neurons, at a rate that is of the same order of magnitude as previously determined for muscle cells. The J-protein DNAJB6 strongly suppresses polyglutamine aggregation in both tissues, consistent with a mechanism in which aggregation is limited by primary nucleation. We confirm that the same mechanism holds true for a construct including the disease-relevant flanking regions of huntingtin exon 1. Altogether, our data reveal that polyglutamine aggregation occurs spontaneously and largely independently of the cellular context, rather than as a consequence of ageing and the associated decline in protein homeostasis.

article.title: Harnessing variation in Drosophila melanogaster reveals different routes to increased infection susceptibility over age and sex-dependent association with lifespan
article.authors: Monteiro-Black, B.; Corbally, M.-K.; Aleksandrowicz, J.; Taggart, A. M.; Langella, F.; Belmonte, R. L.; Mika, P.; Duneau, D.; Regan, J. C.
article.abstract: It is widely accepted that susceptibility to infection increases with age, usually attributed to immune system dysregulation. However, factors beyond decreased resistance mechanisms may increase susceptibility, such as changes to physiological or metabolic processes determining overall tolerance, and this may differ between individuals. We hypothesised that age-related increases in susceptibility reflect changes in both immune system function and disease tolerance, with their relative importance varying by population and sex. We assessed age-related susceptibility to bacterial pathogens in an outbred D. melanogaster population and 22 isolines. We leveraged this variation to investigate age-related infection susceptibility and lifespan, and to estimate frequencies of declines in resistance or tolerance mechanisms. Susceptibility increased early in life, and was widespread across infections and populations. Despite strong correlation between the sexes in baseline susceptibility and its decrease over age, susceptibility at old age did not correlate. Increased susceptibility was associated with impaired resistance (bona fide immunosenescence), but more frequently with reduced tolerance, which could be detected early in life, and remained low. We find susceptibility at old age predicts lifespan in males only. In conclusion, increased infection susceptibility is an early-arising ageing phenotype occurring in both sexes and driving male mortality. Infection susceptibility followed a power-law (Weibull) rather than the exponential (Gompertz) pattern typical of mortality, with each doubling of age approximately doubling susceptibility. We argue that the term 'immunosenescence' should be limited to dysregulation of resistance mechanisms, and consideration of population variation, sex, and ageing of non-immune functions is critical to fully understand age-related loss of pathogen control.

article.title: Creatine phosphagen system regulates energy metabolism and growth of trophoblasts
article.authors: Sah, N.; Zheng, C.; Stein, F. H.; Shaik, W.; Nassoura, M. B.; Mole, L. M.; Rajupalem, R.; Pizzo, D.; Meads, M.; Soncin, F.
article.abstract: The creatine (Cr)-creatine kinase (CK)-phosphocreatine (PCr) system maintains ATP homeostasis in tissues with high energy demands, but its role in early human placental development remains poorly understood. We characterized Cr-CK-PCr system components across gestation and investigated its function in trophoblast development. Proteins involved in Cr biosynthesis, transport, and utilization were examined in first-trimester, second-trimester, and term human placentae (n=3-6/group). Components showed gestational age- and compartment-specific localization. The biosynthetic enzymes AGAT and GAMT localized predominantly to fetal villous mesenchyme and broadly across villous compartments, respectively. CKB was enriched in fetal mesenchyme, whereas CKMT1 was broadly expressed across trophoblast subtypes. The main Cr transporter SLC6A8 was abundant in syncytiotrophoblast early in gestation but shifted predominantly to fetal blood vessels at term. To determine functional importance, primary human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs) were treated with a creatine analog, cyclocreatine (cCr; 0-40 mM), for 48 h. Treatment with 20 mM cCr reduced proliferation (P<0.001), decreased EGFR expression (P<0.05), induced cell-cycle arrest (P<0.0001), and increased apoptosis (P<0.0001). cCr also impaired mitochondrial and glycolytic function (P<0.01) with morphological evidence of mitochondrial stress. Consistently, treatment of primary human trophoblast organoids with cCr reduced organoid growth and EGFR expression (P<0.05). Together, these findings demonstrate that the Cr-CK-PCr system is dynamically expressed across human placental development and that disruption of Cr/PCr metabolism compromises trophoblast bioenergetics, proliferation, and survival, supporting its importance in placental development and providing a foundation for investigating its contribution to pregnancy disorders associated with altered placental energy metabolism.

article.title: Transgenerational pathogen defence extends beyond behavioural avoidance
article.authors: Zwoinska, M. K.; Widjaja, A. N.; Akgül, A. D.; Altan, A. S.; Aydın, D.; Cukurbaglı, D.; Duxbury, E. M.; Harris, I.; Maklakov, A. A.; Renhuldt, N. T.; Venkataramani, A. G.; Lind, M. I.; Chen, H.-y.
article.abstract: Transgenerational plasticity can prepare descendants for environmental stress, but its generality and adaptive value remain unclear. Here we tested for adaptive transgenerational effects of exposure to the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas vranovensis across five Caenorhabditis species. Pathogen exposure reduced rate-sensitive fitness in all five species, but behavioural responses varied across species and generations. In C. elegans, exposed parents and their F2 descendants showed increased pathogen avoidance. In C. remanei, pathogen exposure increased attraction in females, whereas their F2 female descendants showed greater avoidance. We found no F2 behavioural response in C. kamaaina, C. tropicalis or C. briggsae. Remarkably, however, ancestral exposure increased F2 larval survival on the pathogen in C. elegans, C. remanei and C. tropicalis. In C. tropicalis this survival benefit occurred without behavioural avoidance. The two species showing transgenerational avoidance had the closest sequence matches between the bacterial small RNA Pv1 and its candidate neuronal target maco-1, suggesting a possible molecular basis for variation in the response. Our results show that shared susceptibility to a pathogen does not imply similarity in transgenerational response, and that ancestral exposure can benefit descendants without inheritance of pathogen avoidance.

article.title: Ribosome-Associated GTPase Drg1 Links Cytosolic Translation to Mitochondrial Homeostasis
article.authors: Saha, S.; Bhattacharya, A.; Jin, H.
article.abstract: Coordination of the functionalities among key organelles is essential for maintaining the complexity and adaptability of the eukaryotic cell. Functionally versatile proteins, such as GTPases, often assume important roles in this process. A ribosome-binding GTPase called Developmentally-regulated GTP-binding (Drg) protein is a conserved family of GTPases that promotes protein synthesis and regulates cytoskeletal dynamics, suggesting their importance for cell growth and proliferation. Mitochondrial proteostasis requires coordination between cytosolic translation and the targeting, import, and assembly of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins. However, the ribosome-associated factors that support this coordination remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the conserved GTPase Drg1, one of the two Drg paralogues in eukaryotic cells, as a translation factor required for mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular fitness. Human Drg1 and its cofactor Dfrp1 are associated with translating ribosomes and co-sedimented with polysomes. Deletion of Drg1 in HEK293T cells caused altered mitochondrial architecture, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, and impaired expression of a mitochondrially targeted reporter. Re-expression of wild-type Drg1 restored ATP production and reporter expression, whereas a GTPase-deficient Drg1 mutant failed to provide comparable rescue in ATP production, demonstrating that Drg1 catalytic activity is required for its cellular function. Mitochondria-directed APEX2 proximity proteomics further connected Drg1-dependent translation to proteins involved in mitochondrial protein import, respiratory-chain function, and mitochondrial protein synthesis. Reporter analyses indicated that Drg1 loss preferentially compromises productive translation toward the 3' region of the coding sequence. Together, these findings establish Drg1 as a ribosome-associated translation factor that supports the synthesis and homeostasis of proteins required for mitochondrial function. At the molecular level, loss of cellular homeostasis that is caused by compromised translation of cytoplasmically synthesized proteins functionally related to mitochondria underpins the observed phenomenon. Our results reveal a previously underappreciated connection between the cytosolic translation machinery and mitochondrial maintenance and provide a framework for understanding how defects in a conserved translational GTPase impair cellular energy metabolism and physiology.

article.title: A high-throughput nanoscale imaging platform for direct visualization and rapid measurement of telomeres at single-molecule resolution
article.authors: Jackson-Cook C, Gheghiani L, Mikheykin A, Laeken DV, Guest D, Archer K, Riethman H, Reed J.
article.abstract: Abstract Telomere length is a biomarker of aging, cancer and telomeropathies, with some of the strongest health-related associations occurring at the extremes of the telomere-length spectrum. Critically short telomeres can drive chromosome instability, cellular stress and senescence, yet conventional assays largely provide population-average measurements that obscure these biologically important molecules, and the underlying heterogeneity of individual chromosome ends. In addition, amplification bias associated with highly repetitive telomeric sequences and inter-laboratory variability can limit measurement reproducibility. Although emerging technologies provide higher-resolution analyses, they often require high DNA input, specialized sample preparation, or complex instrumentation and bioinformatic tools, restricting broader adoption. Here, we present a high-throughput single-molecule platform that overcomes these barriers through an automated, user-friendly nanoscale imaging workflow compatible with standard genomic DNA preparations. The method combines a unique dual CRISPR-Cas9 telomere boundary labeling strategy with amplification-free magnetic-bead-based enrichment, preserving the native telomere-length distribution while minimizing representation bias. Using only 500 ng of input DNA and 2–4 h of hands-on processing, the assay accurately resolves intact telomeres spanning ~50 bp to >50 kb within the same sample, enabling simultaneous characterization of the full telomere-length spectrum. It also demonstrates high reproducibility across technical replicates and independent operators (ICC up to 0.90). Validation in telomere-length models, replicative aging systems, and clinical biospecimens, together with subtelomeric barcoding for chromosome-arm assignment, establishes a scalable platform for chromosome-resolved telomere profiling, biomarker development, and future clinical implementation in aging, cancer, and telomere biology.

article.title: Gut microbiota modulates hyodeoxycholic acid to inhibit leukemia development.
article.authors: Liu W, Yang J, Chen Y, Chen S, Li J, Yang T, Zhang G, Hu J.
article.abstract: Abstract To explore the role of gut microbiota and bile acid (BA) metabolism in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), we analyzed samples from 29 patients via 16S rDNA sequencing and LC-QTOF-MS, and performed functional studies on Enterococcus faecalis and hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA). Results revealed a dynamic shift in gut microbiota diversity during treatment, which recovered after therapy. Notably, the abundance of Enterococcus at baseline was significantly correlated with clinical response after treatment. Furthermore, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) using E. faecalis reduced in vivo leukemia burden and increased levels of BAs such as HDCA. In vitro analyses demonstrated that HDCA suppresses AML cell growth and promotes apoptosis through inhibition of NF-κB, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cell cycle arrest. These findings were corroborated in a mouse model, where HDCA delayed leukemia progression and improved survival. Clinically, higher baseline serum HDCA correlated with greater gut microbiota α diversity and was associated with complete remission. In summary, Enterococcus levels and baseline HDCA are linked to AML treatment outcomes. E. faecalis FMT ameliorates AML with concurrent rises in fecal HDCA, while HDCA exerts anti-leukemic effects by targeting NF-κB, disrupting mitochondrial integrity, arresting the cell cycle, and triggering apoptosis.

article.title: Histone Modifications at the Intersection of Aging, Neuroinflammation and Metabolism in Alzheimer's Disease.
article.authors: Liang J, Cao H, Ren X, Sha N, Han X, Jiang L, Liu B, Zhao W.
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Aging, neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction are tightly intertwined in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how transient pathological signals become persistent cellular states remains poorly understood. Histone post‐translational modifications (PTMs) provide a dynamic interface between extracellular stimuli, cellular metabolism and chromatin state. This Review examines how canonical histone modifications and emerging metabolite‐derived acylations regulate inflammatory and stress‐responsive programmes across microglia, astrocytes and neurons during aging and AD. We discuss how amyloid‐β, tau pathology, metabolic dysfunction and innate immune signaling converge on histone‐modifying machinery, and how reciprocal interactions between metabolism and chromatin may stabilize disease‐associated cell states. Particular attention is given to cellular senescence and neuroimmune memory, while emphasizing the context dependence of individual histone marks across cell types, genomic regions and disease stages. We further evaluate evidence for causality using three criteria: perturbation, persistence and reversibility. This framework distinguishes chromatin states that accompany ongoing pathology from those capable of sustaining pathological cell states beyond their initiating signals. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies targeting histone‐modifying enzymes, chromatin readers and metabolic inputs to restore chromatin plasticity and promote resolution of chronic neuroinflammation.

article.title: Ancestral tributyltin exposure produces male-specific brown adipose thermogenic dysregulatoin
article.authors: Huang, Y.; Chang, R. C.; Nguyen, K. U.; To, K. T.; Gibbs, M.; Honjoh, H.; Shioda, T.; Blumberg, B.
article.abstract: Obesity is a global health challenge increasingly linked to environmental obesogens. Tributyltin (TBT), a model obesogen that activates PPARgamma and RXR, promotes transgenerational obesity in mice, but whether developmental and ancestral exposure impairs energy balance remains unclear. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) contributes to energy expenditure and thermoregulation through UCP1-dependent and -independent pathways. We tested whether TBT exposure disrupts BAT function in F1 and F3 descendants of exposed F0 dams. We measured body composition before and after high-fat diet (HFD) challenge and assessed resting core body temperature, BAT gene expression, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content, and mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) capacity. TBT-line males accumulated more fat after HFD without changes in lean mass despite similar mass-scaled food intake. Before HFD, core body temperature was lower in F1 and F3 TBT-line males, indicating impaired thermal homeostasis before increased adiposity. Candidate-gene qPCR did not show uniform suppression of thermogenic genes; instead, Ucp1 mRNA increased while Ucp2 mRNA decreased in F1 males, indicating dysregulation. Transcriptomal profiling revealed altered thermogenic signaling and consistent downregulation of mitochondrial electron transport chain genes across F1 and F3 males. Relative mtDNA content was unchanged, whereas complex-specific respirometry revealed reduced complex I- and II-associated respiratory capacity, providing evidence of impaired electron transport. No consistent effects occurred in females. These findings identified an early, male-associated BAT phenotype characterized by thermogenic dysregulation, reduced mitochondrial ETC capacity, and impaired thermal homeostasis. They support a model in which impaired BAT mitochondrial function contributes to later susceptibility to diet-induced obesity.

article.title: The Cardiovascular Benefit of Menopause Hormone Treatment is Age-Dependent in Ldlr-/- Mice
article.authors: Lalisan, C. D.; Gavin, C.; Litts, B.; Zhong, M.; Rein, J. A.; An, J.; Boobalan, R.; Wang, Y.; Van Aelst, A.; Chinnarasu, S.; Xu, Y.; Linton, M.; Stafford, J. M.; Zhu, L.
article.abstract: Background: The risk of Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) increases in women after menopause, coinciding with declining estrogen levels. However, menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) has not consistently reduced ASCVD events in post-menopausal women, despite improvements in lipid profiles. The mechanisms underlying the diminished cardiovascular protective effects of estrogens during MHT remain poorly understood. Methods: Atherosclerosis was established in 11-month-old female Ldlr-/- mice through Western diet feeding. To investigate the effects of menopause and 17{beta}-estradiol (E2) treatment on atherosclerotic burden during lipid normalization, mice were switched to a chow diet and subjected to ovariectomy (OVX) with and without E2 treatment. To determine the contribution of inflammation to ASCVD risk during MHT, a cohort of mice received Ifn{gamma}-/- bone marrow transplant (Ifn{gamma}-/-BM) before hormone treatment. To assess the influence of age on ASCVD risk during MHT, parallel studies were conducted in young mice, beginning at 12 weeks of age. Outcomes included lipid profiles, HDL function, circulating cytokines, atherosclerotic burden, liver lipid metabolic pathways and transcriptomic profiles, and hepatic estrogen receptor signaling. Results: OVX increased atherosclerotic burden compared with sham-operation. E2 treatment following OVX failed to reduce established atherosclerosis in older mice but reduced atherosclerosis in young mice during diet-induced lipid normalization. In older mice, E2 treatment increased circulating IFNγ, impaired HDL antioxidant and cholesterol efflux functions, and promoted inflammatory and vulnerable plaque phenotypes. Suppression of inflammation through Ifn{gamma}-/-BM transplantation restored HDL function and the ability of E2 treatment to reduce atherosclerosis in older mice. In contrast, E2 treatment following OVX in young mice limited inflammation and improved HDL function. E2 treatment increased liver fatty acid metabolic signaling in both older and young mice but increased liver 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) levels only in older mice. This age-dependent response was associated with remodeling of hepatic estrogen receptor (ER) expression, characterized by reduced ERα and increased in G protein-coupled ER expression with aging. Liver transcriptomic analyses identified inflammatory and interferon-associated signatures following OVX+E2 treatment in older mice. qPCR analyses across older and young mice suggested age-associated differences in inflammatory transcripts in response to E2. Conclusions: These findings suggest that aging alters the hepatic response to E2 treatment following ovariectomy, promoting oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling that contribute to persistent systemic inflammation and compromise the ability of E2 to reduce atherosclerosis.

article.title: Assembly and Interfacial Mechanics of Recombinant Surfactant Protein B in Mixed Detergent Systems and Lipid Monolayers
article.authors: Asrat, T. G.
article.abstract: Although surfactant protein B (SP-B) is essential for pulmonary surfactant function, the experimental structure of mature SP-B remains undetermined, and the molecular basis of its function is unclear. Here, we characterize the structural and functional behavior of a recombinant SP-B construct (rSP-B) in DPC/SDS detergent micelles and DPPC/POPG lipid monolayers. Light scattering showed that dilute DPC/SDS (9:1, 0.2% w/v) is intrinsically heterogeneous, containing both micellar (~4 nm) and supramicellar structures (~68-400 nm), consistent with non-ideal surfactant mixing at low detergent concentration. Dialysis resulted in a dominant, reproducible mesoscale structure (~600 nm) in which rSP-B retained predominantly alpha-helical structure (~47%), whereas 200 nm filtration removed most of the protein and helical signal, suggesting that rSP-B is associated with the large assemblies, although the resulting complex sizes exceed the regime typically accessible to solution NMR. In separate detergent-only measurements, higher detergent concentrations (0.5-2% w/v) gave monomodal micelles (3.6-4.1 nm), suggesting that detergent concentration influences assembly size. In parallel, incorporation of rSP-B into DPPC/POPG monolayers stabilized the hysteretic response and attenuated cycling-induced area loss relative to protein-free films, with compressibility signatures consistent with out-of-plane deformation and reversible reorganization of collapsed material. These results inform strategies for optimizing detergent conditions for future structural studies and support a model in which rSP-B may promote retention and reversible reorganization of collapsed interfacial material, potentially through mechanically coupled reservoirs.

article.title: Excessive mitochondrial fission in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury: Pathophysiological relevance and potential cardioprotective modulation by plant-derived interventions and electroacupuncture
article.authors: Li Sun; Xing-Yi Sun; Zi-Han Na; Yi-Jia Liu; Lin Li; Tian-Yu Cao; Xin-Ran Li; Ya-Dong Fan; Gui-Ping Hu; Shuo Wang
article.abstract: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MI/RI) remains an unresolved problem despite reperfusion therapies, including percutaneous coronary intervention. Mitochondria are central mediators of reperfusion-associated cardiomyocyte injury, with excessive fission implicated as a potentially important mechanism linking acute metabolic stress to fragmentation, bioenergetic failure, and cell death. Reactive oxygen species, Ca2+ overload, mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and membrane-potential loss promote dynamin-related protein 1-centered (Drp1-centered) fission, often involving mitochondrial fission factor, mitochondrial fission 1 protein and site-specific Drp1 phosphorylation. By disrupting mitochondrial networks and oxidative phosphorylation, this process contributes to cytochrome c release, apoptosis, microvascular dysfunction and impaired recovery. Impaired mitofusin 1/2-mediated and optic atrophy 1-mediated fusion limits repair and quality control, supporting investigation of this fission-dominant imbalance as a target for cardioprotection. Preclinical studies suggest plant-derived natural products, multi-component botanical preparations and electroacupuncture may influence this imbalance. Reported effects include attenuated Drp1 signaling, altered fusion-protein expression, preserved membrane potential, inhibited permeability transition, reduced oxidative stress and apoptosis, and modulated upstream metabolic/stress-responsive pathways. However, hypoxia/reoxygenation, oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation, non-reperfused ischemia/infarction and stress models provide surrogate or supportive evidence rather than direct evidence of MI/RI. Heterogeneity in models, timing, dosage, readouts, causal validation and botanical quality control limits interpretation. This review examines these mechanisms, interventions and translational priorities. Clinical efficacy and safety of these interventions in MI/RI have not been established.

article.title: Cell-Free Hemoglobin Drives CD163+ Macrophage Reprogramming and Drp1-Dependent Mitochondrial Transfer to Promote Septic Cardiac Dysfunction
article.authors: Yuzhou Xiao; Yingjiao Liao; Yifei Liu; Guanglin Peng; Yinrui Ma; Qianyi Zeng; Ke Sun; Gautam Sethi; Ruijun Tang; He Huang; Rui Song; Bing Chen; Chenyang Duan
article.abstract: Abstract Background Severe trauma is commonly accompanied by secondary infection and multiple organ dysfunction, wherein sepsis and SIMD constitute predominant determinants of fatal outcomes. Despite this, the mechanistic connection between systemic hemolysis and cardiac immune remodeling has yet to be defined. Accordingly, this study was designed to determine whether CFH drives septic cardiac injury and to elucidate the cellular and molecular basis underlying this process. Methods Clinical samples from patients with sepsis, cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse models, single-cell RNA sequencing, metabolomic profiling, high-resolution live-cell imaging, and genetic manipulation were integrated to characterize CFH-mediated cardiac remodeling. Intercellular mitochondrial transfer was dynamically tracked using fluorescence imaging and super-resolution microscopy. A hemoglobin-targeting nanoparticle (HbAb-NP) was developed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of CFH scavenging. Results Circulating CFH was markedly elevated in septic patients and CLP mice and was associated with myocardial hemoglobin deposition, endothelial barrier disruption, cardiac dysfunction, and poor survival. CFH exposure was associated with an increased relative proportion of a metabolically reprogrammed CD163+ macrophage subset through activation of the glycolysis–NF-κB1 signaling axis. These macrophages exhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and transferred damaged mitochondria to endothelial cells via tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), resulting in oxidative stress, impaired mitochondrial respiration, endothelial barrier disruption, and reduced angiogenic capacity. Mechanistically, Drp1 facilitated TNT formation by activating the Cdc42/Rac1–cofilin/profilin pathway to drive actin cytoskeletal remodeling. Therapeutically, HbAb-NP efficiently scavenged circulating CFH, suppressed CD163+ macrophage activation, alleviated endothelial injury, improved cardiac function, and prolonged survival in septic mice. Conclusions This study identifies circulating CFH as a previously unrecognized upstream regulator linking systemic hemolysis to cardiac immune microenvironment remodeling during sepsis. CFH-induced CD163+ macrophage reprogramming and Drp1-dependent pathological mitochondrial transfer establish a macrophage–mitochondria–endothelial injury axis that drives SIMD. Targeting circulating CFH represents a promising therapeutic strategy for sepsis-associated cardiac dysfunction.

article.title: P2RY11–SIRT1–PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic regulation of macrophages drives fin regeneration in zebrafish
article.authors: Yiping Zhou; Lechen Li; Huiyu Hao; Zhouchen Zhang; Lin Zhao; Lifeng Wang; Yakun Ma; Dongyan Chen
article.abstract: Abstract Background Tissue regeneration is an energy-intensive process that requires coordinated mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox homeostasis. Extracellular ATP is rapidly released after tissue injury, but how ATP-derived signals support regenerative repair remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether the purinergic receptor P2RY11 regulates macrophage mitochondrial metabolism and thereby promotes tissue regeneration. Methods Using zebrafish caudal fin regeneration as an in vivo model, we examined regenerative outgrowth, cell proliferation, macrophage accumulation and migration, mitochondrial function, redox status, and metabolic gene expression in p2ry11 -deficient larvae. Genetic ablation and pharmacological inhibition of P2RY11 were combined with macrophage depletion and pathway rescue experiments targeting the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis and PPARγ signaling. Results Loss or inhibition of p2ry11 markedly impaired caudal fin regeneration, reduced injury-induced cell proliferation, and decreased macrophage migratory capacity and accumulation at the wound site. Mechanistically, p2ry11 deficiency disrupted systemic mitochondrial metabolic and redox homeostasis, as evidenced by a reduced NAD⁺/NADH ratio and decreased PGC-1α expression. Importantly, cell-resolved analyses further revealed mitochondrial depolarization, increased mtROS accumulation, and reduced ATP levels specifically in injury-associated macrophages. Systemic antioxidant defense was also compromised, with reduced CAT and SOD activities, decreased GSH content, and suppressed expression of antioxidant-related genes. Pharmacological activation of SIRT1 or PGC-1α restored mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic function and rescued fin regeneration, whereas inhibition of PGC-1α abolished the SIRT1-mediated rescue. Importantly, macrophage depletion eliminated the regenerative benefits of SIRT1–PGC-1α activation, demonstrating that macrophages are essential effectors of this pathway. Treatment with the clinically approved PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone similarly restored macrophage mitochondrial function and rescued regeneration, whereas activation of canonical cAMP–PKA or PKC signaling failed to improve regenerative outcomes. Conclusions These findings identify P2RY11 as an injury-responsive metabolic regulator that promotes tissue regeneration by sustaining macrophage mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox balance through the NAD + –SIRT1–PGC-1α axis. Targeting macrophage mitochondrial fitness may provide a therapeutic strategy for enhancing regenerative repair.

article.title: De novo assembly and characterization of the first complete mitochondrial genome of Prunus humilis based on PacBio HiFi sequencing
article.authors: Song Wang; Pingping Sun; Lei Zhang; Zhengnan Li
article.abstract: Abstract Background Prunus humilis (Chinese dwarf cherry) is a perennial dwarf shrub fruit tree endemic to China with considerable ecological, economic, and medicinal value. Although its chloroplast and nuclear genomes have been studied, its mitochondrial genome remains poorly characterized. Results Based on PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing data, we assembled the mitochondrial genome of P. humilis and obtained a circular assembly representation. The mitogenome was a circular molecule of 491,011 bp, comprising 36 unique protein-coding genes (PCGs), 18 tRNA genes, and three rRNA genes, with a GC content of 45.5%. Notably, comparative analysis across Prunus species revealed that P. humilis lost one gene ( rps19 ) and exhibited the highest level of gene duplication, with eight genes present in two copies ( atp4 , atp6 , atp8 , atp9 , ccmC , cox3 , rps3 , and sdh4 ). Codon usage analysis revealed a strong A/U bias at the third codon position, while RNA editing site prediction indicated that nad4 harbored the highest number of predicted RNA editing sites (43). Phylogenetic analyses based on ML and BI indicated that P. humilis formed a sister lineage to the P. davidiana + P. dulcis clade (UFBoot = 89, PP = 1.0). Comparative analyses revealed conserved syntenic regions and structural variation among Prunus mitogenomes. nad1 , cox2 , and atp1 showed relatively high nucleotide diversity, while 14 PCGs exhibited significant positive-selection signals. Conclusions This study presents the first complete mitochondrial genome of P. humilis , providing a valuable genomic resource for future molecular and evolutionary studies in Prunus . The results reveal substantial structural conservation and variation among Prunus mitogenomes, together with heterogeneous patterns of sequence diversity and selective pressure among mitochondrial genes, providing new insights into mitochondrial genome evolution and diversification within the genus.

article.title: Securing Maternal Identity: Halachic Concerns in the Age of Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy
article.authors: John Loike; Tzvi Flaum; Alan Kadish
article.abstract: Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT) encompasses assisted reproductive technologies designed to prevent the transmission of pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations by combining the DNA in the nucleus (nuclear genome) of the intending parents with another woman’s enucleated egg that provides healthy donor-derived mtDNA. The use of advanced genomic engineering in MRT raises distinct ethical and halachic considerations regarding the ontological status of embryos containing genetic material from more than two individuals. This paper advances an original theoretical protocol, termed biparental mitochondrial replacement therapy (Bi-MRT), that mitigates the central halachic concerns associated with multi-parent embryos. In this protocol, future advances in stem cell technology could be employed to generate an enucleated gamete-like cell containing healthy mitochondria from the husband. The meiotic spindle–chromosome complex from the wife’s oocyte could then be transplanted into this reconstituted gamete, which could be subsequently fertilized with the husband’s sperm for IVF. If technically feasible and developmentally competent, the resulting embryo could potentially be transferred to the wife for gestation. By combining the wife’s nuclear genetic contribution, gestation, and parturition with the husband’s paternal DNA, this framework isolates the third-party mitochondrial contribution as a non-maternal factor, thereby reinforcing the wife’s singular claim to halachic maternity. Biparental MRT therefore represents a theoretical framework that could potentially reduce some halachic concerns associated with conventional MRT, but substantial scientific and safety barriers remain before any clinical application could be contemplated.

article.title: Mitochondrial DNA Lineages of Eurasian Otters (Lutra lutra) in Central Anatolia: A Phylogenetic Bridge Between Asia and Europe?
article.authors: Emrah Aslan; Yasin Demirbaş; Ayça Özkan Koca; Kubilay Toyran; Hakan Soysal; Franz Suchentrunk
article.abstract: The Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra), a semi-aquatic carnivore listed as “Near Threatened” by the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), is widespread across Eurasia but remains poorly studied genetically in various regions. We analyzed the Central Anatolian population along the Kızılırmak River using mitochondrial (mt) DNA from non-invasively collected samples to examine whether Anatolian otters connect phylogenetically typical European and Caucasian lineages and whether Anatolia could have harbored a late-glacial source population for otter migration to Europe via western (Balkan) and/or eastern (east of the Black Sea) routes. Thirty spraints were collected from five localities, including four previously known sites and one newly identified in the Sulakyurt district, northeast of Kırıkkale province. We amplified a short (256 bp) mtD-loop fragment and a longer (820 bp) fragment spanning the Cytb, tRNA-Thr, tRNA-Pro, and D-loop from 14 samples and included all corresponding Lutra lutra mtDNA sequences available in GenBank in our analyses. Six short-fragment samples from Kapulukaya, Kesikköprü, and Kalecik carried the widespread northern Eurasian haplotype Lut1, while eight samples from Kalecik, Kesikköprü, Hirfanlı, and Hamzalı revealed a novel haplotype (H256-TR). The long fragments represented two additional haplotypes (H820-37, H820-38), distributed across the same localities. Median-joining network analysis of the short fragment produced a star-like topology with no clear phylogeographic structuring, whereas the longer fragment resolved two weakly separated phylogenetic groups. Central Anatolian haplotypes were positioned between Far Eastern and northern Eurasian lineages, with H820-38 phylogenetically connecting Caucasian and European haplotypes. This finding is consistent with the hypothesis of possible western and eastern postglacial migration routes from Anatolia to Europe, although broader spatial sampling is needed for confirmation.

article.title: Mitochondrial cristae remodeling in ischemic stroke: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives
article.authors: Dawei Zhang; Hongbo Zhang; Ruoxin Tu; Shuo Zhang; Hao Tian; Yue Meng; Xiaolin Lv; Hongna Yin
article.abstract: Mitochondrial cristae arrange the respiratory machinery within the inner membrane and change as ischemia gives way to reperfusion. Their organization depends on mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system assemblies, optic atrophy 1, adenosine triphosphate synthase, and cardiolipin. Disruption of these systems can impair energy production, facilitate neuronal death, and expose mitochondrial DNA to inflammatory sensors. This review brings structural work together with experimental stroke studies to examine how crista remodeling contributes to injury and recovery. Genetic manipulation of selected regulators has preserved mitochondrial structure and reduced injury in neurons and microglia. Most of these interventions preceded ischemia, leaving the speed and feasibility of repair after stroke onset uncertain. Pharmacological modulation and mitochondrial delivery offer ways to address this gap, particularly around reperfusion. Emerging strategies combine modulation of crista protein assemblies with cardiolipin directed treatment, mitochondrial antioxidant nanomedicine, organelle delivery, and control of local drug exposure. Their therapeutic evaluation can be aligned with distinct opportunities at reperfusion and during subsequent tissue recovery. Progress toward treatment will require evidence that a candidate reaches the affected brain cells, modifies the intended membrane assembly, and produces lasting neurological benefit. The available studies place crista remodeling within neuroprotective pathways and identify the experimental steps needed to evaluate it as a therapeutic target.

article.title: Targeting taurine metabolism improves mitochondrial function in mt-tRNA mutation-associated mitochondrial disease
article.authors: Xingyu Zhuang; Ying Zhao; Jianing Wang; Yan Lin; Jiayin Wang; Weiyue Si; Chuanzhu Yan; Busu Li; Kunqian Ji
article.abstract: Abstract Background Mitochondrial diseases caused by mt-tRNA mutations disrupt oxidative phosphorylation and metabolic homeostasis, but effective treatment options remain scarce. Given the central role of nutrient metabolism in mitochondrial function, we investigated whether metabolite disturbances could reveal actionable therapeutic targets. Methods We conducted integrated transcriptomic and targeted metabolomic analyses in patients with mt-tRNA mutation-related mitochondrial disease, using skeletal muscle biopsies for transcriptome profiling and serum samples for metabolite assessment. The functional relevance of the identified metabolic alteration was tested in mutant cells following taurine supplementation. Results Transcriptomic analysis revealed coordinated upregulation of mitochondrial-encoded respiratory chain genes and downregulation of nuclear-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits, consistent with mito-nuclear transcriptional decoupling. Targeted serum metabolomics demonstrated a 26% reduction in taurine, accompanied by increased expression of genes involved in taurine biosynthesis and transport, suggesting a compensatory adaptation to systemic taurine deficiency. Importantly, taurine supplementation improved mitochondrial respiration, restored membrane potential, increased mtDNA content, and attenuated reactive oxygen species accumulation in mutant cells. Conclusions Our findings identify an association between altered taurine homeostasis and mt-tRNA mutation-associated mitochondrial dysfunction and provide in vitro evidence that taurine can modify selected mitochondrial parameters in an mt-tRNA mutation fibroblast model. These results provide a mechanistic rationale for future clinical studies targeting taurine metabolism in mitochondrial disorders.

article.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in asthma: damage signals sustain airway inflammation and remodeling
article.authors: Yuqian Zhang; Lujia Liu; Mengdi Shi; Yiqiao Li; Suning Mu; Yan Wang; Youpeng Wang
article.abstract: Asthma is a heterogeneous disease characterized by chronic airway inflammation and airway remodeling. Growing evidence suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction is not only a consequence of inflammatory injury but may also contribute to disease persistence and progression. In asthma, mitochondrial redox balance, energy metabolism, Ca 2+ homeostasis, dynamics, biogenesis, and quality control can all become dysregulated. These abnormalities are interconnected and can alter mitochondrial energy supply, structural integrity, and quality maintenance. Mitochondrial damage can increase mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, promote the mislocalization of mitochondrial nucleic acids, alter membrane lipid oxidation and remodeling, and induce the release of mitochondrial proteins and other components. These changes generate diverse mitochondria-derived damage signals that can regulate inflammation-related gene transcription, nucleic acid sensing, and inflammasome activation. More broadly, mitochondrial abnormalities also alter immune cell function, airway epithelial repair, smooth muscle cell accumulation, and extracellular matrix production. Together, these effects may contribute to persistent airway inflammation and airway remodeling. This review summarizes the major forms of mitochondrial dysfunction in asthma. It also examines how these abnormalities generate mitochondria-derived damage signals, engage inflammatory sensing, and alter immune and airway structural cell functions.

article.title: Mitochondrial transfer and transplantation in cardiovascular diseases: from signaling pathways to targeted delivery strategies
article.authors: Yao Xie; Yue Liu; Shasha Xing
article.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial dysfunction drives the pathogenesis and progression of various cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). Research has demonstrated that approximately 95% of energy in the heart is supplied by mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and mitochondria also act as regulators of endothelial cell function, including metabolism, angiogenesis, and survival. Accordingly, mitochondrial-targeted therapies have garnered considerable research interest in CVD treatment. In contrast to traditional drug-based mitochondrial-targeted strategies, mitochondrial transfer and transplantation, as emerging innovative therapeutic approaches, hold great therapeutic promise for alleviating multiple CVDs. This article systematically reviews the molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks of endogenous/intrinsic mitochondrial transfer pathways (tunneling nanotubes, extracellular vesicles, etc.), and comprehensively summarizes the latest preclinical laboratory research, and preliminary early human clinical studies of artificial mitochondrial transplantation in major CVDs, including myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury, myocardial infarction (MI) and heart failure (HF). We further discuss the current critical challenges and potential risks associated with the clinical translation of this strategy, and propose targeted optimization directions and future research perspectives for its clinical application.

article.title: Global Mitochondrial Diversity and Distribution of Taenia hydatigena (Cysticercus tenuicollis) Lineages Across Geographic and Host Groups: A cox1-Based Analysis of Shared and Widespread Haplotypes
article.authors: Mughees Aizaz Alvi; Warda Qamar; Muhammad Saqib; Sarmad Hanif; Hilal Ahmad Parray; Ahmed M. Hassan; Muhammad Umar Zafar Khan; Kostadin Pavlov Kanchev; Baraa Hussni Falemban; Sheryar Afzal; Anwar M. Hashem; Hong-Bin Yan
article.abstract: Taenia hydatigena is a widely distributed taeniid tapeworm of veterinary significance that circulates in transmission cycles among canid definitive hosts and various domestic and wild ungulates. Mitochondrial studies have shown significant genetic variation within this species; however, the geographical and host restrictions of these mitochondrial lineages are not yet fully understood. In this study, we analyzed the global mitochondrial diversity and phylogeographic distribution of T. hydatigena lineages in geographic and host groups based on a cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (cox1) sequence dataset obtained from the GenBank database. A total of 406 sequences were assembled, and were used for the population genetic analyses. Mitochondrial diversity and lineage distribution were characterized using haplotype and nucleotide diversity, neutrality statistics, country- and host-associated variation, median-joining networks, and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction. The global dataset included 123 haplotypes, with high levels of haplotype diversity (Hd = 0.897) and comparatively low levels of nucleotide diversity (π = 0.00898). Haplotype frequencies were highly skewed, with 79 of them represented by a single sequence, whereas the most common haplotype, Hap-3, contained 124 sequences. Country-based analyses showed significant mitochondrial diversity, as well as geographically widespread and geographically restricted haplotypes, but no country-specific clustering pattern. There were eight different host categories for 364 sequences for which host information was available, and the haplotype diversity (Hd) was high (0.907), whereas the nucleotide diversity (π) was low (0.00926). Major haplotypes were common among several host species, especially sheep and goats, and mitochondrial variants within major haplotypes were shared with dogs and other wild animals. The maximum-likelihood phylogeny identified a monophyletic group of T. hydatigena and showed high levels of intraspecific mitochondrial variation but no obvious geographical structure in the largest mitochondrial subclades. All Tajima’s D, Fu’s Fs, Fu and Li’s D, and Fu and Li’s F statistics were negative for the pooled dataset. These are results that show a departure from the expectations of neutral models, but should not be interpreted as evidence for demographic expansion, as they represent a mixture of geographically and biologically heterogeneous GenBank records with unequal sampling and potentially non-independent sequences. In conclusion, the available GenBank data indicated a high mitochondrial haplotype richness, as well as the presence of widespread and geographically restricted cox1 haplotypes and haplotype sharing between recorded host and geographic categories. Unbalanced host and country representation, possible non-independence of sequence records, and host and geographic origin are each potential sources of confounding that reduce the power to make inferences concerning population connectivity and host-associated structure. These results offer a comparative model to understand the distribution of mitochondrial variation in T. hydatigena and point to the need for a sampling methodology that is both geographically distributed and standardized, as well as longer mitochondrial and nuclear sequence data, for sympatric hosts.

article.title: Methylglyoxal Impairs Mitochondrial Bioenergetics and Microglial Functions
article.authors: Taketo Taguchi; Pamela Maher
article.abstract: Aging is accompanied by a progressive disruption of brain homeostasis, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this age-associated deterioration remain poorly understood. Microglia play a critical role in maintaining brain homeostasis by clearing cellular debris and neurotoxic protein aggregates. Here, we investigated the effects of methylglyoxal (MG), a highly reactive endogenous metabolite that accumulates with aging, on microglial functions using the murine microglial cell line BV2. We assessed the effects of MG exposure on multiple aspects of microglial biology in both control and bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-treated cells, including phagocytic activity, cellular proliferation, cytokine secretion, mitochondrial bioenergetics, mitochondrial membrane potential, and intracellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. We found that MG significantly impaired mitochondrial bioenergetics, leading to reduced cellular energy production, and markedly suppressed multiple essential microglial functions, including phagocytosis. Given the high reactivity of MG with arginine, we also investigated whether arginine depletion contributes to these functional impairments. Arginine depletion recapitulated the impairment of mitochondrial bioenergetics and microglial function induced by MG, demonstrating that arginine availability is a critical determinant of microglial metabolic fitness and immune function. These findings suggest that the age-associated accumulation of MG impairs mitochondrial bioenergetics and microglial functions, thereby potentially accelerating neurodegenerative processes.

article.title: Baicalein improves cisplatin resistance in gastric cancer through OMA1/OPA1 axis mediated mitochondrial dynamics.
article.authors: Yu C, Yu C.
article.abstract: Chemoresistance represents a major obstacle to the successful treatment of gastric cancer (GC). This study aimed to investigate whether baicalein can help overcome cisplatin resistance in GC and explore the involvement of the OMA1/OPA1 axis in this effect. Treatment with baicalein significantly increased mitochondrial fission and ROS levels in AGS cells, reducing ATP production and sensitizing GC cells to cisplatin. Intriguingly, treating AGS cells with the combination of baicalein and cisplatin significantly increased OMA1 expression and reduced OPA1 expression. Mechanistically, we identified a signaling axis linking OMA1 to OPA1 and mitochondrial fission in GC. Moreover, OMA1 overexpression in AGS/DDP cells significantly increased mitochondrial fission and ROS levels, decreased the expression of the OPA1 protein and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), and reduced ATP production. Consistently, cell viability and cell apoptosis assays showed that OMA1 overexpression enhanced sensitivity to cisplatin in AGS/DDP cells. Taken together, this study indicated that baicalein improved cisplatin resistance in GC through OMA1/OPA1 axis-mediated modulation of mitochondrial dynamics. These findings support the repurposing of baicalein as a potential agent to reverse cisplatin resistance in GC. Furthermore, the results illuminate how OMA1 regulates mitochondrial dynamics and advocate for combining OMA1 overexpression with chemotherapy in GC.

article.title: Betulinic acid attenuates obesity-associated cardiac remodelling by modulating mitochondrial quality control, ferroptosis-associated signalling, and calcium-regulatory pathways.
article.authors: Uddandrao VVS, Kothai R, Asokan BR, Sengottuvelu S, Kumar U, Sakthivel KM, Brahmanaidu P.
article.abstract: Obesity-associated cardiac remodelling (OACR) is characterized by metabolic, structural, mitochondrial, oxidative, and molecular alterations that may contribute to progressive cardiac dysfunction. However, the interplay among mitochondrial quality control, ferroptosis, and calcium homeostasis in obesity-associated cardiac injury and remodelling remains incompletely understood. This study investigated whether betulinic acid (BA) attenuates obesity-induced myocardial injury by modulating these interconnected pathways. Male Sprague-Dawley rats were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks to induce cardiac injury and remodelling and treated with BA (40 mg/kg, orally) for 6 weeks. Cardiac morphology, metabolic parameters, myocardial bioenergetic parameters, oxidative stress, iron homeostasis, and markers associated with mitochondrial quality control, mitochondrial dynamics, ferroptosis, and calcium regulation were assessed using biochemical, histopathological, mRNA, and protein expression analyses. Molecular docking provided hypothesis-generating predictions of potential interactions between BA and selected regulatory proteins. HFD-induced obesity was associated with alterations in mitochondrial quality-control, ferroptosis-associated, and calcium-regulatory signalling markers, including changes in the SERCA2a-CaMKIIδ axis. BA improved metabolic abnormalities, increased myocardial ATP content and the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and attenuated oxidative injury and iron accumulation. These effects were accompanied by increased PINK1, Parkin, MFN2, GPX4, SLC7A11, and SERCA2a expression and decreased DRP1, ACSL4, and CaMKIIδ expression. BA attenuated OACR, accompanied by changes in mitochondrial quality-control, ferroptosis-associated, and calcium-regulatory proteins. These findings indicate that modulation of these interconnected pathways may contribute to the attenuation of OACR.

article.title: Deciphering the effects of aging on Alzheimer’s disease based on mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation
article.authors: Yamei Luo; Haoli Yu; Jun Zhang; Zhihong Wu; Haiyan Zhang
article.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD), a neurological disorder characterized by progressive deterioration of cognitive function, has complex pathogenic mechanisms and lacks curative therapies with proven efficacy. Aging and inflammatory responses, which play indispensable roles in the onset and progression of AD, are closely intertwined with mitochondrial dysfunction. During aging, a series of degenerative alterations, including accumulated mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, disrupted mitochondrial quality control (MQC) and disturbed energy metabolism, further induce structural mitochondrial damage. This damage causes the leakage of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and activates numerous downstream inflammatory signaling pathways. In brain tissue, inflammatory cytokines, which continuously facilitate blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption, aberrant activation of microglial cells, tau protein hyperphosphorylation, as well as Aβ accumulation, drive an endlessly amplified neuroinflammatory cascade that leads to irreversible neuronal damage and fuels the initiation and progression of AD. In this review, we clarify the regulatory effects of aging on AD pathogenesis through the mitochondrial dysfunction-chronic inflammation axis and ultimately focus on mitochondrial-targeted therapies, with future outlooks for AD treatment provided.

article.title: Gastrodin combined with donepezil alleviates cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease mice by improving mitochondrial function through AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 axis
article.authors: Junwen Wang; Jing Wu; Fenrong Liang; Shulei Huang; Longfei Liu; Ying Huang; Yiming Wang
article.abstract: Objective This study aims to explore whether gastrodin (Gas) combined with donepezil (Don) has a neuroprotective effect on Alzheimer’s disease (AD) mice by regulating the AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis. Methods HT22 cells were transfected with SIRT3 siRNA or control siRNA. Cells were then treated with the AMPK inhibitor, Don, Gas, or their combination. Subsequently, HT22 cells were treated with Amyloid beta 1–42 (Aβ 1–42) to induce an in vitro AD model. Cell viability was detected by CCK8 assay. DCFH-DA fluorescent probe was used to evaluate cell reactive oxygen species (ROS). Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) content was detected by luciferase chemiluminescence method. Cell membrane potential was measured by flow cytometry. For in vivo experiments, WT mice and APP/PS1 mice were treated with Don, Gas or a combination of drugs. Morris water maze test, Y-maze test and novel object recognition test were used to evaluate the cognitive impairment of mice. The pathological changes of hippocampus were detected by HE staining, and the expression of Aβ protein in hippocampus and cortex was detected by IHC. In addition, the protein and mRNA expressions of APP, Tau, and AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis were determined by Western blot and RT-QPCR. Results Gas combined with Don significantly improved cognitive dysfunction, reduced Aβ plaque deposition in the cortex and hippocampus, up-regulated AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 axis, and inhibited the abnormal phosphorylation of Tau and APP in APP/PS1 mice compared with the model group and the Don group ( p < 0.05). In vitro cell experiments confirmed that the combination of the two drugs could improve cell viability, inhibit cell apoptosis, restore ATP level, reduce ROS accumulation, stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve mitochondrial function ( p < 0.05). Molecular experiments and complementary experiments showed that Gas combined with Don activated AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis ( p < 0.05). Silencing SIRT3 or inhibiting AMPK could reverse the protective effect of the combined regimen ( p < 0.05). Conclusion Gas combined with Don can maintain mitochondrial homeostasis through AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 pathway, alleviate AD-relaated pathological damage, and exert neuroprotection.

article.title: Sequential Mitochondrial Transplantation Abrogates Agmatine-Mediated Neuroprotection Against 6-OHDA Toxicity in SH-SY5Y Cells
article.authors: Volkan Tekin; Levent Elmas; Zehra Çiçek; Besra Özmen Yelken; Elçin Yenidünya Konuk
article.abstract: Objective: Parkinson disease (PD) involves dopaminergic neuron loss from mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. We investigated the combined, sequential effects of mesenchymal stem cell–derived mitochondrial transplantation (MitoTr) and pharmacological agmatine modulation in a PD–like undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cellular model. Methods: Undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA; 350 μM) for 24 hours and sequentially treated with mitochondria (5 or 10 μg/mL) and agmatine (100 μM; 2 hours post-MitoTr). Cell viability was assessed via MTT assays (n = 8 independent experiments). Total-lysate cytochrome c ELISA (n = 3) and Western blots for DJ-1, REDD1, and α-synuclein (n = 4) were performed across 4 core groups. Results: 6-OHDA significantly reduced viability compared with Control (mean [SEM], 0.50 [0.05] vs 1.00 [0.04]; P .99). Conversely, MitoTr-containing groups showed significantly lower viability than Control, Agmatine, and Agmatine + 6-OHDA groups (P .05). Total-lysate cytochrome c was significantly elevated only in the triple-combination group compared with the Control group (mean [SEM], 36.01 [3.65] versus 22.63 [1.08] ng/mL; P = .03). Conclusions: Postinjury agmatine rescued 6-OHDA-induced viability loss, but sequential MitoTr followed by agmatine caused an additional marked reduction in viability rather than synergistic neuroprotection. Molecular alterations remained exploratory and nonsignificant. This MitoTr-associated loss may reflect antiproliferative effects in neuroblastoma-derived cells, underscoring the need for optimized protocols and nonmalignant models.

article.title: Enhanced mitochondrial respiratory metabolism in UV-damaged HDF cells based on metabolomics analysis of fermented Galla rhois gallnut extract
article.authors: Jiaying Wu; Ning Wang; Denghui Chen; Yi Zhang; Jingxia Sun; Xiao Zhang; Guanlin Li; Xiang Li; Hu Huang
article.abstract: UV-induced photoaging disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis in skin cells, which in turn exacerbates skin aging. In this study, we developed a novel fermented Galla rhois gallnut extract (FGRE) using Lactiplantibacillus plantarum with mitochondrial respiratory homeostasis amelioration. Biochemical assays showed that FGRE exhibited stronger antioxidant and anti-elastase activities than the unfermented extract. Using Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test, 1% FGRE significantly enhanced mitochondrial respiratory function in UVB-irradiated human dermal fibroblast (HDF) cells compared to that with the unfermented extract. In addition, 1% FGRE increased the ATP content and NAD + /NADH ratio and regulated the transcription level of fusion and fission genes in UVA-induced HDFs. Furthermore, the non-targeted metabolomics analysis revealed that differential metabolites were predominantly enriched in amino acid metabolic pathways, and 24 differential metabolites were putatively identified. Among these, the differential metabolites leucinic acid, urolithin A, and urolithin M5 were quantitatively determined. Notably, 1 μg/mL leucinic acid (equivalent to the concentration in 1% FGRE) ameliorated mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction and promoted the ATP production in UV-induced HDFs. Therefore, leucinic acid was considered as one of the potentially bioactive metabolites of FGRE.

article.title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic and Regulatory Network Analyses Identify a Putative HNF4A–OXR1 Association Linked to Podocyte Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Diabetic Kidney Disease
article.authors: Zhenkun Yang; Shimin Jiang; Wen Cui; Jiahui Zhou; Wenge Li
article.abstract: Podocyte injury is a central pathological event in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), but the mitochondrial regulatory mechanisms underlying podocyte dysfunction remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human renal biopsies in GSE195460 with podocyte-specific differential expression, functional enrichment, mitochondrial gene annotation, co-expression network analysis, machine learning feature selection, pseudotime analysis, in silico knockout, transcription factor enrichment, motif analysis, and molecular docking; findings were externally evaluated in GSE209781. Podocytes showed prominent disease-associated transcriptomic perturbation, with 677 exploratory cell-level differentially expressed genes and enrichment of cytoskeletal, adhesion, developmental, oxidative phosphorylation, and metabolic pathways. Thirty-one mitochondrial-related differentially expressed genes were identified, and OXR1 was prioritized as a candidate regulatory hub based on consistent downregulation, network centrality, machine learning selection, and external validation. HNF4A was predicted as an upstream regulator linked to OXR1 and other mitochondrial targets. In silico OXR1 perturbation increased the predicted injured-state probability from 15% to 82%, while promoter motif analysis provided additional computational support for a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship. These findings highlight OXR1 as a candidate associated with podocyte mitochondrial dysfunction in DKD and suggest a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship.

article.title: TFAM Expression, rs1937 Variant, and Mitochondrial DNA Copy Number in Egyptian Myocardial Infarction Patients
article.authors: Sherin Sobhy El naidany; Heba F. Khader; Asmaa Abdelkarim Kenawy; Mohammed G. Elhelbawy; Zahraa Azab Mohamed Abouelatta; Hoda Ahmed Abdelmoneim; Reham Abdulla Aboukhalil; Wael Tawfik; Mai A. H. Abouelenin
article.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a fatal condition that causes damage to the heart muscle by abruptly stopping blood flow and oxygenation. Mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNA CN) show an increased rate of association with development of several human diseases and malignancies. This paper, therefore, aims to identify the possible relation among mtDNA CN and its regulating gene TFAM (expression of the gene and rs1937 polymorphism) as markers in myocardial infarction among Egyptians. A total of 200 participants were enrolled and divided into two groups. Group 1 included 100 myocardial infarction patients with ST-segment elevation (STEMI) recruited from from the Coronary Care Unit (CCU) of Menoufia University Hospitals, while group 2 included 100 Controls. Blood samples were collected from all participants immediately after diagnosis of MI and before beginning therapy. TFAM SNP (rs1937) was determined by the allelic discrimination TaqMan technique, and mtDNA CN and TFAM gene expression were detected using real-time quantitative PCR in 100 MI patients and 100 controls. TFAM mRNA expression and mtDNA copy number were profoundly reduced in MI patients than controls. Analysis of genotype showed that the TFAM rs1937 variant distribution was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The C allele and the GC genotype were substantially more frequent in the patients’ cohort (p = 0.006 and 0.005, respectively). The GC genotype of the TFAM polymorphism (rs1937) showed a preliminary association with MI in STEMI patients. Limitations of this study are the absence of longitudinal pre-MI or post-recovery data. TFAM mRNA expression and mtDNA copy number were measured in whole blood without adjustment for leukocyte subpopulations or platelet counts. Small number of C carriers of TFAM rs1937 variant and absence of CC genotype limited statistical power and requires replication in larger Egyptian cohort. These findings suggest that decreased TFAM gene expression and mtDNA CN were significant biomarkers associated with acute myocardial infarction in STEMI patients.

article.title: Natural Medicines Targeting Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3: A Narrative Review of Cellular and Molecular Events
article.authors: Mwafaq Kmail; Noor Asyikin Suaidi; Jin Han Chin; Lee Wei Lim; Kah Hui Wong
article.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also known as Machado-Joseph disease, is the most common autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia and is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration for which no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutics are currently available. Mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central pathogenic mechanism in SCA3, making it a promising therapeutic target. This narrative review aims to evaluate the published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. This review summarizes published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3 in preclinical studies. The reviewed studies suggest the therapeutic potential of Glycyrrhiza inflata, Codonopsis pilosula, Ginkgo biloba, Poria cocos, Pueraria lobata, Rehmannia glutinosa, Curcuma longa, Hericium erinaceus, Astragalus membranaceus, Hemerocallis citrina, caffeic acid, and resveratrol in targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. These natural medicines were reported to regulate multiple mitochondrial-associated pathways, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, mitochondrial bioenergetics, mitochondrial dynamics, mitochondrial quality control, and mitochondria-mediated apoptosis, thereby improving neuronal survival and mitochondrial function in experimental SCA3 models. In conclusion, natural medicines targeting mitochondrial dysfunction represent promising preclinical candidates for further investigation in SCA3. However, further mechanistic investigations, well-designed clinical trials, and optimization of pharmacokinetic properties are required to facilitate their translation into clinical practice.

article.title: A Mito-CoQ10-TPP Nanocarrier Hybrid Enhances the Therapeutic Efficacy of Mitochondrial Transplantation in Alzheimer’s Disease
article.authors: Nitika Sindhu; Smita Jain; Swapnil Sharma; Swati Paliwal
article.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial dysfunction is an early pathological aspect of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) that promotes oxidative stress, leading to amyloid β-plaque formation and neurofibrillary tangles. Thus, targeted mitochondrial therapy and mitochondrial transplantation have emerged as promising therapeutic strategies. However, excessive oxidative stress and neuroinflammation in the microenvironments of the AD brain limit the functional and stable integration of transplanted mitochondria. In this study, we have engineered a Mito-CoQ10-TPP hybrid nanocarrier by conjugating triphenylphosphonium (TPP), a lipophilic cation, with Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) and localized it to mitochondria isolated from healthy cortical brain cells. This nanocarrier hybrid was administered via a single intravenous (IV) dose to streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD in mice. A comprehensive evaluation of mitochondrial function, amyloid burden, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, biogenesis, and behavior revealed that CoQ10-TPP conjugation significantly improved the mitochondrial transplantation efficacy in the amelioration of AD. Thus, conjugating the antioxidant CoQ10 with mitochondrial transplantation significantly improved the overall therapeutic efficacy, indicating the use of the Mito-CoQ10-TPP hybrid nanocarrier as a promising therapeutic strategy.

article.title: Piezoelectric Tm‐ZnO Nanoparticles Reprogram Neutrophils by Modulating Mitochondrial Homeostasis for Osteoarthritis Therapy
article.authors: Chengxiao Liu; Ruqi Wang; Zhaowenbin Zhang; Ruiqing Wang; Xiaowei Wu; Yuxuan Liu; Zhengliang Wang; Ruomei Li; Chunlong Zhang; Bin Li; Bing Fang; Chen Yang; Lunguo Xia
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Osteoarthritis (OA) is increasingly recognized as a chronic inflammatory disorder driven by immune dysregulation, with early neutrophil infiltration associated with a pro‐inflammatory phenotype and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis. However, whether restoring neutrophil mitochondrial function can reprogram their inflammatory state and ameliorate OA remains unclear. Distinct from previous piezoelectric strategies for OA that primarily focus on chondrocytes or macrophages, this study focuses on neutrophil mitochondrial immunometabolism. Here, we report piezoelectric thulium‐doped zinc oxide (Tm‐ZnO) nanoparticles that associate with neutrophil mitochondria to restore mitochondrial homeostasis and reprogram neutrophil polarization. The ultrasmall size and positive surface charge of Tm‐ZnO facilitate mitochondrial association, while its enhanced piezoelectric properties (14‐fold increase in piezoelectric coefficient) enable activation by low‐intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), generating localized bioelectric cues. This stimulation reduces mitochondrial ROS, enhances oxidative phosphorylation, and is associated with suppression of HIF‐1/NF‐κB signaling, thereby promoting neutrophil polarization from a pro‐inflammatory N1 state toward a reparative N2 phenotype. In vitro and in vivo, Tm‐ZnO+LIPUS attenuates synovial inflammation, restores chondrocyte anabolic activity, limits matrix degradation, and facilitates cartilage repair. Together, these findings establish a mitochondria‐associated piezoelectric strategy for bioelectric reprogramming of neutrophil immunometabolism and highlight its therapeutic potential for OA and other chronic inflammatory diseases.

article.title: Polymer-specific nanoplastic exposure, mitochondrial dysfunction, and depressed ejection fraction in humans
article.authors: Alberta Maria Maddalena Palazzo; Lucia Scisciola; Manuela Giovanna Basilicata; Nunzia D’Onofrio; Pasquale Paolisso; Angelo Fenti; Francesco Prattichizzo; Celestino Sardu; Eduardo Sommella; Valentina Golino; Marta Belmonte; Asad Zia; Claudio Marra; Cristiano Amarelli; Laura Graciotti; Gianluca Fulgenzi; Fabiola Olivieri; Rosalba La Grotta; Antonio Ceriello; Maria Luisa Balestrieri; Bruno D’Agostino; Carmine Lubritto; Pasquale Iovino; Claudio Napoli; Pietro Campiglia; Emanuele Barbato; Philip Landrigan; Michelangela Barbieri; Raffaele Marfella; Giuseppe Paolisso
