article.authors: Fen Xiong; Kaiyuan Jiang; Xiaoqing Yan; Tian Tang; Xinran Wang; Yiwen Peng; Ruoxin Guan; Xi Zhang; Chen Li; Hongchang Gao
article.abstract: Background: Cognitive impairment is a clinically relevant neurological complication of diabetes, yet its metabolic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to determine whether fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a fasting-responsive metabolic hormone, mediates the neuroprotective effects of intermittent fasting (IF) in diabetes-associated cognitive impairment, and to explore the underlying mechanisms. Methods: Streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type 1 diabetes-associated cognitive impairment (T1DCI) mice were used together with FGF21 genetic deletion and exogenous FGF21 supplementation. Cognitive function, neuronal injury, hippocampal lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, protein acetylation, and SIRT3-associated deacetylation were evaluated. Results: IF significantly increased FGF21 levels in serum and hippocampus and improved cognitive deficits, whereas these effects were attenuated in FGF21-deficient mice. FGF21 supplementation improved cognitive performance and attenuated neuronal damage, accompanied by MAPK-related signaling changes. Lipidomic analysis revealed decreased phosphatidylcholine and triacylglycerols in the hippocampus of T1DCI mice, which were partially restored by FGF21. Consistently, FGF21 increased the expression of LPIN3, DGAT2, and CHPT1, key enzymes involved in PC and TAG biosynthesis. FGF21 also improved mitochondrial function and was associated with reduced protein acetylation, while SIRT3 inhibition attenuated these effects. Conclusions: These findings suggest that FGF21 contributes to the neuroprotective effects of IF in diabetes-associated cognitive impairment, potentially through coordinated regulation of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function.

article.title: Mitochondrial mutation m.1555A>G and aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss in neonates: an integrative review
article.authors: P. E. Edison; M. J. Sankar; Michael Hall
article.abstract: Objective To evaluate the evidence related to the association between aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss and the mitochondrial mutation m.1555A>G, and to examine the potential clinical utility of pharmacogenetic prescription of aminoglycosides in neonates. Methods An integrative literature review of m.1555A>G mutation and aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss in neonates, analysed using the Wilson-Jungner framework of population-based preventive screening. Results The evidence base was observational and methodologically heterogeneous. Across population-based and epidemiological newborn cohorts, the study-level median frequency of m.1555A>G was 0.2% (range 0%–0.3%), with regional and ethnic variation. In a prospective multicentre study, aminoglycoside exposure was weakly associated with failed newborn hearing screen (NBHS) in carriers (OR: 1.26, 95% CI: 1.07–1.49, p = 0.0058). Pure tone hearing impairment was detected at 3 years in a very-low-birthweight carrier with prior exposure. Pilot data support both the analytical validity of prenatal screening using buccal swabs or blood samples and the feasibility of rapid NICU genotyping to inform aminoglycoside prescribing. Population-based genetic screening offers the potential for early carrier identification; however, long-term audiological surveillance, economic viability, and ethical considerations remain important areas for future investigation. Conclusion Aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss fulfills the criteria for preventive screening, including a latent preclinical period, available m.1555A>G genotyping tools, and an actionable aminoglycoside avoidance. Although screening appears feasible and early data support the validity of available tools, the clinical utility remains uncertain. Genetic screening may be considered as either a universal component of NBHS programmes or a targeted strategy informed by risk stratification. (family history, NICU admission, aminoglycoside predisposition). Further research on the clinical utility and effectiveness of screening methods is needed to inform neonatal aminoglycoside policy.

article.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in Parkinson's disease and aging
article.authors: Xiaoyu Lu; Zhiyan Huang; Zhongming Ying
article.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder for which advancing age is the major risk factor. Aging and PD share several features, including chronic neuroinflammation and pathological protein accumulation. This overlap suggests that mechanisms driving the aging process may also contribute to the onset and progression of PD. In this narrative review, we examine mitochondrial dysfunction as a shared feature of aging and PD, focusing on energy production, calcium buffering, apoptosis, inflammation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. The literature reviewed here suggests shared alterations in mitochondrial dynamics, increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) instability, NAD + depletion, Complex I inhibition, redox imbalance, and disrupted calcium homeostasis. We also summarize mitochondria-targeted interventions investigated in PD.

article.title: Mitochondrial stress-signaling networks in male reproductive dysfunction: redox, inflammatory, and cell-death integration with context-dependent modulation by melatonin
article.authors: Qi Qi; Jingsheng Luo; Xuejiao Ren; Lin Jiang; Tianhui Liu; Wei Liu; ChangJie Bao; Meiyan Sun; Hongxun Fu
article.abstract: Mitochondria integrate bioenergetic, redox, calcium, inflammatory, and cell-death signals during cellular stress, but their position within male reproductive injury is highly dependent on cell type and initiating insult. This critical narrative review examines mitochondrial stress-signaling networks in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, developing germ cells, and spermatozoa, with particular attention to their context-dependent modulation by melatonin. Physiological reactive oxygen species (ROS) participate in steroidogenesis and sperm function, whereas excessive or mislocalized ROS can interact bidirectionally with mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, impaired quality control, and regulated cell death. Across toxicant, metabolic, inflammatory, thermal, ischemic, aging, and cryopreservation models, mitochondria can therefore function as conditional integrative signaling hubs rather than universal initiating causes. Melatonin-associated responses intersect with these networks through MT1/MT2 signaling, redox-sensitive processes, chemical interactions with reactive species, and mitochondria-associated mechanisms, with reported effects on mitochondrial function, inflammatory amplification, apoptosis, and ferroptosis- or pyroptosis-associated injury. However, molecular co-variation is distinguished from causal signaling, and lipid peroxidation or inflammasome activation alone is not considered definitive evidence of ferroptosis or pyroptosis. Human evidence remains limited relative to animal, ex vivo, and cell-culture studies. We propose an evidence-calibrated initiation–amplification–progression framework in which mitochondria integrate stress signals dynamically and melatonin acts as a context-dependent experimental modulator rather than an established reproductive therapy.

article.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
article.authors: Ahmad A. Cluntun; Joseph R. Visker; Jesse N. Velasco-Silva; James Carrington; Luis Cedeño-Rosario; Giulia C. Napoli; Ji Eon Kim; Thirupura S. Shankar; Marisa J. Brothwell; Rana Hamouche; Álvaro J. Narbona-Pérez; Jing Ling; Ashish G. Toshniwal; Hayden K. Low; Corey N. Cunningham; David R. Eberhardt; Jing Li; Claire E. Stanley; Queren A. Alcantara; Tarun Yadav; Ryan L. Maves; Wojciech I. Swiatek; Nicholas A. Offei; Bhavya Blaze; Sumangala P. Shetty; Dipayan Chaudhuri; Tingting Hong; Jeffery D. Rothstein; Deborah M. Muoio; Joao A. Paulo; Steven P. Gygi; Eleni Tseliou; Sutip Navankasattusas; James E. Cox; Katsuhiko Funai; Stavros G. Drakos; Jared Rutter; Gregory S. Ducker
article.abstract: Abstract The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

article.title: Mitochondrial ROS and Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: Mechanistic Interplay and Links to Regulated Cell Death
article.authors: Lice Wang; Kai Cao; Haozhe Cheng; Zhong Fang
article.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) develops through interacting mechanical, matrix, nutritional, inflammatory and age-related processes. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitophagy participate in some of these contexts, but current evidence does not place mitophagy failure at the start of every degenerative trajectory. Most mechanistic studies have been performed in nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. In these models, mechanical overload, inflammatory mediators and oxidant stress can depolarize mitochondria, disturb fission–fusion balance and increase mtROS. Mitophagy can limit injury when damaged cargo is selected and delivered through a competent lysosomal pathway; accumulation of pathway markers during blocked flux, or mitochondrial clearance that is not matched by renewal, need not be protective. The most extensive mechanistic literature concerns apoptosis and senescence. Evidence linking mitochondrial quality control to pyroptosis and ferroptosis is growing but remains model-dependent, whereas direct evidence for necroptosis is comparatively sparse. We use a capacity-matching framework to organize these findings around damage burden, cargo selection, lysosomal completion and mitochondrial renewal within the regional metabolic constraints of the disc. This is an interpretive framework rather than a newly identified pathway. Its purpose is to define testable conditions under which mitophagy is likely to be protective, insufficient or maladaptive, while preserving the distinction between NP-derived evidence and the more limited evidence from annulus fibrosus and cartilage endplate cells.

article.title: Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids differentially regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation during Western diet feeding in male Ldlr −/− mice
article.authors: Siyun Kim; Sung Gi Noh; Minje Ji; Tomas Vence; Lidan Gao; Oliver Otoko; Frank C. Nichols; Christopher N. Blesso; Oh Sung Kwon
article.abstract: Abstract The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome‐derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD‐fed Ldlr −/− mice. Male Ldlr −/− mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy‐associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross‐sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid‐supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross‐sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome‐derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. image Key points Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet‐fed Ldlr − / − mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid‐supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) and interleukin 6 (IL‐6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross‐sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

article.title: Ginsenoside Rg1 Alleviates Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Partially Through Regulating ABCB1-Mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
article.authors: Xu W, Ye J, Dong K, Cao Z, Zhu Y, Li L, Huang B.
article.venue: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology
article.abstract: ABSTRACT To investigate the protective effects of ginsenoside Rg1 on lung injury in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and to elucidate the underlying mechanism involving ATP‐binding cassette subfamily B member 1 (ABCB1)‐mediated regulation of mitochondrial function. A COPD rat model was established by cigarette smoke exposure, followed by in vivo administration of different doses of ginsenoside Rg1. ABCB1 knockdown was achieved by tail vein injection of short hairpin RNA (shRNA). Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) and Masson staining were performed to evaluate lung histopathology and collagen deposition. Pulmonary function was assessed by measuring inspiratory resistance (Ri), dynamic lung compliance (Cdyn), and the ratio of forced expiratory volume at 0.3 s to forced vital capacity (FEV 0 . 3 /FVC). In vitro, cigarette smoke extract (CSE) was used to induce injury in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells, followed by Rg1 treatment and ABCB1 overexpression or knockdown. Advanced glycation end products–receptor for advanced glycation end products (AGEs–RAGE) and early growth response protein 1–c‐Jun N‐terminal kinase (EGR1–JNK) signaling pathways were detected. In COPD rats, Rg1 markedly attenuated alveolar structural destruction and collagen deposition, decreased Ri, increased Cdyn and FEV 0 . 3 /FVC. ABCB1 knockdown partially reversed these protective effects. In HBE cells, Rg1 enhanced cell viability, restored mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced apoptosis, decreased ROS accumulation, and rescued intracellular ATP depletion. Rg1 inhibited the activation of the AGEs–RAGE and EGR1–JNK pathways in a manner associated with upregulation of ABCB1 expression. Ginsenoside Rg1 enhances mitochondrial function partially through upregulation of ABCB1 expression, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction in COPD rats and CSE‐treated HBE cells.

article.title: Mitochondrial Genome Variation in Breast Muscle of Tibetan Fragrant Chickens Across an Altitudinal Gradient and Its Association with Meat Quality
article.authors: Zengwen Huang; Jing Wang; Jun Li; Dayong Si; Zengpeng Lü; Gang Shu; Zhiqiang Hu; Chaoyun Yang
article.abstract: This study aimed to characterize the mitochondrial (MT) genome of Tibetan fragrant chickens along an altitudinal gradient and to relate it to meat quality. Eighteen 150-day-old male chickens were selected from three groups (LX, 1500 m; MX, 2800 m; HX, 3500 m; n = 6 each; six birds were randomly chosen from 30 reared per group) and subjected to whole-genome resequencing (reference: Gallus gallus GCA_000002315.5). Ninety MT variants (85 polymorphic; transition/transversion 83:7) were identified, comprising 58 coding (42 synonymous, 16 non-synonymous), 20 D-loop/non-coding, 10 rRNA and 2 tRNA sites; no MT insertions/deletions or structural variants were found. The 18 birds clustered into three maternal lineages (A, B, C) that were only partially structured by altitude (A more frequent at low altitude; B at mid and high altitude). A neighbour-joining tree with 12 Gallus mitogenomes placed the population close to Gallus gallus gallus and Chinese local breeds. Fifteen heteroplasmic sites were detected, with 16S rRNA nt3946 (G/C/A) heteroplasmic in all birds. Relative mtDNA copy number did not differ among groups (p = 0.52). Meat quality varied with altitude (highest protein and lowest fat at 2800 m; highest inosine monophosphate at 3500 m) but not with maternal lineage, suggesting that the observed phenotypic differences are associated mainly with altitude of rearing rather than with maternal mitochondrial lineage, and that the MT genome contributes standing genetic variation rather than a direct functional basis for these differences.

article.title: Maternal Genetic Diversity and Population Structure of Four Jordanian Subpopulations Revealed by Mitochondrial DNA Variation
article.authors: Almuthanna K. Alkaraki; Hiba T. Alqaissi; Tuqa R. Abu-Alhayjaa; Eman N. Alabbas; Reham I. Ghawanmeh; Mohammad B. Alsliman; Mazhar S. Al Zoubi
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: Jordan’s geographical position at the crossroads of the Southern Levant, Arabian Peninsula, and Africa has contributed to its complex demographic and population interactions and genetic admixture. This study aimed to investigate the maternal genetic structure among four Jordanian subpopulations: Fellahin (Farmers), Bedouins (Nomads), Alnawar (Banu Murra), and Beer Al-Saba Bedouins. Methods: A total of 192 unrelated participants, 48 from each subpopulation, were analyzed after required ethical approvals. Three mitochondrial DNA regions (the D-loop, cytochrome b, and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1) were amplified and sequenced. The predicted maternal haplogroups were assigned using the online HaploGrep 3 tool. Further genetic structure and diversity analyses were assessed through Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) analysis based on the FST distance matrix, along with a Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA). The studied subpopulations were also compared with other populations from the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula, North Africa, East and West Africa, and Europe. Results: The most frequent predicted haplogroup was U in Fellahin (18.75%) and Bedouins (22.92%), H in Alnawar (Banu Murra) (18.75%), and U in Beer Al-Saba Bedouins (20.83%). Maternal genetic diversity was high among the four studied subpopulations, with an average value of 0.9. MDS analysis placed the Jordanian subpopulations within the broader maternal genetic landscape of the Levant and Arabian Peninsula, while also revealing population-specific differentiation, particularly among the Bedouins of Beer Al-Saba. PCoA further showed substantial overlap among Fellahin and Bedouins, partial differentiation of Beer Al-Saba Bedouins, and broader dispersion among Alnawar (Banu Murra) individuals. Interestingly, in comparison with selected Roma subgroups, Alnawar (Banu Murra) showed greater similarity in the predicted mitochondrial haplogroup composition with other Jordanian groups than most of the selected Roma reference populations. Conclusions: The obtained results showed substantial maternal genetic diversity within the studied Jordanian subgroups and highlight the influence of distinct demographic histories on the mitochondrial variation. The study also provides additional mtDNA data that may support future development of population-specific mitochondrial reference datasets for forensic applications in Jordan.

article.title: MitImpact 4: a genome-wide resource for the interpretation of coding and non-coding mitochondrial DNA variants
article.authors: Agnese Giovannetti; Alessandro Napoli; Niccolò Liorni; Francesco Petrizzelli; Tommaso Biagini; Antonio Gasbarrini; Viviana Caputo; Tommaso Mazza
article.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial DNA variants are a frequent cause of inherited disease, yet their computational interpretation has focused almost exclusively on the 13 protein-coding genes. Variants in tRNA and rRNA genes, which carry a disproportionate share of the known pathogenic alleles, have remained a diagnostic blind spot, because their effect depends on RNA structure rather than on protein sequence and few dedicated predictors exist. MitImpact 4 removes this asymmetry. The database now covers all 49 704 single-nucleotide variants that can occur in the mitochondrial genome and reports their functional consequence, phylogenetic conservation, local mutational constraint, and population frequency in gnomAD, HelixMTdb, and ToMMo. Missense variants are annotated with APOGEE 2 and with newly added predictors, including AlphaMissense, ESM1b, VARITY, and LIST-S2, while tRNA and rRNA variants receive predictions from nAPOGEE, our RNA-specific model, alongside MitoTIP and PON-mt-tRNA. For both classes, scores are accompanied by posterior probabilities of pathogenicity that can be used within the ACMG/AMP framework for mitochondrial DNA. Clinical annotation from ClinVar and MITOMAP, including ClinGen expert-panel classifications, is integrated in a redesigned interface that also annotates user-submitted VCF files. MitImpact 4 is freely available at https://mitimpact.mcb2lab.org.

article.title: Manipulation of ER-mitochondria interactions with mitofusin modulators reduces cardiac damage during myocardial infarction in mice.
article.authors: Axelrod JL, Nichtová Z, Schneider T, Lee J, Pekson R, Qin D, Ghazi M, Kumar V, Margulets V, Kirshenbaum LA, Santulli G, Csordás G, Calvert JW, Kitsis RN.
article.abstract: Mitofusin (MFN) 1 and MFN2 are large outer mitochondrial membrane GTPases. Dimerization of MFNs on adjacent mitochondria mediates mitochondrial fusion. MFN2, but not MFN1, also resides at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)/sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) membrane, and dimerization of MFNs on ER/SR and mitochondria tethers the two organelles. Here we report that cell-permeable peptides that perturb MFN conformations regulate myocardial infarct size by impacting ER/SR-mitochondria interactions and Ca 2+ transfer independently of changes in mitochondrial fusion. MFN activators increase ER/SR-mitochondria proximity, promote ER/SR to mitochondria Ca 2+ transfer and exacerbate infarct size in mice, with effects dependent on MFN2, but not MFN1, and on mitochondrial calcium uniporter, which transports Ca 2+ into the mitochondrial matrix. Conversely, although ER/SR-mitochondria proximity is not affected, MFN inhibitors reduce mitochondrial Ca 2+ transfer and infarct size, even when their administration is delayed until reperfusion. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of acutely modulating ER/SR-mitochondria interactions and Ca 2+ dynamics and suggest that pharmacological MFN inhibition may provide a new therapeutic strategy to limit cardiac damage during reperfused myocardial infarction.

article.title: Cancer as a syntrophic cellular consortium established by fatty acid oxidation–primed mitochondria and carrier macrophages
article.authors: Abhijit Deonath
article.abstract: The escalating clinical link between cardiovascular disease and subsequent cancer suggests a systemic etiology beyond the sole purview of somatic mutation. This article reviews emerging evidence through a novel lens: cancer as a syntrophic cellular consortium, where metabolic stratification, driven by fatty acid oxidation (FAO)-primed mitochondria and mediated by carrier macrophages, establishes functionally distinct, metabolically interdependent cellular subpopulations. Stressed cardiomyocytes eject metabolically “primed” mitochondria. These organelles are engulfed by macrophages, transforming them into pathogenic “mito-macrophages” that act as mobile systemic carriers. These mito-macrophages instigate malignancy through mitochondrial transfer to recipient cells, inducing profound metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. Within individual cells, the transferred mitochondria establish distinct intracellular oxidation zones fueled by FAO, juxtaposed with hypoxia zones favoring glycolysis. This primary compartmentalization scales up within the evolving tumor: cells from oxidation zones adopt a “leader” phenotype, characterized by high FAO, metabolic flexibility, and invasive capacity, while cells from hypoxia zones become “follower” phenotypes, relying on glycolysis and contributing to bulk tumor growth. Critical intercellular signaling pathways between these emerging “leader” and “follower” populations are central to establishing, maintaining, and propagating this obligate, syntrophic cross-feeding hierarchy, ensuring tumor progression. This framework bridges cardiac stress and distal cancer, elucidating how metabolic and epigenetic imprinting dictates cellular roles within a structured malignant consortium. Reconceiving cancer as such a syntrophic system offers new avenues for therapeutic intervention, targeting metabolic instigators and the signaling axes that define its consortium partners. This framework synthesizes established biological mechanisms into a novel, testable hypothesis and is presented as such. Direct experimental evidence for several of the proposed linkages—particularly long-distance macrophage-mediated trafficking of cardiomyocyte-derived mitochondria, and the FAO-primed state—remains to be established.

article.title: Biointerface‐Customized Nanomodulators Induce Mitochondria‐Specific Dysfunction to Reprogram Tumor Immunity
article.authors: Xueyan Zhen; Yuxin Chen; Linhao Li; Tingting Zhang; Min Li; Runting Wang; Yihan Sun; Jiaqi Li; Shurui Ma; Renyue Zhou; Sicen Wang; Xiaoyu Xie
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Tumor mitochondria regulate cancer progression and immune evasion. However, current therapeutic strategies lack the subcellular precision required to selectively induce immune‐beneficial mitochondrial dysfunction without causing systemic toxicity. Here, we report a biointerface‐customized nanomodulator (C/C‐HP@M2M‐TPP), developed through a biointerface‐engineered strategy (BES), that integrates sequential targeting and controlled activation to induce mitochondria‐specific dysfunction and reprogram tumor immunity. Through a customized biointerface coating, the nanomodulators achieve preferential tumor accumulation and mitochondria‐directed subcellular localization. Co‐delivered calcium ion donors and efflux inhibitors cooperatively induce mitochondrial ion interference and dysfunction, which is further amplified by photothermal activation. This localized mitochondrial interference promotes immunogenic cell death and robust antitumor immune activation, resulting in potent tumor regression in mice. Integrated single‐cell transcriptomic and proteomic analyses further identify mitochondrial disruption as a key mechanistic driver of tumor immune reprogramming. This work establishes biointerface‐customized nanomodulation as a subcellular immunomodulatory therapeutic strategy in vivo.

article.title: DUSP26 Regulated by YY1 Lactylation Couples Osteogenesis and Angiogenesis by Dephosphorylating PMPCB at Y141 and Activating Mitophagy in BMSCs
article.authors: Yunpeng Lv; Feng Wu; Xiongjie Liang; Chong Liu; Wenhui Guo; Kejian Zhang; Jiawen Niu; Wenjie Jiang; Hongjian Xu; Anlong Jiang; Yang Zheng; Enming Yu; Xintao Wang; Jinglong Yan; Jingjun Xia; Chengchao Song
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) support bone formation through osteogenic differentiation and pro‐angiogenic paracrine activity, but the mechanisms coordinating these functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we identified dual‐specificity phosphatase 26 (DUSP26) as a regulator of BMSC osteogenesis and mitochondrial homeostasis. DUSP26 expression increased during osteogenic differentiation and was reduced in osteoporotic femoral tissues. p300 gain‐ and loss‐of‐function experiments, together with analysis of the Yin Yang1(YY1) K183R mutant, supported the conclusion that p300‐regulated YY1 lactylation contributes to DUSP26 transcriptional activation. DUSP26 interacted with the mitochondrial processing peptidase subunit beta(PMPCB) and reduced its tyrosine phosphorylation, with mass spectrometry and mutational analyses implicating Y141 as involved in this regulation. Functional assays supported a model in which DUSP26 limits mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP)‐mediated PTEN‐induced kinase 1 (PINK1) processing and promotes PINK1‐dependent mitophagy, thereby supporting mitochondrial homeostasis. DUSP26 enhanced osteogenic differentiation and the pro‐angiogenic activity of BMSC‐conditioned medium(CM), whereas its knockdown impaired bone formation and reduced type H vessels in vivo. Furthermore, BMSC‐derived exosomes carrying a runt‐related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) promoter‐driven DUSP26 plasmid produced preferential transgene expression in osteogenic‐lineage cells and attenuated ovariectomy‐induced bone loss in mice. These findings link lactylation‐associated transcriptional regulation to mitochondrial protein processing and support further preclinical evaluation of DUSP26‐directed approaches for osteoporosis.

article.title: Isovitexin Attenuates Aβ-Induced Neurotoxicity by Activating SKN-1/Nrf2 Signaling and Suppressing Ferroptosis in Caenorhabditis elegans Models of Alzheimer’s Disease
article.authors: Mengjiao Hao; Dongni Wu; Lingli Sun; Xingfei Lai; Ruohong Chen; Zhenbiao Zhang; Qiuhua Li; Suwan Zhang; Xi Zheng; Dongli Li; Shili Sun
article.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
article.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction, while effective therapeutic interventions remain limited. Epidemiological evidence indicates that tea and flavonoids with antiaging properties lower AD risk. In this study, untargeted metabolomic profiling identified isovitexin as a differentially abundant flavonoid in postfermented dark tea (DT), and Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) AD models were employed to evaluate its anti-AD potential and elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. The results showed that isovitexin significantly extended lifespan, reduced Aβ accumulation, and improved neuromuscular function, demonstrating marked neuroprotective effects. Mechanistically, isovitexin mitigated Aβ-triggered toxicity through SKN-1 signaling, accompanied by the attenuation of Aβ-evoked ferroptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction. Collectively, these results broaden the therapeutic potential of dark tea flavonoids and support further investigation of isovitexin as a candidate for mitigating Aβ-induced neurodegeneration.

article.title: AI-Based Grading of Facial Aging Signs and Prediction of Visible Age From Standardized Facial Images: Algorithm Development and Internal Evaluation Study.
article.authors: Frederic Flament; Panagiotis-Alexandros Bokaris; Tao Li; Aurelie Abric; Sileye Ba; Julien Despois; Hussein Jouni; Laudine Bertrand; Paul Michel; Thomas Dauxerre; Diala Haykal; Hughes Cartier
article.abstract: BACKGROUND: Facial appearance influences visible age (VA), defined here as the age perceived by others; this perception-based outcome differs from chronological age and biological age. Human evaluation of facial aging signs can be time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability. A standardized AI-based approach might offer a more reproducible assessment of visible facial aging in digital dermatology research. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop and evaluate an AI-based process for automatically grading facial aging signs and predicting the VA of participants from standardized full-face images. METHODS: Evaluation of full-face photographs of 468 North American women aged 18 to 80 years recruited in Dallas and Phoenix, Texas. Fifteen trained experts, including dermatologists, graded 13 aging signs using Skin Aging Atlas scales. A separate, naïve group of 253 North Americans aged 20 to 60 years, recruited in New York City, estimated the VA of each participant. For each sign, facial areas were pulled out using facial landmarks and fed into ResNet-based regression models, which were trained to match the averaged expert scores. The automated facial sign grading models were tested on 90% of the image set, and the remaining 10% was used for evaluation. Results were assessed using the mean absolute error, the proportions of estimates within 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 grading units of the expert reference, and Spearman correlations between chronological age, human-assessed VA, and predicted visible age (PVA). RESULTS: The mean absolute error was below 0.3 grading units for 11 of the 13 facial aging signs. The average proportion of automatic gradings within 1 grading unit of the expert reference was about 98% for participants of East Asian ancestry group, 96% for participants of African ancestry group, and 97% for participants of European ancestry group. Human-assessed VA correlated strongly with real age (r=0.94, 95% CI 0.928-0.950; P<.001), although participants were perceived as around 10 years older than their real age, on average. The AI-PVA also correlated strongly with the human-assessed VA (r=0.93, 95% CI 0.917-0.941; P<.001), with approximately 70% of estimates within 5 years. CONCLUSIONS: The AI-based system showed low grading errors across most facial aging signs and also a fairly strong relationship between the PVA and human-assessed VA under standardized image acquisition conditions. Consequently, the system could provide a reproducible digital outcome for facial aging research and future longitudinal monitoring. However, external validation across separate populations, in men, and across image acquisition devices is required before clinical and consumer-facing implementation. As the predicted visible age is derived from quantified clinical facial signs, it reflects measurable features of visible facial aging, while its relationship with biological age and overall health remains to be established through future studies integrating biological biomarkers.

article.title: Ginsenoside Rb1 alleviates uterine aging via AMPK-mediated mTOR inactivation.
article.authors: Zhou P, Wang Y, Cheng M, Deng F, Liu F, Chen X, Ning K, Mo D, Zeng Z, Huang Z, Dong Y, Wang Y, Zhang C, Qiao J, Yu Y, Pan H, Li R.
article.abstract: Uterine aging impairs fertility and reproductive health, but the underlying pathogenic mechanisms and effective treatment strategies remain elusive. Defective endometrial decidualization and implantation failure are hallmarks of uterine aging, which can be driven by cellular senescence, especially in endometrial stromal cells (EnSCs). Rb1 has been reported to relieve cellular senescence by suppressing oxidative and inflammatory pathways. However, whether Rb1 functions in alleviating uterine aging remains uncertain. Here, we demonstrate that Rb1 can attenuate oxidative stress, senescence, and apoptosis in the EnSCs of the aging human endometrium and murine uterus. Further proteomic analysis reveals that Rb1 safeguards against endometrial aging by regulating mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)-related pathways. Rb1 treatment results in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and AMPK-mediated suppression of the mTOR-nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) signaling loop, thereby ameliorating aging-related phenotypes. Collectively, our findings illustrate that Rb1 alleviates uterine aging by attenuating endometrial stromal cell senescence and suppressing AMPK-mTOR-NF-κB-driven inflammatory signaling. Rather than selectively eliminating senescent cells, Rb1 primarily targets senescence-associated dysfunction and restores endometrial homeostasis, highlighting its potential as a senescence-modulating therapeutic strategy for uterine aging.

article.title: Toward a comparative endocrinology of aging: insights from insects
article.authors: Jiangtian Chen; Fernando G. Noriega; Marc Tatar
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Insulin-like signaling modulates aging and lifespan in insects. Here, we discuss a novel view of this control: insulin hormone in the adult regulates the production of the sesquiterpenoid juvenile hormone (JH) that in turn acts as the systemic regulator of aging and lifespan. Work in Drosophila establishes that insulin signaling is allatotropic – it stimulates the production and secretion of JH from the corpora allata. JH then exerts systemic effects on adult survival through its control of specific proteins, translation and proteostasis. The interdependent functions of insulin and JH allow reproduction and longevity to be coupled in many insects or decoupled in social insects with long-lived queens and in some long-lived genetic mutants of Drosophila. Features of these insulin-regulated life history syndromes are also found in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Recognizing the systemic role of JH in aging provides grounds to search for analogous systems in mammals that might modulate human lifespan.

article.title: The Skin–brain Axis in Cutaneous Aging: Neurobiological Foundations and Clinical Implications
article.authors: Ahmad Taha Khalaf; Haitham Bader; Waseem H. Q. Alkhaffaf; Yahya D. M. Zakaria; Omar Y. Abdullah; Mohammed N. S. Al-Mallah
article.abstract: The skin– brain axis is a bidirectional neuroimmunoendocrine axis connecting psychological stress, brain signaling, immune responses, and skin homeostasis. A hypothetical link between dysregulation of this network and skin ageing is neurogenic inflammation, oxidative stress, cellular senescence, inflammaging, and activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. This dysregulation is increasingly recognized as associated with mechanisms of skin ageing, including neurogenic inflammation, oxidative stress, cellular ageing, inflammaging, and activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. This review focuses on the neurobiological mechanisms underlying cutaneous ageing and emphasizes the role of neurocutaneous receptors, neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and neuro-signaling pathways in the stress response. It also examines emerging trends, such as 'neurocosmetics' including peptides that act on neurocutaneous pathways to stimulate regeneration, stress-modulating peptides, and myorelaxant peptides. This review provides new insight into the skin–brain axis as a potential model for better understanding stress-related skin ageing by combining intrinsic and extrinsic skin ageing with neurobiology. There are a variety of neuroactive cosmetic strategies, with some having mechanistic and preliminary clinical evidence, while others do not and require controlled, randomized studies with objective markers. Future preventive and therapeutic strategies to regulate neuroimmune and neuroendocrine signaling to preserve skin homeostasis and reduce stress-induced skin ageing may be available.

article.title: Distinct Epigenetic Responses to Aging and Short‐Term High‐Fat Diet in Hepatic Lipid Metabolism Genes in Male and Female Mice
article.authors: Annalena Frank; Sascha Tierling; Beate Czepukojc; Sonja M. Kessler; Thomas Hentrich; Michael Kohlstedt; Johannes Haybaeck; Christoph Wittmann; Jessica Hoppstädter; Julia Schulze‐Hentrich; Alexandra K. Kiemer
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aims Aging is associated with widespread epigenetic remodelling that contributes to metabolic alterations in the liver. High‐fat diet (HFD) represents a major environmental perturbation affecting hepatic metabolism, yet its specific impact on age‐associated epigenetic changes remains unclear. Here, we investigated in male and female mice whether HFD induces epigenetic changes similar to or distinct from those observed during aging, with a particular focus on DNA methylation (5mC) and hydroxymethylation (5hmC) in key lipid metabolism genes. Methods We combined re‐analysis of published RNA‐sequencing datasets from young and aged mouse livers with targeted epigenetic and metabolic profiling in a short‐term HFD model. Results In our study, we identified a consistent age‐associated transcriptional upregulation of lipogenic genes, including fatty acid synthase ( Fasn ) and stearoyl‐CoA 9‐desaturase ( Scd1 ), accompanied by reduced DNA methylation and gene‐specific alterations in 5hmC. In contrast, HFD exposure resulted in increased gene‐body methylation with reduced expression of these genes, alongside shifts in fatty acid composition indicative of altered lipid metabolism. Analyses of samples from male and female mice showed sex‐specific differences. Notably, the applied HFD model did not induce overt lipid pathology, suggesting that these changes reflect early metabolic adaptation rather than advanced disease states. Conclusions Together, our findings indicate that HFD induces an epigenetic and transcriptional response in hepatic lipid metabolism genes that differs from and in part opposes age‐associated patterns. These results support a model in which short‐term dietary lipid excess triggers distinct regulatory mechanisms rather than simply recapitulating epigenetic aging.

article.title: A Bi‐Adjuvant Senolytic Nanovaccine Modulating Dendritic Cell Senescence Ameliorates Aging‐Related Metabolic Dysfunction
article.authors: Qingxu Song; Xiaoxue Du; Wenbo Dong; Ying Wang; Xiaojing Wang; Qiliang Yin
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Senolytic vaccines hold promise for eliminating senescent cells, but their efficacy is limited by poor seno‐antigen immunogenicity and age‐related dendritic cell (DC) dysfunction. Here, we engineered an active biomaterial‐enabled bi‐adjuvant senolytic nanovaccine (CK5‐GC‐NV) by co‐assembling CpG oligodeoxynucleotide with a fusion protein of the seno‐antigen Gpnmb and a cationic spider silk protein variant (CK5). Beyond antigen delivery, the CK5 scaffold acts as an intrinsic senomodulator associated with the downregulation of mitotic kinases Aurka/b and a concomitant decrease in senescence‐associated PI3K/AKT phosphorylation in DCs. This intervention attenuates aged DC phenotypes, restores antigen cross‐presentation, and synergizes with CpG to elicit potent cytotoxic T‐lymphocyte responses against senescent targets. Across multiple aging mouse models, CK5‐GC‐NV immunization orchestrated targeted clearance of Gpnmb + senescent adipocytes, profoundly ameliorating metabolic dysfunction and extending lifespan. This multifunctional biomaterial platform integrates seno‐antigen immunogenicity enhancement with the restoration of aged DC function, providing a promising proof‐of‐concept for antigen‐directed gerotherapeutics.
