Peripheral biomarkers: including decreased ETC complex activity, increased MDA and 8-OHdG, altered purinergic enzymes, and elevated mtDNA reflect systemic bioenergetic stress. Emerging interventions targeting mitochondrial cofactors (creatine, CoQ10, carnitine, NAC), metabolic strategies (ketogenic diet), and immunomodulatory or purinergic pathway modulators show promise. CONCLUSIONS: Emerging evidence suggests that systemic bioenergetic dysregulation may contribute to the pathophysiology of BD. Integrating mitochondrial, metabolic, and inflammatory biomarkers with neuroimaging may enable biologically informed patient stratification and precision therapeutics aimed at restoring energetic homeostasis. Large, standardised multicenter studies are required to translate these findings into clinical practice.

article.title: Ciliary-Mitochondrial Crosstalk in Cancer: Mechanistic Links Between Primary Cilium Dysfunction and Mitochondrial Reprogramming in Tumor Progression and Metastasis
article.authors: Bonab MA, Tofighbakhsh Y, Shokri M, Behnam B.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: Primary cilia are microtubule-based sensory organelles that coordinate key oncogenic signaling pathways, including Hedgehog, Wnt, PDGF, and TGF-β. Mitochondria, traditionally viewed as bioenergetic hubs, also regulate redox balance, calcium homeostasis, apoptosis, and metabolic plasticity. Emerging evidence demonstrates that these organelles are functionally coupled, forming a bidirectional ciliary-mitochondrial axis that influences cancer progression and metastasis. Disruption of ciliogenesis, often through IFT88 or KIF3A loss, impairs mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and promotes a glycolytic, biosynthetic phenotype. Conversely, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), and altered dynamics feedback to regulate ciliary assembly and signaling. Key mechanistic nodes include calcium flux, AMPK-ULK1 signaling, ROS-mediated communication, and the recently identified NDUFAF2-ARMC9 bridge linking mitochondrial metabolism to ciliogenesis. This crosstalk converges on pathways that drive epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, cancer stemness, migration, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. In the tumor microenvironment, hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, immune signaling, and extracellular vesicles further modulate this axis, contributing to metabolic heterogeneity and metastatic dissemination. Importantly, the relationship between cilia and cancer is context-dependent: cilia can be tumor-suppressive in some malignancies yet support oncogenic signaling in others. These insights suggest that targeting ciliary function, mitochondrial metabolism, or their intersection may offer novel therapeutic opportunities. This review synthesizes current evidence on ciliary-mitochondrial crosstalk, highlights unresolved mechanistic questions, and proposes an integrated framework for understanding how this organellar axis shapes cancer evolution and treatment response. We propose that integrated ciliary-mitochondrial signatures represent highly promising novel cancer biomarkers capable of predicting tumor plasticity, metastatic risk, and therapeutic response beyond conventional single-organelle or genomic markers.

article.title: Motile vesicles (MoVes) are a cancer cell migration-associated extracellular vesicle population.
article.authors: Tsering T, Nadeau A, Ghasemi M, Mousovich-Neto F, Tobias G, Chen Y, Kienzle L, Dickinson K, Douanne N, Serganova I, Zappasodi R, Matei I, Lyden D, Burnier JV.
article.abstract: Migrating cancer cells release diverse extracellular vesicles (EVs) that carry cargo capable of influencing tumour progression and intercellular communication. However, the mechanisms by which intracellular components are incorporated into EVs remain poorly understood. Here we identify and characterize a previously undescribed population of large EVs (2-5 μm), termed motile vesicles (MoVes), that are generated during active cancer cell migration and associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Comparative analyses across EV populations show that MoVes display distinct ultrastructural features, molecular composition and sedimentation behaviour. Live-cell imaging and scanning electron microscopy reveal that MoVes arise from trailing-edge retraction during mesenchymal migration and are actively shed by cancer cells but rarely by non-transformed cells. MoVes contain genomic DNA spanning the genome of the parent cell, recapitulating its mutational landscape, as well as organelles and proteins associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Moreover, MoVes-associated mitochondrial cargo can enhance oxidative phosphorylation in recipient cells. Together, these findings identify MoVes as a cancer cell migration-associated EV population capable of disseminating genomic DNA and organelles.

article.title: mito-overview: a mitochondrial report software
article.authors: Gai, X.; Ahuja, K.; LOPES, E. N.
article.abstract: Interpreting mitochondrial DNA variation requires relating allele representation and genomic annotation to the sequencing evidence available for each sample. We developed mito-overview to integrate mitochondrial coverage, candidate allele fractions, genomic annotations and long read co-occurrence in mitochondrial genomic reports. Analysis of a subset of public GM12878 long read data from Vandiver and colleagues Cas9 enrichment study of full-length mitochondrial genomes (SRR18110025) identified 16 candidate variants. Among these candidates, co-occurrence analysis showed that m.8860A>G and m.14831G>A occurred together in all 366 jointly callable query names, demonstrating how mito-overview extends individual allele measurements to quantify shared read support between mitochondrial sites. Analysis of public GM11906 short read data (GSE142741), pooled from three single-cell ATAC-seq libraries, recovered the previously characterized disease-associated m.8344A>G variant in MT-TK at an alternate allele fraction of 72.1% (740 of 1,027 callable observations). The recovered variant identity and MT-TK assignment agree with Lareau and colleagues original study, providing a disease-relevant example of mito-overview combined candidate detection and genomic annotation. We also examined ONT data from blood, fibroblast and muscle of one patient using a separate internal workflow. Heteroplasmy was estimated from alternate allele fractions calculated separately for each tissue. The respective analyses yielded 90, 52 and 60 candidates, with 19 candidate identities shared across all three lists. For these shared candidates, the tissue-specific estimates enabled examination of both variant presence and allele representation across the sampled tissues, illustrating the application of mitochondrial genomic reports to heteroplasmy assessment in disease research. By combining candidate identification with allele measurements, genomic annotations and shared read support, mito-overview enables researchers to examine which variants are observed, their representation within a sample and their co-occurrence with other mitochondrial alleles. These complementary measurements support the selection and characterization of candidate variants for further study in mitochondrial disease research.

article.title: Alpha- and Gamma-Synuclein Proteins Define Complementary Metabolic and Invasive Programs in Melanoma Development, Progression, and Prognosis
article.authors: Marquez MM, Malizia F, Zanotti L, Mian M, Ponce PM, Mamberto M, Avila A, Laluce NC, Farré C, Binolfi A, Bustelo X, Anselmino L.
article.abstract: Abstract Melanoma, a highly aggressive skin cancer, remains a major clinical challenge due to its metastatic capacity and resistance to therapy. Synuclein proteins — alpha-synuclein (αS) and gamma-synuclein (γS), traditionally studied in neurodegeneration — are increasingly recognized as contributors to melanoma progression, yet whether they define distinct tumor cell states or act through shared mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we show that SNCA and SNCG are robustly anti-correlated across independent transcriptomic and proteomic cohorts and at single-cell resolution, marking two complementary malignant cell states. Both synucleins support melanoma proliferation, migration, and invasion, and are internalized by melanoma cells in a prion-like manner that enhances tumor growth in vitro and in vivo. Functionally, however, αS and γS diverge along distinct axes. αS is transcriptionally coupled to a MITF-linked mitochondrial program and functionally sensitizes complex I: its silencing improves mitochondrial bioenergetics and blunts the response to a second respiratory challenge, while exogenous fibrils impair it, alongside a corresponding shift in pigmentation. γS instead sustains an integrin-FAK-Rac1-MAPK signaling axis and β-catenin regulation that drives invasive behavior; its silencing reduces MAPK output and confers cross-resistance to three mechanistically distinct therapeutic agents — cisplatin, vemurafenib, and paclitaxel. These opposing programs converge on a shared differentiation axis: SNCG-high cells define a dedifferentiated, MITF-low, invasive malignant subpopulation that is independently associated with shorter progression-free interval in stage IIC melanoma. Collectively, these findings establish αS and γS as functionally distinct, mechanistically convergent regulators of a metabolic-versus-invasive cell-state dichotomy in melanoma, nominate SNCG as a candidate prognostic biomarker, and identify complex I sensitization and FAK/MAPK signaling as candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities.

article.title: SHED-Derived Exosomes Attenuate Alzheimer's Disease Pathology in iPSC-Derived Cerebral Organoid Model
article.authors: Elyasi L, Chołoniewska A, Lutostańska E, Mierzwa N, Sulejczak D, Macias M, Szybińska A, Gawlik-Zawiślak S, Woźniak M, Filipek-Gliszczyńska A, Bednarska-Makaruk M, Zaremba J, Żekanowski C, Wężyk M.
article.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Developing disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) that go beyond single-target monoclonal antibodies is a pressing translational priority. Stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED) and their exosomal cargo represent a promising biological therapy. To bridge the gap between basic exosome research and clinical application, we evaluated SHED-derived exosomes in human-relevant 2D and 3D patient-derived models. Methods: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D cortical neurons and 3D cerebral organoid models were generated from patients representing both familial AD (FAD; PSEN1) and sporadic AD (SAD). Models were treated with SHED-derived exosomes. Pathological markers including p181-tau, Aβ42, and Aβ40 were quantified, functional excitotoxicity was assessed via N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)-induced calcium dynamics, and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) were measured. High-throughput microRNA (miRNA) profiling was performed to identify functional exosomal cargo. Results: SHED exosome treatment demonstrated genotype-specific efficacy, selectively reducing p181-tau levels and restoring the p181-tau/Aβ42 ratio in FAD lines while elevating the protective Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio across both FAD and SAD backgrounds. Functionally, treatment prevented NMDA-induced calcium overload, accelerated intracellular calcium clearance, and suppressed stress-induced mitochondrial ROS. High-throughput profiling identified enriched therapeutic miRNAs (hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-16-5p, and hsa-miR-191-5p) targeting key networks in tau hyperphosphorylation and amyloid processing. Discussion: SHED-derived exosomes attenuate key AD pathologies and functional excitotoxicity in human 2D and 3D organoid models. These findings provide translational validation for exosome-based therapeutics, helping close the knowledge gap in multi-target biological treatments for dementia.

article.title: Mechanical stress-induced release of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA activates RIG-I to drive osteogenic differentiation in aortic disease
article.authors: Graef, M.; Bender, F.; Dudek, S.; Vasileiadou, P.; Soler, S.; Schlee-Guimaraes, T. M.; Steinheuer, L. M.; Spitzer, J.; Thurley, K.; Nowak, R. P.; Maser, K.; Schmidt, S.; Goody, P. R.; Schlee, M.; Zimmer, S.; Nickenig, G.; Zillinger, T.; Bartok, E.; Hartmann, G.
article.abstract: Background: Gain-of-function mutations in RIG-I and MDA5 (RIG-I-like receptors, RLR) cause Singleton-Merten syndrome, an interferonopathy with early aortic calcification. Here we set out to study a possible involvement of RIG-I-like receptor signaling in the formation of aortic valve stenosis in general. Methods and results: We investigated whether mechanical stress-induced RLR activation promotes osteogenic differentiation and calcification of primary human aortic cells, whether such RLR activation drives the development of aortic valve stenosis in vivo, and whether inhibition of downstream JAK/STAT activation ameliorates aortic valve stenosis. We found that activation of primary human aortic interstitial cells by exogenous RIG-I- and MDA5 agonists induced a type I interferon response and an osteogenic program including increased expression of BMP-2 and BSP2, and promoted calcification. These effects were RIG-I/MDA5 or MAVS-dependent, as assessed by CRISPR/Cas9 knockouts. The stress-granule protein G3BP1 and the Wnt receptor FZD5 were induced downstream of RLR activation and were required for osteogenic gene expression and calcification. To assess a potential endogenous source of RIG-I activation, mechanical stretch mimicking valvular tissue stress was applied in cell cuture, which induced a significant RIG-I-dependent interferon response. Sequencing of highly purified preparations of double-stranded RNA from stretched cells demonstrated a predominant mitochondrial origin of double-stranded RNA, and depleting mitochondrial RNA abolished the stretch-dependent response. The JAK/STAT inhibitor ruxolitinib suppressed the RIG-I-induced response including the expression of osteogenic factors in vitro. In a murine wire-injury model of aortic stenosis, MAVS deficiency attenuated valvular morphological changes and improved hemodynamic parameters. Ruxolitinib attenuated hemodynamic progression, prevented aortic stenosis development, and improved survival. Conclusions: Altogether, our results demonstrate that the mechanical-stress-induced release of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA activates RIG-I signaling in aortic interstitial cells, thereby driving osteogenic differentiation and calcification via a MAVS- and G3BP1-dependent pathway. JAK/STAT inhibition with ruxolitinib mitigates this process in a mouse model of aortic valve stenosis, identifying a candidate therapeutic strategy.

article.title: Aβ42 oligomers disrupt calcium homeostasis via Piezo1 and induce neurotoxicity in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells
article.authors: Meng W, Zhang J, Zhang S, Shi Y, Wang H.
article.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits an intricate and multifactorial pathogenesis. Existing research on amyloid-β (Aβ)-triggered neurotoxicity has predominantly centered on neuronal apoptosis, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial damage. The role of biomechanical signaling, a vital regulatory mechanism in neuronal physiological homeostasis and AD pathological progression, remains largely uncharacterized in the context of Aβ-mediated neurotoxicity. Here, differentiated SH-SY5Y, neuron-like cells, were used to examine the Aβ42 oligomers induced cellular mechanics alteration and the abnormal activation of mechanosensitive ion channels. Aβ42 oligomer adsorption increases cellular Young's modulus, which is associated with sustained intracellular Ca 2+ elevation mediated by Piezo1. Subsequently, the overloaded Ca 2+ induces mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, YAP/TAZ signaling activation, cytoskeletal remodeling, dynamic changes in cellular stiffness, and finally a cell death through caspase-4-mediated non-canonical pyroptosis. These findings support an Aβ42-Piezo1-Ca 2+ -cytoskeletal remodeling axis that links altered neuronal mechanics to neurotoxicity and identify Piezo1 as a potential target for further investigation in AD.

article.title: Beyond Glycemic Control: The Pleiotropic Role of GLP-1RAs and Melatonin in Combating Neuroinflammation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
article.authors: Reiter RJ, Sharma R, Simão VA, Chuffa LGdA, Carloni S, Gentile C, Balduini W, Manucha W.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and impaired protein homeostasis form interconnected pathological networks in acute central nervous system injury and chronic neurodegenerative disease. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), originally developed for metabolic disorders, exhibit neuroprotective activity in experimental models through effects on neuronal survival, metabolic adaptation, and inflammatory signaling. Melatonin complements these actions through mitochondrial redox protection, preservation of bioenergetics, and circadian regulation. This narrative review examines the pharmacological diversity and central nervous system accessibility of GLP-1RAs, including emerging multi-receptor agonists, and their convergence with melatonin on AMPK, sirtuin–PGC-1α, and mitochondrial quality-control networks. Evidence from stroke, traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and type 2 diabetes-associated cognitive decline highlights opportunities to translate these mechanisms into neuroprotective strategies. Experimental efficacy, exploratory cognitive findings, and existing clinical experience provide a foundation for further investigation, while heterogeneous clinical outcomes help define appropriate populations, endpoints, and treatment conditions. A mitochondrial-support framework is proposed in which melatonin may preserve the cellular environment needed for GLP-1RA-mediated metabolic and survival responses. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide a promising foundation for developing combined GLP-1RA–melatonin strategies to preserve mitochondrial function, attenuate neuroinflammation, and support cognitive and functional recovery.

article.title: Porcine astrovirus induces endoplasmic reticulum stress-mediated autophagic degradation of MAVS to inhibit type I interferon production.
article.authors: Lv Y, Feng X, Du Y, Shao S, Ouyang K, Chen Y, Wei Z, Huang W, Qin Y.
article.abstract: Porcine astrovirus (PAstV) infection predominantly results in diarrhea and encephalitis in suckling piglets, yet the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, the PAstV1-GX1 strain, previously isolated, was utilized to infect PK-15 cells. The results demonstrated that PAstV infection induced pronounced endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, as evidenced by the upregulation of HSPA5/GRP78 expression, and macroautophagy/autophagy, indicated by the increased conversion of MAP1LC3/LC3 from LC3-I to LC3-II and decreased expression of SQSTM1/p62. Pharmacological mitigation of ER stress effectively suppressed autophagy, suggesting that PAstV facilitates autophagy via ER stress. Further mechanistic investigations identified that PAstV infection selectively activated the EIF2AK3/PERK-EIF2S1/eIF2α-ATF4 pathway within the unfolded protein response, establishing this pathway as the pivotal upstream signal mediating autophagy. Through the screening of viral proteins, the capsid protein was identified as the primary viral component responsible for inducing ER stress and autophagy. This protein was concurrently localized to both mitochondria and the ER, where it interacted with the MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein). The capsid protein facilitated the degradation of MAVS via the autophagy pathway and an apoptosis-related pathway in a non-classical, caspase-3-independent manner, thereby suppressing the production of type I interferons. Modulating ER stress, autophagy, or apoptosis greatly impacted the capsid protein's suppression of type I interferons. This suggested that the capsid protein hindered type I interferon production by triggering ER stress, which activated autophagy and possibly apoptosis, resulting in MAVS degradation. These insights lay the groundwork for understanding PAstV's pathogenic mechanisms and aid in developing new antiviral treatments. article.title: Macrophage GLUD1 is Essential for Redox Balance and Immune Homeostasis in Cardiac Injury.
article.authors: Jin T, Lai C, Zhou Q, Wang R, Tong Y, Chen W, Rabrenovic N, Zhang T, Ren X, Huang C, Chen J, Li R, Yu L, Mazzone M, Zhang W, Fu G, Shang M.
article.abstract: Excessive free radical production and dysregulated immune responses contribute to myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (IR) injury. However, the mechanisms by which macrophages regulate reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis and orchestrate immune responses during IR injury remain elusive. Here, we show that glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (GLUD1) expression is induced in monocytes from patients with acute myocardial infarction after interventional therapy and in cardiac-recruited macrophages from mice subjected to IR injury. GLUD1-deficient macrophages exacerbate IR injury by increasing mitochondrial ROS accumulation and amplifying pro-inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, GLUD1 deficiency leads to mitochondrial ROS accumulation due to reduced NADPH/NADP + and GSH/GSSG ratios during IR injury. Elevated mitochondrial ROS inhibits PHD2 activity, stabilizing HIF-1α and enhancing NF-κB signaling, promoting the release of pro-inflammatory factors and exacerbating myocardial damage. Systemic activation of GLUD1 or adoptive transfer of monocytes pre-treated with a GLUD1 activator preserved cardiac function and mitigated IR injury. These findings highlight macrophage GLUD1 as a critical regulator of redox balance and immune homeostasis, presenting a promising therapeutic target for alleviating IR injury and preserving cardiac function.

article.title: Neutrophil-Derived Arg1 Impairs CD8 + T Cell Activity in Sepsis Through mTOR-Mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
article.authors: Peng Q, Yang L.
article.abstract: Background This research aimed to elucidate the contribution of Arginase 1 (Arg1) to pediatric sepsis progression, specifically impacting the effector functions of CD8 + T lymphocytes. Methods Arg1 expression was assessed in venous blood from pediatric sepsis patients ( n = 21) and healthy volunteers ( n = 21). Pharmacological inhibition of Arg1 was achieved using Nor-NOHA in both sepsis patients-derived neutrophils and LPS-stimulated healthy neutrophils, followed by co-culture with CD8 + T cells. Sepsis-derived neutrophils were also treated with hArg1 monoclonal antibody (mAb). CD8 + T cell viability, exhaustion markers (PD-1/TIM-3), mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production, autophagy, and inflammatory cytokine secretion were systematically evaluated. Results Arg1 expression was markedly upregulated in sepsis patients correlated positively with neutrophil counts but negatively with CD8 + T cell numbers and mitochondrial function. Strikingly, CD8 + T cells from Arg1-high patients exhibited increased PD-1 + TIM-3 + double-positive populations. Both Nor-NOHA-mediated Arg1 inhibition and hArg1-mAb neutralization significantly restored CD8 + T cell mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), ATP production, and effector cytokine secretion, while concurrently reducing PD-1/TIM-3 expression. Conclusion Our findings indicate that overexpression of Arg1 derived from neutrophils leads to a highly inflammatory response suggesting that Arg1 is a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in pediatric sepsis.

article.title: Cancers relax selection on charge at the mitochondrial complex I quinone cavity
article.authors: Sung, J.-Y.; Cheong, J.-H.
article.abstract: Mitochondrial complex I translocates protons through hydrated channels whose connectivity and electrostatics are both defined by structure, but whether they are distinctly constrained is unknown. From a 2.39 cryo-EM structure modelling 2,945 ordered waters, we built the proton wire of the seven mtDNA-encoded ND subunits and scored all 40,166 missense substitutions on two near-orthogonal axes (r = 0.17): electrostatic shift at proton-loading sites, and topological disruption of the wire. Across 858 germline variant sites, loading sites (0.51) and cut vertices (0.67) are both depleted. In tumours only loading sites are enriched (1.42 TCGA, 1.67 PCAWG, 1.29 MSK-IMPACT), a 3.06-fold difference tested as a wire class tissue-type interaction (P = 3.6 10-). It survives adjustment for conservation, burial and coverage, and is concentrated in ND1 within 15 of the quinone cavity, not spread along the proton path. Selection separates charge from connectivity, without establishing a fitness benefit.

article.title: Beyond Chronological Age: Circadian Disruption, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, and the Biology of Female Reproductive Aging
article.authors: Warda Abubakar; Laiba Rehmat
article.venue: Journal of Women's Health, Reproductive Medicine and Physiology
article.abstract: Female reproductive aging involves progressive follicular depletion, declining oocyte competence, and changes in reproductive endocrine function. This narrative review examines the potential interactions between circadian regulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress in ovarian aging. Evidence on sleep timing, shift work, ovarian clock genes, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and redox homeostasis is considered. Although these processes share pathways involved in cellular metabolism and stress regulation, direct evidence that circadian disruption accelerates ovarian reserve depletion or shortens reproductive lifespan in humans remains limited. The proposed circadian–mitochondrial relationship should therefore be considered a testable hypothesis rather than an established causal pathway. Longitudinal human studies integrating objective circadian measures, ovarian reserve markers, mitochondrial assessments, and reproductive outcomes are needed to clarify these interactions and their clinical significance.

article.title: Beyond Mitochondrial Fission: Emerging Roles of Drp1 in Skeletal Muscle Physiology and Disease
article.authors: Kai Zou; Nicolas J. Berger; Zhenqi Zhou; Benjamin A. Kugler
article.abstract: Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is best recognized as the primary regulator of mitochondrial fission. However, emerging evidence indicates that Drp1 is a multifaceted regulator of skeletal muscle physiology whose functions extend well beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial fission. Recent studies have identified novel roles of Drp1 in regulating substrate utilization, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species signaling, respiratory complex assembly, and mitochondrial-to-nuclear signaling, including mechanisms independent of its canonical fission activity. Importantly, Drp1 regulation in skeletal muscle is highly context-dependent, as both excessive and insufficient Drp1 activity can disrupt skeletal muscle homeostasis. For example, excessive Drp1 activation and mitochondrial fragmentation are associated with insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and neuromuscular diseases, whereas severe or prolonged Drp1 deficiency impairs mitochondrial quality control, bioenergetics, induce muscle atrophy, and compromise the exercise training adaptations. Therefore, the biological consequences of Drp1 modulation are highly context dependent and influenced by the metabolic and physiological state of skeletal muscle. In this review, we summarize the molecular regulation and emerging functions of Drp1 in skeletal muscle, with particular emphasis on fission-independent mechanisms and Drp1 dysregulation in metabolic and neuromuscular diseases. We further discuss pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies for modulating Drp1 signaling and highlight emerging approaches for skeletal muscle-specific targeting. Collectively, current evidence supports a paradigm in which skeletal muscle Drp1 functions as a multifaceted regulator of mitochondrial and skeletal muscle homeostasis, highlighting the therapeutic potential of modulating Drp1 activity to optimize mitochondrial and muscle health across different physiological and pathological contexts.

article.title: Nanoformulations of Asiatic Acid and Asiatic Acid-enriched Fraction of Centella asiatica Preserve Mitochondrial and Dopaminergic Integrity in Cellular and MPTP-induced Mouse Models of Parkinson's Disease.
article.authors: Chinthu V Saji; Goutam Chandra; K P Mohanakumar; Rajesh A Shenoi
article.abstract: The therapeutic potential of asiatic acid (AA), a bioactive constituent of Centella asiatica, is limited by its poor aqueous solubility and low oral bioavailability. Nano-enabled phytomedicine offers a strategy to improve the formulation characteristics of AA through enhanced stability, cellular uptake, and sustained release. Here, we developed poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) nanoformulations containing AA (nf-AA) and an AA-enriched ethyl acetate fraction of C. asiatica (EXT; nf-EXT) and evaluated their neuroprotective effects in MPP+-treated differentiated SH-SY5Y cells and an MPTP-induced mouse model of PD. Mice were orally pretreated with AA (50 mg/kg), nf-AA (50 mg/kg), EXT (100 mg/kg), or nf-EXT (100 mg/kg) for five consecutive days before MPTP-administration. nf-AA and nf-EXT were prepared using double-emulsion solvent evaporation, and characterized for size, encapsulation efficiency, and drug release. In vitro neuroprotective effects were established in MPP⁺-treated, neuronally differentiated SH-SY5Y cells. In vivo validation was performed in C57/BL6 mice with MPTP-induced parkinsonism, through behavioural, neurochemical, and molecular assessments. The nanoformulations (~ 85-105 nm) exhibited high encapsulation efficiency (> 80%), sustained release up to 48 h and enhanced cellular uptake in normal physiological conditions. Compared with free phytochemicals, nf-AA and nf-EXT significantly reduced intracellular and mitochondrial oxidative stress, restored mitochondrial membrane potential and integrity, while preserving the levels of dopaminergic markers tyrosine hydroxylase (up to 3.9-fold) and dopamine transporter proteins (up to 4.8-fold) in MPP+-treated SH-SY5Y neurons. In vivo, pretreatment with nanoformulations improved motor behaviour, maintained striatal dopamine levels by normalizing its metabolism and restored TH, Nrf2 and PGC-1α expression by approximately three-fold compared with the MPTP-treated group, with nf-EXT showing greater recovery. Together, these findings demonstrate that PLGA nanoformulation improves the cellular delivery and neuroprotective efficacy of AA and EXT, supporting further investigation of this approach for PD.

article.title: Role of the ACTH-SF1/NR5A1-NRF2 axis in glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical cell death through mitochondrial ROS accumulation
article.authors: Naohiro Uchida; Namiko Kawamura; Hironobu Umakoshi; Maki Yokomoto-Umakoshi; Tazuru Fukumoto; Norifusa Iwahashi; Masamichi Fujita; Aya Fujimoto; Kaede Saito; Yuta Hiraike; Fumiya Takahashi; Takashi Baba; Masahide Seki; Yutaka Suzuki; Yoshihiro Ogawa
article.abstract: Abstract Exogenous glucocorticoids are widely used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, yet the prolonged administration often leads to adrenocortical atrophy and subsequent adrenal insufficiency. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical atrophy remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that adrenocortical alterations in dexamethasone (DEX)-treated mice are similar to those in human adrenocortical tissues adjacent to cortisol-producing adenoma. During DEX treatment, marked cell death occurs, being restricted to the adrenocortical zona fasciculata (ZF), as a result of reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction; the pathological changes are all attenuated by co-administration of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In DEX-treated mice, ACTH deficiency impairs nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-dependent redox homeostasis in ZF cells. Activation of the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway, a downstream signaling of ACTH stimulation, increases gene expression of steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1; NR5A1) in cultured adrenocortical cells in vitro, where it binds directly to the Nrf2 promoter and enhances its transcription, thereby promoting antioxidant gene expression to maintain redox homeostasis. This study highlights the role of the ACTH-SF1-NRF2 axis in glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical cell death through mitochondrial ROS accumulation, thereby providing a clue to a new therapeutic strategy to prevent or treat secondary adrenal insufficiency during glucocorticoid excess.

article.title: Hippocampal Glial Alterations Are Associated with Mitochondrial Changes and Reduced Glucocorticoid Receptor Density in Suicides
article.authors: Andrea Judith Vázquez-Hernández; Yali Escribano-Cadena; Julio César Morales-Medina; Amira Flores; Laura Alejandra Mendoza-Larios; Roberto Cuauhtémoc Mendoza-Morales; Humberto Nicolini; Hiram Tendilla-Beltrán; Fernando García-Dolores; Gonzalo Flores
article.abstract: Suicide is a major public health concern frequently associated with depressive disorders and neurobiological alterations within the hippocampus. This study investigated biomarkers related to neuroinflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and mitochondrial labeling in the CA1 region of the hippocampus of young and adult individuals of Mexican ancestry who died by suicide. Postmortem hippocampal CA1 samples were obtained from young and adult suicide cases and age-matched controls. Cellular markers of microglia (ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1, Iba1) and astrocytes (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP), neuronal density, glucocorticoid receptor expression, and mitochondrial labeling were evaluated and compared among groups. Suicide cases exhibited increased microglial and astrocyte cell density indicated by increased Iba1 and GFAP immunoreactivity in both age groups. In contrast, mitochondrial labeling and glucocorticoid receptor immunoreactivity were reduced in suicide cases, regardless of age. Additionally, a significant reduction in neuronal density was detected exclusively in young individuals who died by suicide. Together, these findings indicate age-independent alterations in glial immunoreactivity, mitochondrial labeling, and glucocorticoid receptor expression, alongside reduced neuronal density in the hippocampal CA1 region of younger suicide cases, supporting the involvement of neuroinflammation-related processes in suicide. Despite the limited sample size, these findings provide insight into potential neurobiological mechanisms underlying suicide and may contribute to the identification of biomarkers and therapeutic targets for individuals at risk.

article.title: Differentiating sulfite intoxication and mitochondrial-related encephalopathy in neonates: a review
article.authors: Andrea Gropman; Gregory M. Enns; Jerry Vockley
article.abstract: Abstract Introduction Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MoCD), isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency (ISOD), and primary mitochondrial disorders (MDs) are rare conditions that can cause life-threatening seizures and rapidly progressive encephalopathy in the neonatal period. Overlapping clinical presentations, biochemical abnormalities, and imaging findings can make differentiation challenging. Main body We highlight both the shared and distinct aspects of the pathogenesis, clinical features, and diagnostic evaluation of MoCD, ISOD, and MDs. All three can present with neonatal encephalopathy, intractable seizures, and hypotonia, due to impaired energy metabolism and mitochondrial function. However, their underlying molecular etiologies lead to differences in their metabolic signatures, neuroimaging patterns, and disease trajectories. Primary MDs result from over 400 pathogenic variants in nuclear or mitochondrial DNA that lead to respiratory chain deficiencies. In contrast, MoCD and ISOD disrupt sulfite oxidase activity through pathogenic variants in the molybdenum cofactor synthesis or sulfite oxidase genes, respectively. MoCD and ISOD typically manifest in the first days of life with severe seizures and rapid neurological decline, while MDs show a more variable age of onset, with cases presenting in the neonatal period associated with poor prognosis. Other frequent manifestations among these disorders include feeding difficulties and neuroimaging patterns. MoCD and ISOD predominantly affect the central nervous system and eyes, whereas MDs often involve multiple organ systems. A definitive diagnosis relies on a combination of neuroimaging, metabolic testing, and confirmatory genomic analysis. Conclusions Prompt diagnostic evaluation in suspected cases of MoCD, ISOD, or MDs is essential to guide early therapeutic interventions or supportive care, which are associated with prolonged patient survival and improvements in neurological outcomes.

article.title: Impact of SPAK Deficiency on Glomerular Injury and Mitochondrial Homeostasis in Adriamycin-Induced FSGS
article.authors: CHIEN-WEI HUANG; HSIN-HUNG CHEN; JIN-SHUEN CHEN
article.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is characterized by podocyte injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic remodeling. STE20/SPS1-related proline-alanine-rich kinase (SPAK), a downstream component of WNK signaling, regulates renal ion transport and has been implicated in inflammatory and stress responses. This study examined the impact of SPAK deficiency on renal injury and mitochondrial homeostasis in Adriamycin-induced FSGS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight-week-old male wild-type and global SPAK knockout C57BL/6 mice received a single intravenous injection of Adriamycin (18 mg/kg) or saline and were followed for four weeks. Renal function, proteinuria, glomerular histology, podocyte markers, mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and targeted metabolic profiles were assessed using biochemical assays, histology, immunohistochemistry, TUNEL staining, western blotting, quantitative PCR, and LC-MS-based metabolomics. RESULTS: Adriamycin induced proteinuria, serum creatinine elevation, glomerulosclerosis, and reduced nephrin and podocin expression in both wild-type and SPAK knockout mice. The severity of renal functional and histological injury was comparable between the two FSGS groups. SPAK deficiency was associated with baseline mitochondrial and apoptotic abnormalities, including reduced ATP5A1 expression and increased TUNEL-positive cells. In FSGS kidneys, SPAK deficiency did not restore ATP5A1, OPA1, PGC-1α, redox balance, or glycolytic remodeling, and SPAK-knockout FSGS mice exhibited greater apoptosis than wild-type FSGS mice. CONCLUSION: SPAK deficiency modifies mitochondrial and apoptotic responses but does not attenuate Adriamycin-induced glomerular injury. These findings suggest that SPAK contributes to glomerular homeostasis and that its role in kidney injury is context-dependent.

article.title: Clinical and genetic spectrum in a cohort of patients with suspected mitochondrial disease
article.authors: Doina Secu; Daniela Blanita; Natalia Usurelu; Calin Deleanu; Alina Nicolescu; Victoria Sacara
article.abstract: Introduction : Mitochondrial diseases (MDs) are a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders affecting oxidative phosphorylation, characterized by diverse neuromuscular and multisystemic manifestations, whose clinical variability and genetic complexity necessitate a comprehensive, multidisciplinary diagnostic approach. Aim : This study aims to explore the phenotypic and genotypic spectrum of patients with suspected MD, focusing on mitochondrial genome variations to improve diagnostic accuracy and support genetic counseling. Materials and methods : We analyzed 240 patients with a Nijmegen mitochondrial disease score (NMDS) ≥3, with 90 individuals undergoing comprehensive clinical, biochemical, neuroimaging, and genetic assessments. Descriptive statistics were applied to summarize clinical and biochemical data, while inferential analyses, including chi-square tests and regression models, were employed to explore genotype-phenotype associations. Results : The study delineated a multifaceted clinical spectrum, with neuromuscular dysfunction as the predominant hallmark, evidenced by a high prevalence of developmental delay (88.9%), hypotonia (77.8%), and exercise intolerance (63.3%). Patients with mitochondrial involvement displayed a significantly greater burden of neurological (seizures: 71.9% vs. 43.1%, p =0.009) and cardiac abnormalities (37.5% vs. 15.5%, p =0.018), underscoring their diagnostic relevance. Genetic analysis identified gene variants associated with the patients’ phenotypes in 35.6% of cases, with Complex I being the most frequently affected, emphasizing its pivotal role in mitochondrial dysfunction and disease severity. Conclusion : Our findings highlight the genetic and clinical heterogeneity of MDs, emphasizing the importance of integrating molecular, biochemical, and neuroimaging data to enhance early diagnosis and facilitate personalized treatment strategies.

article.title: Intranasal Mitochondria-Targeted Rosmarinic Acid Selenium Nanoparticles Restore Mitochondrial Function and Attenuate Dopaminergic Neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s Disease
article.authors: Gajanan Balaji Paul; Anjuman Nanda; Rakesh K. Singh; Awesh K. Yadav
article.abstract: Abstract Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and α-synuclein pathology, highlighting the need for mitochondria-targeted neuroprotective strategies. Here, we developed a mitochondria-targeted intranasal nanotherapeutic system comprising rosmarinic acid (RA)-loaded selenium nanoparticles (RASNPs) surface-functionalized with triphenylphosphonium (TPP)-conjugated chitosan (TCS-RASNPs) to enhance nose-to-brain delivery and improve mitochondrial function. TCS-RASNPs exhibited a spherical morphology, a uniform particle size distribution (140.13 ± 0.40 nm), a narrow polydispersity, and a positive surface charge (33.7 ± 0.75 mV), indicating good colloidal stability. Spectroscopic characterization confirmed successful RA loading and surface functionalization. Moreover, TCS-RASNPs enhanced antioxidant activity and sustained drug release compared with free RA and unmodified RASNPs. In neuronal cells, TCS-RASNPs significantly enhanced neuronal survival, reduced apoptosis, attenuated intracellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential under 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+)-induced neurotoxicity. Confocal microscopy further confirmed efficient mitochondrial localization of TCS-RASNPs. Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies demonstrated prolonged retention of RA and significantly higher brain RA levels following intranasal administration. In 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced Parkinsonian mice, TCS-RASNPs increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, reduced α-synuclein (SNCA) expression, and normalized oxidative stress biomarkers in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and striatum (STR) regions. Together, these findings demonstrate that TCS-RASNPs facilitate mitochondrial targeting and nose-to-brain delivery, thereby representing a promising nanotherapeutic approach for the management of PD.

article.title: Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α signaling pathway: Molecular mechanisms from mitochondrial function regulation to the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases
article.authors: Miaoyan Tang; Jing Miao
article.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial dysfunction is considered a central factor in the onset and progression of various neurodegenerative diseases. Sirtuin 1 is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-dependent deacetylase that senses changes in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide/reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide ratio and activates the transcriptional coactivator peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α through deacetylation. Activated peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α subsequently interacts with multiple transcription factors to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, mitochondrial dynamics, autophagy, energy metabolism, and antioxidant defense, thereby playing a critical role in maintaining mitochondrial functional homeostasis. Preclinical studies have shown that neurodegenerative diseases are frequently accompanied by downregulation of the expression or activity of key components of the Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α pathway, whereas activation of this pathway can ameliorate associated mitochondrial dysfunction and exert neuroprotective effects. This article systematically elucidates the pivotal role of the Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α pathway in neurodegenerative diseases from the perspectives of molecular structure, interaction mechanisms, and regulation of mitochondrial function, aiming to provide a theoretical foundation for the development of novel multi-target drugs and intervention strategies.

article.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
article.authors: Srividya Chandrasekhar; Rachael McMinimy; Andrew G. Manford; Eddie Wehri; Christine L. Gee; Caitlyn Miller; Baris Bingol; John Kuriyan; Julia Schaletzky; Michael Rapé
article.abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

article.title: Perturbation of Melatonin Signaling Modulates Respiration and Mitochondrial Gene Expression in Arabidopsis thaliana During Photooxidative Stress
article.authors: I. A. Bychkov; N. A. Shugaeva; A. G. Shugaev; N. V. Kudryakova; V. V. Kusnetsov
article.abstract: Abstract Melatonin (MT) is a critical regulator of mitochondria that affects bioenergetics, dynamics, and gene expression, and effectively protects them from oxidative stress. In this study we elucidated the role of the putative melatonin receptor CAND2/PMTR1 in mitochondrial respiration and the melatonin-mediated expression of mitochondrial genes under high light (HL) stress. Disruption of CAND2 and its associated partner GPA1 in Arabidopsis thaliana resulted in an increase in the respiration rate predominantly due to cytochrome respiration (CP), in contrast to wild type (WT) plants and 35SCAND2 overexpressing line in which an increase of alternative respiration (AP) prevails. MT treatment decreased AP activation under HL and reduced the overall leaf respiration rate, however, these effects were less pronounced in cand2 and gpa1 mutants. Increase in an AP capacity under HL stress positively correlated with an increase in transcript accumulation of the alternative oxidase (AOX) genes ( AOX1a , AOX1d ). At the same time, under stress conditions, the expression of the studied CP genes ( cob, cox1 ) and the ATPase gene ( atp6-1 ) was suppressed. MT treatment completely removed this inhibition, but only in WT and 35SCAND2 plants. Moreover, cand2 showed elevated steady state transcript levels of genes associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, suggesting an initial stress state of the mutant. The effects of exogenous melatonin on mitochondrial gene activity were mainly dependent on CAND2 receptor activity, although some genes were regulated by melatonin independently of CAND2, indicating the multiple mechanisms of melatonin perception in plants. Thus, disruption of MT signaling has a significant impact on mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial gene expression.

article.title: Huaier Attenuates Renal Injury in Type 2 Diabetic Nephropathy by Ameliorating Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Inhibiting Tubular Epithelial Cell Apoptosis
article.authors: Yucan Guan; Xiaoying Bai; Xianping Wei; Tao Ding; Ping Luo; Ping Nie
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a major microvascular complication of Type 2 diabetes, with renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs) apoptosis playing a pivotal role in its progression. The aqueous extract of Trametes robiniophila Murr. (Huaier) has shown renoprotective effects, but its specific molecular mechanisms in DN remain to be fully elucidated. Objective This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic effects of Huaier aqueous extract on DN and verify whether its anti‐apoptotic mechanism is mediated through the Wnt/β‐catenin pathway using the pathway activator SKL2001. Methods In vivo, KKAy Type 2 diabetic mice were treated with Huaier (5 g/kg/day) for 12 weeks to evaluate renal function and histopathology. In vitro, HK‐2 cells were treated with high glucose and palmitate (HG + PA) to induce injury. The Wnt/β‐catenin pathway activator SKL2001 was employed to determine if activating this pathway could abolish the protective effects of Huaier. Results Bioinformatics analysis indicates that the regulation of apoptosis is the primary mechanism by which Huaier improves DN. In vivo, Huaier reduced UACR and improved renal histopathology in KKAy mice. Consistently, TUNEL staining and molecular analysis confirmed that Huaier significantly suppressed RTECs apoptosis within the renal tissues. In vitro experiments demonstrated that Huaier significantly inhibited HG + PA‐induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and RTECs apoptosis. Notably, the administration of SKL2001 effectively reversed these protective effects, leading to increased β‐catenin expression and elevated apoptosis levels despite Huaier treatment. Conclusion Huaier aqueous extract mitigates RTECs apoptosis and renal injury in Type 2 diabetic nephropathy by suppressing the Wnt5a/β‐catenin signaling pathway.

article.title: Mitochondrial complex IV disruption is a detrimental pathology conferring ssusceptibility to alzheimer’s disease
article.authors: Jing Tian; Kun Jia; Yanting Chen; Tienju Wang; Lan Guo; Russell H. Swerdlow; Heng Du
article.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) is an integral part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial function. In contrast to the long-standing recognition of its dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the exact role of CIV deficit in the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disorder remains poorly defined. In this study, by incorporating clinical resources, mouse- and human-based models of AD risk, and a genetic approach to bypass defective CIV via the ectopic expression of alternative oxidase (AOX), we examined whether CIV deficits are a pathogenic driver of or a beneficial adaptation to AD-associated pathologies. Our results showed a clinicopathological association between neuronal CIV dysfunction and pathological characteristics of AD. Further experiments linked defective CIV to the development of mitochondrial dysfunction and synaptic loss in the tested mouse- and human-based models of AD risk. In addition, a reciprocal relationship between CIV dysfunction and amyloid pathology was determined. Lastly, a proteome-wide association study (PWAS) using genetic data from large-scale AD cohorts identified that downregulation of COX11, a crucial CIV assembly factor, confers susceptibility to AD risk. Collectively, our findings suggest that CIV dysfunction is a detrimental pathology contributing to AD-associated mitochondrial and neuronal damage. The dual role of CIV dysfunction, both as a consequence of and a contributor to amyloid toxicity in AD pathogenesis, further justifies the therapeutic potential of strategies targeting CIV deficits to diversify the tools for prevention and treatment of this neurodegenerative disorder.

article.title: Differential redox-mitochondrial adaptation to ultra-high-dose-rate irradiation in astrocytes and glioma cells
article.authors: Giulia Rosini; Elisa De Santis; Riccardo Nieri; Matteo Paolini; Filippo Rossi; Silverio Sbrana; Esther Ciarrocchi; Andrea Cavalieri; Fabiola Paiar; Fabio Di Martino; Eleonora Vannini; Mario Costa; Beatrice D’Orsi
article.abstract: Abstract FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) delivers radiation at ultra-high dose rates (UHDRs) and has been reported to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying the ‘FLASH effect’ remain incompletely defined. FLASH-RT has been associated with differential normal and tumor tissue responses in preclinical studies, although the early cellular processes induced under these conditions remain incompletely understood. Here, we compared FLASH-RT versus conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in murine glioma GL261 cells and primary healthy astrocytic cultures, focusing on redox dynamics, mitochondrial function, bioenergetics, and transcriptional stress programs. Using real-time kinetic assays, flow cytometry, Seahorse analysis, and gene expression profiling, we found that in healthy astrocytes FLASH-RT reduced acute ROS accumulation, limited cell death, and was associated with greater preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential and respiratory capacity compared with CONV-RT. FLASH-RT was also associated with sustained induction of cell-cycle checkpoint and senescence-associated transcripts. In GL261 cells, FLASH-RT produced a lower initial ROS peak followed by continued ROS accumulation over time and enhanced G2/M accumulation, together with persistent mitochondrial depolarization and respiratory suppression. Annexin V analysis at 8 Gy revealed comparable levels of Annexin V positivity between FLASH- and CONV-RT, whereas FLASH-treated cells showed greater G2/M accumulation and metabolic dysfunction, consistent with altered cell-cycle progression rather than enhanced Annexin V-defined cell death. Pharmacological modulation with DPQ, Calpeptin, Nec-1 and zVAD differentially affected mitochondrial bioenergetic parameters across irradiation modalities and cell types, providing functional evidence for the potential contribution of distinct stress- and cell-death-associated signaling pathways to radiation-induced metabolic dysfunction. Similar stress responses were also observed in human U87 glioblastoma cells, where FLASH-RT induced stronger ROS accumulation, greater Annexin V positivity, and alterations in NAD⁺ levels associated with mitochondrial respiratory impairment compared with CONV-RT. Collectively, these data indicate that FLASH-RT elicits cell-type-specific redox–mitochondrial responses associated with relative preservation of mitochondrial function in healthy astrocytes and prolonged metabolic stress and altered cell-cycle dynamics in glioma cells, highlighting distinct early adaptations to FLASH irradiation in astrocytic and glioma models.

article.title: Prognostic significance of SLC25A28 and its associations with mitochondrial metabolism and immune features in glioma
article.authors: Wangyang Yu; Yue Yang; Wenli Guo; Yafeng Wang; Jinsong Bai; Chen Li
article.abstract: Background SLC25A28 encodes the mitochondrial iron transporter mitoferrin-2, but its prognostic relevance and biological associations in glioma remain incompletely characterized. We investigated its clinical significance and relationships with metabolic, ferroptosis-related and immune features across glioma cohorts. Methods SLC25-family genes were screened in CGGA and TCGA, followed by survival analysis and meta-analysis across nine GlioVis cohorts. Clinical Cox models, prognostic scores and grade/IDH subgroups were evaluated. Metabolic, immune and curated ferroptosis-related signatures were examined using clinically adjusted models, and immune-cell and checkpoint analyses underwent false-discovery-rate correction. SLC25A28 expression was assessed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting. Results Lower SLC25A28 expression was associated with unfavorable clinicopathological features and shorter overall survival (pooled hazard ratio, 1.91; 95% confidence interval, 1.46–2.50; I² = 84.9%). Exploratory analyses supported survival associations in both IDH-mutant and IDH-wild-type subgroups of CGGA and TCGA, although findings within glioblastoma varied. Positive oxidative-phosphorylation associations persisted after grade/IDH adjustment in both pooled cohorts; within glioblastoma, this association was supported in CGGA but not TCGA. Ferroptosis-related transcriptional associations were also detected, with consistent all-glioma WikiPathways results across sensitivity analyses in TCGA but scoring-method and cohort dependence in regulator signatures. Immune-cell differences survived correction for 10 of 22 populations in CGGA and 16 of 22 in TCGA, and three checkpoint genes showed positive correlations in both cohorts. qRT-PCR and Western blotting confirmed lower SLC25A28 expression in U87 and U251 cells than in normal human astrocytes. Conclusions SLC25A28 is a candidate prognostic biomarker associated with mitochondrial metabolism, ferroptosis-related transcriptional features and immune features in glioma. Multi-cohort survival evidence and clinically adjusted molecular associations support further evaluation of its prognostic and biological relevance. Subtype-specific clinical validation and functional investigations will help define its clinical utility and biological role.

article.title: In Silico Evidence for Enterobactin-Facilitated Ferric Iron Import into Mitochondria via ATP Synthase Alpha Subunit Binding
article.authors: Abeg Dutta; Anutthaman Parthasarathy; Ganesh Pandian Namasivayam
article.abstract: Research on mitochondrial iron metabolism has largely focused on Fe(II), as it is relatively soluble and readily available under physiological conditions. By contrast, the role of Fe(III) remains less well understood. Its poor solubility and tendency to form potentially harmful ferric hydroxides mean that it must remain bound to suitable ligands or chaperones during transport. Canonically, iron is delivered to cells via transferrin (Tf), which binds the transferrin receptor (TfR1) for receptor-mediated endocytosis. Acidification of endosomes releases Fe(III), which is then reduced to Fe(II) by STEAP3 and transported into the cytosol by DMT1, forming a labile iron pool for mitochondrial use. However, the direct trafficking of Fe(III) into mitochondria has remained unexplored. Here, we propose a potential model for Fe(III) uptake into mitochondria through enterobactin, a bacterial siderophore known to influence host iron metabolism. Using in silico docking with AutoDock Vina and AlphaFold2-derived mitochondrial F-type ATP synthase structures, we observe that Fe(III)- enterobactin complexes yield docking scores comparable to Fe(II)-enterobactin complexes at the ATP synthase alpha subunit. In addition, enterobactin itself adopts compatible binding poses at the protein surface. These observations are consistent with a possible interaction framework but do not establish a dissociative mechanism for iron delivery within the mitochondrial matrix. These docking analyses support the structural plausibility of an enterobactin-associated ferric iron interaction with the mitochondrial ATP synthase alpha subunit. Although these findings do not establish a specific transport mechanism, they raise the possibility of an alternative route for mitochondrial iron trafficking. Further experimental work is needed to determine whether this pathway operates in cells and how it contributes to iron homeostasis. More broadly, the proposed model suggests a possible connection between microbial siderophores and mitochondrial iron handling, with potential physiological and pathological relevance.

article.title: A Damage‐Gated Small‐Molecule Chimera Selectively Enhances Mitophagy by Coupling Dysfunctional Mitochondria to Autophagy
article.authors: Ratislav M. Ozhiganov; Ekaterina А. Guseva; Alexander Yu. Rudenko; Konstantin G. Lyamzaev; Sofya Y. Sokolskaya; Julia A. Golubeva; Maria V. Belopolskaya; Nadezda V. Andrianova; Olga V. Fadeeva; Elena О. Morgun; Elena A. Tukhovskaya; Marina S. Kazakova; Vladimir M. Pavlov; Daria K. Yagoda; Elena I. Marusich; Rose‐Lys Zaranaina; Valeriya B. Vays; Irina M. Vangeli; Egor Y. Plotnikov; Maxim L. Lovat; Lora E. Bakeeva; Arkady N. Murashev; Vladimir I. Polshakov; Olga A. Dontsova; Peter V. Sergiev
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Mitophagy is a central mitochondrial quality‐control pathway, and its pharmacological activation is considered to be geroprotective. However, its small‐molecule activators act indirectly by perturbing metabolism or mitochondrial function, limiting selectivity and increasing toxicity. Here, we describe a chemical biology strategy for activating damage‐responsive mitophagy using bifunctional small molecules that couple mitochondrial recognition to the recruitment of the autophagic machinery. We designed and synthesized a focused library of chimeric molecules and identified MG‐1 as a lead compound. It had minimal effects on basal autophagy but markedly enhanced autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance under conditions of mitochondrial stress. Biochemical analyses, together with fluorescence and electron microscopy, showed that MG‐1 promotes lysosomal degradation of damaged mitochondria without acting as a direct mitochondrial uncoupler. MG‐1 was well tolerated across experimental systems and improved locomotor performance in a zebrafish model of MPTP‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings establish damage‐gated small‐molecule chimeras as a promising approach for selective control of mitochondrial quality.
