article.title: Urolithin A Attenuates Noise-induced Hearing Loss and Is Associated With Increased Cochlear Mitophagy Markers
article.authors: SUNG IL CHO; EU-RI JO; JEONGHYUN OH
article.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is a prevalent cause of sensorineural hearing impairment, in which mitochondrial dysfunction plays a key pathogenic role. Mitophagy is essential for maintaining mitochondrial quality control. This study investigated whether urolithin A (UA), a known mitophagy inducer, protects against NIHL. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight-week-old CBA/J mice were divided into three groups: control, noise + saline, and noise + UA (10 mg/kg). NIHL was induced by exposure to broadband noise (100 dB SPL, 2 h). UA was administered intraperitoneally before and after noise exposure. Auditory function was evaluated using auditory brainstem response (ABR). Mitophagy-associated markers and mitochondrial function were assessed by Western blotting, quantitative real-time PCR, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) integrity analysis, ATP measurements, and immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence. RESULTS: UA treatment significantly reduced auditory threshold shifts compared with the untreated group. The expression levels of mitophagy-related proteins and genes, including PINK1, Parkin, and BNIP3, were significantly increased in the UA-treated group. In addition, UA restored ATP levels following noise exposure. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analyses demonstrated enhanced formation of mitophagosomes and mitophagolysosomes in the cochlea, including the organ of Corti and the spiral ganglion, in the UA-treated group. CONCLUSION: UA attenuates NIHL by enhancing mitophagy-associated markers and preserving mitochondrial function in the cochlea. These findings suggest that pharmacological activation of mitophagy may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for NIHL.

article.title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia Aggravates the Pyroptosis of Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells Through Regulating Mitophagy‐Mediated NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation
article.authors: Yuwei Zhang; Hongyan Tai
article.venue: Journal of Biochemical and Molecular Toxicology
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)‐induced renal injury is triggered by chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Our previous article has revealed that CIH triggers the pyroptosis of renal tubular epithelial cells through the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, whereas the mechanism by which CIH activates NLRP3 inflammasome remains elusive. Rats and HK‐2 cells were exposed to CIH to establish CIH models. Histopathological staining, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine (Scr) levels were examined to assess renal injury. Western blot and immunofluorescence assay were used to assess proteins related to NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptosis and mitophagy. Mitochondrial membrane potential and production of ROS and ATP were examined to evaluate mitochondrial function. CCK‐8, LDH release and ELISA assays were performed to assess cell injury and inflammation. Mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi‐1) was applied for a rescue assay. CIH induced renal injury and suppressed mitophagy in vivo, evidenced by worsening pathological features, elevated Scr and BUN levels, reduced colocalization of Tom20 with LC3B, and downregulated expression of LC3‐II/I ratio, Atg5, PINK1 and Parkin. PINK1 overexpression restored mitophagy by enhancing colocalization of mitochondria with LC3B, upregulating LC3‐II/I ratio and Atg5, and restored mitochondrial function of CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells through enhancing mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing ROS production and increasing ATP content. PINK1 overexpression alleviated cell viability, inflammation and NLRP3 inflammasome‐mediated pyroptosis in CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells, which were partly abolished by Mdivi‐1. PINK1 attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome‐mediated pyroptosis in CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells partially through restoring mitophagy and mitochondrial function, providing potential therapeutic strategies for OSA‐related kidney diseases.

article.title: Universal protein immobilization and digestion reactor facilitates deep quantitative proteomic analysis of single Caenorhabditis elegans individuals
article.authors: Wenjia Zhang; Yingyue Wang; Jiayu Tang; Lingxiao Weng; Guoquan Yan; Mingxia Gao; Xiangmin Zhang
article.abstract: Abstract Single-organism proteomics can reveal heterogeneity masked by population-level measurements, but deep profiling of individual Caenorhabditis elegans remains challenging because of low protein input, inefficient extraction through the collagen-rich cuticle, and lengthy sample processing. Herein, we present SPIDR-C (single-organism protein immobilization and digestion reactor for C. elegans), a streamlined workflow enabling deep single-worm proteomics. SPIDR-C seamlessly integrates worm disruption, strong surfactant-assisted extraction, covalent protein immobilization, in-reactor sample cleanup, and rapid enzymatic digestion in a single-tube, transfer-free format. Built from commercially available insert tubes and requiring neither microfluidic devices nor custom instrumentation, the workflow is low-cost, easy to operate, and compatible with standard liquid chromatography (LC) autosamplers, allowing parallel batch processing of multiple samples within 2 h. By coupling aggressive extraction with LC−MS/MS-compatible cleanup, it enabled identification of more than 7100 proteins from a single adult worm, representing one of the deepest single-worm proteomes reported to date. Across eight single-worm-equivalent technical replicates, the median protein-abundance CV was 13.34%, with pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients above 0.977. We applied SPIDR-C to a high-glucose and high-fat (HGHF) model as an exploratory demonstration of its analytical utility, where single-worm proteomics captured HGHF-associated proteome alterations and individual-level heterogeneity under the same dietary challenge. Proteome profiling further pointed to two candidate HGHF-associated response patterns: one marked by higher abundance of ER proteostasis-related proteins and the other characterized by stronger lipid- and membrane-associated remodeling. Thus, SPIDR-C provides a practical strategy for deep single-organism proteomics and facilitates the investigation of molecular heterogeneity in complex low-input biological samples.

article.title: Photocatalytic Conversion of Volatile Fatty Acids into H₂ and C 1 –C 6 Alkanes over Cu 2 O/BiPO 4 p-n Heterojunctions: Insights into Radical Intermediate Coupling
article.authors: Qingtao Chen; Xiangdong Shi; Xianghai Rao; Mingyang Zhu; Xiaoyun Qin; Dan Luo; Fenghua Chen
article.abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic conversion of biomass-derived volatile fatty acids (VFAs) into H 2 and hydrocarbons remains challenging, largely because the product distribution is governed by the selective coupling of alkyl radical intermediates generated via the photo-Kolbe reaction. Herein, we synthesized a series of Cu 2 O/BiPO 4 p-n heterojunction composites with varying Cu 2 O loadings (1–15 wt%) and evaluated their performance for converting acetic (HAc), propionic (HPr), and butyric acid (HBu) into H 2 and C 1 –C 6 alkanes under UV irradiation. The p-n heterojunction is proposed to facilitate charge separation and to influence the oxidative power of photogenerated holes, thereby affecting the decarboxylation of carboxylates to generate alkyl radical intermediates (·CH 3 , ·CH 2 CH 3 , ·CH 2 CH 2 CH 3 ), whose subsequent coupling pathways dictate the product selectivity. The optimized CBP-9 (9 wt% Cu 2 O) delivered a 2.49-fold higher total H 2 /alkane yield than pristine BiPO 4 from HAc, with 85.71% total organic carbon removal within 4 h. For HPr and HBu, the yields of ethane/butane and methane/propane were enhanced by 2.27- and 1.67-fold, respectively. Mechanistic studies based on photoluminescence, transient photocurrent, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy indicate that the p-n junction promotes spatial charge separation and improves stability. The catalyst retained > 85% of its initial activity after five cycles. This work provides insights into radical intermediate coupling in the photocatalytic conversion of VFAs over Cu 2 O/BiPO 4 heterojunctions, demonstrating the potential for directly converting wet biomass residues into H 2 -enriched fuel gases.

article.title: Comparative Proteomic Analysis of Hypoxic Adaptation Reveals Conserved and Species-Specific Responses in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium bovis
article.authors: María Mercedes Bigi; Magdalena Portela; Laura Inés Klepp; Rosana Valeria Rocha; Elizabeth Andrea García; Crisitina Lourdes Vazquez; Federico Carlos Blanco; Rosario Duran; Fabiana Bigi
article.abstract: Abstract Tuberculosis, caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, remains a major global health concern. While M. tuberculosis and M. bovis share similar pathogenic mechanisms, important differences in disease progression and adaptive responses have been observed. Hypoxia is a critical stressor during latent infection, however, the comparative molecular adaptations of these two species under oxygen-limited conditions remain incompletely understood. In this study, we used the Wayne gradual oxygen depletion model to investigate the cellular proteomes of the reference strains M. bovis AF2122/97 and M. tuberculosis H37Rv under hypoxic and aerobic conditions. Our analysis revealed that pathways involved in acyl-CoA generation constitute a conserved response to hypoxia in both species. Proteins associated with lipid metabolism and stress responses, particularly members of the DosRST regulon, emerged as hallmarks of hypoxic adaptation in both strains. Notably, a greater number of DosRST- and EHR-regulated proteins showed an increase in abundance in M. bovis than in M. tuberculosis . Lipid metabolism and cell envelope remodeling were central features of the hypoxic response in both species, consistent with observed changes in PDIM A and PDIM B levels. Both species also showed accumulation of proteins involved in molybdenum metabolism, whereas remodeling of nitrogen metabolism was a prominent feature specific to the M. bovis response. These findings support the notion that pathogenic mycobacteria rely on lipid utilization to maintain energy homeostasis and redox balance under oxygen-limited conditions, and that cell envelope remodeling may contribute to long-term survival. The identified species-specific differences in metabolic adaptation and PDIM modulation provide new insights into the distinct physiological responses of M. tuberculosis and M. bovis during hypoxic stress.

article.title: A Small Molecule Drug, Formoterol Fumarate, Potently Reverses Anemia
article.authors: Laurie Glimcher; Shrestha Ghosh; Shengze Xu; Merve Akyol; Shaokun An; Ha Eun Choi; Mileena Nguyen; Jae-Won Cho; Edward Doherty; Gregory Petsko; Martin Hemberg
article.abstract: Abstract Anemia is a major societal health risk that greatly lowers quality of life in roughly a quarter of the world population1. However, current treatments are effective in only a subset of patients with hematological malignancies and disorders2,3. We have identified dynamic surface expression of β2-adrenoceptors in erythroid progenitors at various stages of differentiation. Here, we report that formoterol fumarate (FF), a highly selective β2-adrenoceptor agonist, promotes erythroid differentiation in the bone marrow and spleen to enhance hemoglobin and hematocrit levels in peripheral blood, thereby reversing anemia. FF treatment at very low doses via multiple routes of administration confers striking survival benefits in lethal hemolytic anemia. FF also boosts red blood cells in mouse models of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)/acute myeloid leukemia, chronic kidney disease (CKD), hemolytic stress-induced anemia, and in naïve mice at steady state. Furthermore, FF augments erythropoiesis in human stem cells derived from bone marrow aspirates of MDS patients. Mechanistically, FF promotes erythropoiesis partly via HIF-1α and associated hypoxia-responsive genes along with induction of mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby suggesting that the therapeutic relevance of FF may reflect its specific ability to induce coordinated HIF-1α and mitochondrial programs in addition to general β₂ activation. Importantly, we have developed a unique capsule formulation of FF that markedly reverses anemia when dosed orally in mice. Our study uncovers FF-driven stimulation of β2-adrenenoceptors as a new therapeutic strategy for treatment of anemia associated with MDS, CKD and hemolytic stress.

article.title: Heterogenous Aging of Local Tissues Is a Major Contributor to the Age-Related Decline in Glycosaminoglycans and Fracture Toughness of Cortical Bone
article.authors: Savannah Heath; Ashley Ridoutt; Michael Reyes; Keying Ye; Jean X. Jiang; Xiaodu Wang
article.abstract: Abstract Bone fragility fractures increase with age as bone toughness declines, potentially in part due to the loss of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). However, the mechanisms linking GAG depletion to bone quality remain unclear, partly due to the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of bone remodeling during aging. During bone remodeling, newly formed secondary osteons and older interstitial tissue are randomly distributed throughout the bone, each with distinct material properties. This microstructural heterogeneity adds complexity to studying age-related changes in bone quality that cannot be explained by donor age alone. This study hypothesized that the age-related decline in bulk bone fracture toughness originates from changes in local tissue GAGs with tissue aging and is amplified by an increasing proportion of old tissue relative to new tissue with advancing donor age. To test this, local tissues in human cortical bone samples across different ages and sexes were analyzed using Raman spectroscopy, DMMB, Alcian blue, histomorphometry, microcompression, and fracture toughness testing. The results showed that compositional and mechanical properties of local tissues changed significantly with tissue age, but not with donor age or sex. The volume fraction of old tissue as well as GAG heterogeneity (FWHM) increased significantly with donor age. Furthermore, age-related changes in bulk bone GAG content were strongly correlated with bone fracture toughness. These findings suggest that age-related loss of bone quality arises from the combined effects of tissue age-dependent deterioration in local properties and donor age–dependent accumulation of older tissue.

article.title: Intervention-Type-Specific Effects on Healthy Aging of Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
article.authors: Aeyoung Cho; Bomgyeol Kim; Gyeoul Jeong; Harim Lee; Kyung Hee Lee
article.abstract: Abstract Background and Objectives Healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment requires preserving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning to sustain their independence and quality of life. However, existing interventions vary in design, delivery format, and composition, and evidence regarding their effectiveness across these three core domains remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify the most effective intervention types for specific domains of healthy aging. Research Design and Methods Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from October 2015 to June 2026. Randomized controlled trials reporting at least two outcomes—among physical capability, cognitive function, or psychosocial well-being—were reviewed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool. A dependency-aware multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with trial-clustered robust inference was conducted in R, supplemented by moderator tests, prediction intervals, sensitivity analyses, reporting-bias assessments, and GRADE evaluations. Results Multicomponent interventions were associated with beneficial effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, whereas group-based interventions showed beneficial effects across all three domains and a significantly greater effect on cognitive function than individually delivered interventions. Despite substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses. Discussion and Implications The observed advantages of group-based delivery, particularly for cognitive function, and multicomponent approaches for cognitive and psychosocial outcomes highlight the domain-specific nature of intervention effects. These findings support tailoring intervention delivery and component configuration to the targeted domain rather than applying a uniform approach to healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment.

article.title: Oral Health in an Aging Population: Emerging Challenges for Geriatric Dentistry
article.authors: Warda Abubakar; Laiba Rehmat
article.venue: Journal of Oral Health and Dental Therapeutics
article.abstract: Dental care systems all over the globe are changing as the population is getting older. Retention of natural teeth is greater for older people than for previous generations; however, they are also experiencing an increasing burden of decayed teeth at the root, periodontal disease, problems with oral mucous membranes and dry mouth, and are more likely to have polypharmacy and multimorbidity. This is further complicated by frailty, cognitive impairment, and functional dependence. Oral health is now being associated with systemic impacts such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and quality of life. However, dental care is still not well linked to medical and long-term care, and very few dental practitioners have formal geriatric training. In this editorial, the primary challenges identified in geriatric dentistry include oral changes due to medications, periodontal-systemic interactions, tooth loss, access to care, and shortage of dental professionals. It outlines future research such as the use of non-invasive methods, teledentistry, interprofessional collaboration, and prevention policy change.

article.title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
article.authors: Samuel D Anderson; Jordan Jomsky; Nikhil N Chaudhari; Nahian F Chowdhury; Xiaoyu Rayne Zheng; Andrei Irimia; Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
article.abstract: Estimating brain age (BA) from T1-weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

article.title: Reversing amorphous aging associated with resistance drift in phase-change memory via atomistic rejuvenation
article.authors: Kaiqi Li; Xuanguang Zhang; Jian Zhou; Bin Liu; Zhimei Sun
article.abstract: Resistance drift in the amorphous RESET state limits phase-change memory (PCM) for multilevel storage and neuromorphic computing. Most mitigation strategies slow the drift rather than reverse the structural aging that develops after programming. Here, we use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with a Y–Sb–Te neuroevolution potential to examine atomistic rejuvenation in Sb–Te-based glasses. Aging and rejuvenation are quantified using potential energy, radial distribution functions, global Steinhardt order parameters, ring statistics, and homopolar bonding, which track short-range relaxation, topological ordering, and bond rearrangement. Binary Sb–Te models first establish competing thermal pathways: low-temperature annealing promotes energetic relaxation and ordering, whereas high-temperature reheating followed by requenching restores higher-energy, less-aged amorphous states while avoiding prolonged residence in the crystallization-prone window. In Y-doped Sb2Te3, Y reduces energetic relaxation, delays four-membered-ring ordering, and reduces bonding fluctuations while preserving reversible rejuvenation. Device-scale simulations further show that rejuvenation pulses reset key aging-sensitive descriptors in a 6.5 × 105-atom mushroom-cell PCM model. These results demonstrate that atomistic rejuvenation can reverse aging-sensitive structural features in Sb–Te-based PCM glasses, providing a structural route toward mitigating resistance drift.

article.title: Neurovascular-immune-clearance remodeling in brain aging
article.authors: Yuxin Liu; Ronghao Yang; Haocai Chang
article.abstract: Brain aging involves concurrent changes in cerebral vessels, immune regulation, and waste clearance, yet these processes are often studied separately. This fragmented approach limits understanding of how dysfunction in one system influences the others and contributes to age-related neurological disorders. This review summarizes current evidence on the neurovascular-immune-clearance axis, focusing on neurovascular unit deterioration, impaired glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic transport, neuroimmune remodeling, and the cell-specific mechanisms that connect these processes. We further compare their shared and disease-dependent roles in Alzheimer’s disease, vascular cognitive impairment, and late-life depression. Available imaging, fluid, proteomic, and epigenetic biomarkers are evaluated for their ability to measure different components of this axis, and emerging interventions are organized according to their predominant effects on vascular support, clearance function, immune signaling, and cellular senescence. Current evidence indicates that brain aging is characterized by interacting and partially compensable functional bottlenecks rather than a single linear pathological pathway. Integrating these mechanisms provides a framework for interpreting heterogeneous aging phenotypes, selecting complementary biomarkers, and developing mechanism-guided interventions. Future progress will depend on longitudinal human validation and direct demonstration that target engagement produces durable neurological benefit.

article.title: Beyond age prediction: a task-oriented framework for evaluating molecular aging clocks.
article.authors: Halimureti Simayijiang; Pei Ye; Liuli Zhang; Jiacheng Wu; Zhuo Li; Ying Long
article.abstract: Biological age estimation is increasingly used in aging research, but evaluation often relies too heavily on mean absolute error (MAE) against chronological age. We conducted a narrative review of major molecular aging clocks and propose an operational framework that links clock selection to the intended task. Applications are organized into four tasks: chronological-age estimation, age-independent deviation, future disease or mortality risk, and longitudinal monitoring of aging pace or intervention response. For each task, the framework specifies the target construct, output, preprocessing and confounding checks, validation metrics, and interpretation limits. A complementary four-layer model distinguishes relatively stable molecular measures, pace-of-aging measures, dynamic functional markers, and organ-specific vulnerability. Published examples illustrate why no single metric is sufficient: low age-prediction error does not establish clinical relevance, and strong risk association does not establish responsiveness to intervention. Aging clocks should therefore be evaluated as task-bound measurement tools, with explicit attention to calibration, discrimination, reliability, transportability, uncertainty, and incremental value. This framework is intended to support transparent model selection, reporting, and interpretation rather than designate a universally superior clock.

article.title: Magnesium in Skin Aging, Wound Healing, and Some Specific Dermatologic Disorders: A Narrative Review on Biological Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and Therapeutic Perspectives
article.authors: Ligia J. Dominguez; Valentina Caputo; Francesco Saverio Ragusa; Nicola Veronese; José Luis Pérez-Albela; Vania Flora Vásquez-López; Santiago Rodas-Regalado; Mario Barbagallo
article.abstract: Magnesium is the second most abundant intracellular cation and an essential cofactor for more than 600 enzymatic reactions involved in cellular metabolism, energy production, nucleic acid synthesis, protein translation, and immune regulation. Emerging experimental evidence suggests that magnesium contributes to several processes involved in skin homeostasis, including keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, epidermal barrier integrity, collagen synthesis, oxidative balance, and innate and adaptive immune responses. Magnesium deficiency is common but often underrecognized, particularly among persons at higher risk including older adults and persons with gastrointestinal disorders, type 2 diabetes, chronic alcohol use, or certain medication exposures. This deficiency has been implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of several dermatologic diseases through mechanisms involving chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, impaired wound repair, endothelial dysfunction, and immune dysregulation. This review summarizes the current understanding of magnesium biology in skin physiology and critically examines experimental and clinical evidence linking altered magnesium status to inflammatory, autoimmune, and degenerative skin disorders, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne vulgaris, rosacea, chronic urticaria, wound healing disorders, diabetic foot ulcers, alopecia, and skin aging. The review also discusses the therapeutic potential of oral and topical magnesium formulations, including their proposed mechanisms of action, clinical efficacy, safety profile, and current limitations of the available evidence. Although preclinical studies support a role for magnesium in skin health, clinical evidence remains limited by heterogeneous study designs and a lack of high-quality randomized trials. Future research should prioritize standardized biomarkers and robust clinical studies to clarify the therapeutic potential of magnesium and identify patients most likely to benefit from magnesium-based interventions in dermatologic disorders.

article.title: Lactobacillus johnsonii attenuates ovarian aging by remodeling the gut–ovary axis
article.authors: Jiamin He; Qiwen Wang; Luyi Chen; Yadong Qi; Dingjiacheng Jia; Jilei Xu; Qingyi Wang; Yao Jiang; Jian Zhou; Yong Sun; Ruochen Yan; Lan Wang; Tongyao Hou; Zheng Kuang; Min Jin; Liangjing Wang; Shujie Chen
article.abstract: Abstract Reproductive aging, accompanied by abnormal levels of sex hormones, affects overall health and poses a particular threat to women. Gut microbiota plays a key role in regulating host aging and is promising for alleviating reproductive aging. Here, we found that gut commensal Lactobacillus johnsonii ( L. johnsonii ) declined in accordance with ovarian failure in female aging mice. Restoring L. johnsonii partially rescued hormone levels in age‐ or chemically‐ induced ovarian decline murine models, thereby reversing cognitive decline and extending lifespan. Indole‐3‐propionic acid (IPA), the bioactive metabolite of L. johnsonii , promoted granulosa cell proliferation to upregulate sex‐steroid output by activating the AhR‐YAP signaling pathway. L. johnsonii ‐derived LdhA was identified as the essential enzyme for indole‐3‐lactic acid (ILA) biosynthesis, thereby increasing downstream IPA. In addition, significant positive correlations were observed between ovarian function and fecal L. johnsonii , as well as IPA levels. These findings establish L. johnsonii as a promising probiotic strategy for alleviating ovarian aging through microbiota‐derived metabolite signaling along the gut–ovary axis.

article.title: Lipids at the meningeal-tumor interface: aging, anatomical niches, and meningioma biology
article.authors: Michele Cerasuolo; Nicholas Giulio Raccagni; Simone Laguardia; Gary Antonio Barahona Rodriguez
article.abstract: Meningiomas exhibit substantial molecular, anatomical, and microenvironmental heterogeneity, yet the spatial organization of their lipid biology remains poorly understood. Emerging lipidomic studies demonstrate extensive remodeling of membrane, signaling, and mitochondrial lipid classes, with profiles varying according to molecular genotype, histopathological grade, and potentially patient characteristics. In parallel, developmental, single-cell, and spatial studies have revealed the meninges and meningiomas as regionally organized systems comprising distinct stromal, vascular, immune, and neoplastic populations. Here, we integrate these lines of evidence and propose the aging meningeal lipid niche as an anatomically grounded framework for understanding lipid biology across the meningioma–meningeal interface. We examine the dural attachment and tumor–bone interface, perivascular niche, immune-enriched regions, tumor core, and tumor–brain boundary as candidate metabolic compartments in which cellular composition, vascular access, extracellular architecture, and inflammatory signaling may shape local lipid states. We further consider how aging may modify these environments through remodeling of the meningeal extracellular matrix, lymphatic function, immune composition, and lipid homeostasis, while distinguishing direct evidence in meningioma from mechanistic inference. A central limitation of current studies is their reliance on bulk tissue, which precludes confident attribution of lipid signals to specific anatomical and cellular sources. We therefore outline a spatially resolved strategy integrating anatomically registered sampling with mass spectrometry imaging, histopathology, molecular classification, and single-cell or spatial transcriptomic approaches. This framework provides testable hypotheses to determine whether meningioma lipid states reflect tumor-intrinsic programs, anatomically defined microenvironments, aging-associated remodeling, or interactions among these determinants, and how these states relate to invasion, recurrence, edema, and treatment resistance.

article.title: JWA as a context-dependent redox regulatory hub linking stress responses with aging hallmarks and age-related diseases
article.authors: Yaning Wu; Ning Zhang; Hui Sun; Heng Fang; Guangli Yan; Xijun Wang
article.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
article.abstract: JWA (also known as ARL6IP5) is an evolutionarily conserved multifunctional protein increasingly implicated in redox homeostasis and cellular stress adaptation. Its functions intersect with redox homeostasis through signaling pathways including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), and adenosine 5′-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), as well as interactions with key proteins such as X-ray repair cross-complementing 1 (XRCC1), nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4), and excitatory amino acid carrier 1 (EAAC1) involved in oxidative-stress adaptation. As a redox-responsive regulatory protein and mediator, JWA exhibits context-dependent roles in disease pathogenesis: in oncology, it acts as a tumor suppressor by mitigating oxidative stress-induced DNA damage and reversing chemoresistance, with reduced expression correlating with poor prognosis in gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and other malignancies; in neurobiology, it exerts neuroprotective effects through suppression of ferroptosis, regulation of glutamate homeostasis, and proteostasis-related mechanisms, with the strength and direction of redox involvement varying across experimental contexts; beyond these fields, JWA regulates intestinal barrier integrity, radiation response, and adaptation to environmental oxidants (Cd, B [a]P, H 2 O 2 ), while specific polymorphisms influence redox-related disease susceptibility. As a potential aging-associated regulator, accumulating evidence suggests that JWA expression or activity may change during aging, although age-, tissue-, and disease-specific patterns remain incompletely defined. Current evidence links JWA dysregulation to oxidative stress and tissue dysfunction in several age-associated diseases, whereas its direct roles in the aging process remain insufficiently established. This review, centered on redox regulation as the unifying framework, comprehensively synthesizes current knowledge on JWA’s multifunctional roles across disciplines, highlights its potential as a candidate redox-related biomarker and experimental therapeutic target, and proposes an evidence-based research framework for future investigation and translation. By emphasizing JWA’s role in maintaining redox balance and its regulatory function in aging process and age-related diseases, we provide novel insights into its significance in future clinical-development considerations and offer directions for targeting redox dysregulation in refractory diseases.

article.title: Impact of UV Aging and Casein Corona Formation on the Physicochemical Properties and Size-Dependent Cytotoxicity of Polystyrene Micro- and Nanoplastics
article.authors: Emine Merve Canga; Raphaela O. G. Ferreira; Aoife Gowen; Jun-Li Xu
article.abstract: Abstract Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) undergo aging and interact with biomolecules before human ingestion, yet their combined effect on cytotoxicity remains poorly understood. This study investigated how UV-C aging and casein (CN) corona formation altered the physicochemical properties and cytotoxicity of polystyrene (PS) particles across three sizes (50 nm, 1 μm, and 90 μm). Physicochemical characterization revealed distinct responses across the three nominal particle sizes. Following UV aging, the mean hydrodynamic diameter of 50 nm PS nanoparticles (NPs) increased from 51 to 419 nm, while its carbonyl index (CI) increased approximately 6-fold. The CI of 1 μm PS significantly increased from 0.084 to 0.477, and its mean hydrodynamic diameter decreased by 10%. UV aging did not significantly change the mean diameter or CI of 90 μm PS. CN corona formation shifted particle ζ-potentials toward less negative values, particularly for UV-aged PS particles. In cytotoxicity assays (carried out over 48 h, with MNP concentration 100 μg/mL), 50 nm PS induced the strongest reduction in Caco-2 metabolic activity (32–43% loss) across all treatments, compared with 14–29% for the larger-particle groups. Transmission electron microscopy confirmed endosomal internalization of all 50 nm NPs. No significant membrane damage or oxidative stress was observed, suggesting a sublethal, nonlytic mechanism. These findings highlight that evaluating MNP surface properties, integrating photooxidative aging and protein interactions, is critical for assessing their biological responses.

article.title: Neuronal receptor remodeling in the aging periosteum: From single-cell atlases to regenerative targets
article.authors: Ziyu Liu; Jianguo Qi; Yong Liu; Hongshang Chu
article.abstract: Abstract The periosteum is the most densely innervated compartment of the skeleton and harbors periosteal stem cells expressing a broad repertoire of neuronal receptors traditionally associated with the nervous system. This narrative review aimed to map the neuronal receptor landscape of the periosteum and its age-dependent remodeling, and to evaluate the therapeutic implications of these receptors for age-related skeletal disorders. Literature was identified using a structured, PRISMA-informed search strategy across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from database inception. Eligible studies addressed neuronal receptor expression or signaling in periosteal tissue, periosteal stem and progenitor cells, or bone. Additionally, an exploratory reanalysis of the publicly available GSE297256 single-cell transcriptomic dataset was performed to contextualize the literature synthesis; no unpublished data were included. The literature synthesis delineated seven major neuronal receptor families in periosteal homeostasis: semaphorin-neuropilin, neurotrophin-Trk, Slit-Robo, adrenergic, cannabinoid, purinergic, and sensory neuropeptide systems. Restricting the analysis to bona fide neuronal receptors, 29 receptor genes were actively transcribed in periosteal stem cells, with neuropilin 2 ( Nrp2 ) ranking highest by a composite score integrating expression magnitude, detection frequency, and cell-type specificity. In exploratory cell-level analysis, Nrp2 expression showed a progressive age-associated increase from young (log1p mean 1.35) to middle-aged (1.85) to old (2.70) mice, concomitant with a decline of Postn-expressing Osteo-X progenitors and activation of stress-response genes ( Mt1 , Mt2 , Gadd45b , and Cebpd ), and was associated with dysregulation of the axon guidance ligand Slit2, downregulation of osteocalcin-associated genes ( Bglap and Bglap2 ), and predicted upstream regulation by the vitamin D receptor, implicating a vitamin D receptor- Nrp2 axis in periosteal aging. Age-related periosteal dysfunction, including cambium layer thinning, progenitor decline, and impaired progenitor-immune crosstalk, paralleled this receptor dysregulation. Neuronal receptor modulation, including Bdnf -TrkB, Sema3a-Nrp1 , and Nrp2 -targeted strategies, emerges as a promising multimodal approach for skeletal regeneration and aging intervention, warranting functional and clinical validation.

article.title: Oocyte-specific OMC1 is required for maintaining chromosome cohesion through reproductive life
article.authors: Sakie Iisaka; Shuhei Yoshida; Ryuki Shimada; Tappei Mishina; Sayoko Fujimura; Manami Koshiguchi; Ryuichi Kimura; Shinya Oki; Kimi Araki; Tomoya S. Kitajima; Kei-ichiro Ishiguro
article.abstract: Nature Aging, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43587-026-01245-5 Mammalian oocytes undergo prolonged meiotic arrest during which sister chromatids are linked by cohesin complexes. Cohesion deterioration during aging results in aneuploidy. Here, Iisaka, Yoshida et al. identify OMC1 as an oocyte-specific protein that preserves chromosome cohesion throughout reproductive life. The loss of OMC1 accelerates age-related aneuploidy.

article.title: PAPEL DA ENFERMAGEM NA PROMOÇÃO DO ENVELHECIMENTO SAUDÁVEL: REVISÃO DE LITERATURA THE ROLE OF NURSING IN PROMOTING HEALTHY AGING: A LITERATURE REVIEW PAPEL DE LA ENFERMERÍA EN LA PROMOCIÓN DEL ENVEJECIMIENTO SALUDABLE: REVISIÓN DE LA LITERATURA
article.authors: Ana Carla Pereira Galvão; Ana Paula Mascarenhas Figueredo; Williany Kelly Teixeira Alves; Kiria Vaz da Silva Hamerski
article.abstract: O envelhecimento populacional tem ampliado a necessidade de ações de saúde voltadas à promoção de um envelhecimento saudável e à manutenção da qualidade de vida da pessoa idosa. Este estudo teve como objetivo descrever o papel da enfermagem na promoção do envelhecimento saudável, considerando ações de cuidado, prevenção de doenças e promoção da qualidade de vida do idoso. Trata-se de uma revisão de literatura, de caráter descritivo, realizada a partir da análise de estudos científicos relacionados à atuação da enfermagem no cuidado à pessoa idosa. Os resultados evidenciaram que a enfermagem desempenha papel fundamental no cuidado integral e humanizado, na prevenção de doenças e agravos, na educação em saúde e no acompanhamento das condições de saúde. Destacou-se ainda a importância das intervenções de enfermagem para o fortalecimento da autonomia, independência, participação e qualidade de vida da pessoa idosa. Conclui-se que a atuação da enfermagem contribui para um envelhecimento mais ativo, autônomo e saudável, especialmente por meio de ações de promoção da saúde, prevenção de agravos e cuidado integral.

article.title: Biological functions and emerging interplay of FGF21 and GDF15 in metabolic diseases and aging
article.authors: Laura Salmón-Gómez; Susanne Keipert; Victoria Catalán; Amaia Rodríguez; Sara Becerril; Gema Frühbeck; Javier Gómez-Ambrosi
article.abstract: Abstract Metabolic diseases and age-related disorders represent a major global health burden driven by the increasing prevalence of obesity and obesity-associated complications. These disorders are characterized by chronic disturbances in energy homeostasis. A key feature linking metabolic disease and aging is the activation of stress-related pathways, which contribute to progressive metabolic dysfunction. Among the endocrine mediators of cellular stress, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) have emerged as key regulators of metabolic homeostasis. Both are induced by similar stress conditions, including nutrient imbalance, inflammation, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and are elevated in pathophysiological conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and aging. FGF21 and GDF15 also share overlapping regulatory pathways and complementary functions, suggesting a potential coordinated regulation and functional interplay. However, the extent and physiological relevance of this possible interrelationship remain incompletely understood. This review summarizes current knowledge on the regulation, tissue sources, and signaling mechanisms of FGF21 and GDF15 across metabolic diseases and aging, with particular attention to their roles as mediators of adaptive metabolic responses and their overlapping biological actions. We further discuss their context-dependent effects under acute and chronic stress and their relevance as biomarkers of metabolic dysfunction and disease progression. Collectively, this work highlights FGF21 and GDF15 as integrated stress signals linking cellular stress to systemic metabolic adaptation, providing a conceptual framework for understanding their cooperative roles and regulation in metabolic and age-related diseases, which may have therapeutic potential.

article.title: Integrated Single‐Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Convergence on a Senescence‐Associated B Cell–MIF Signaling Axis in Joint Aging and Osteoarthritis Progression
article.authors: Weida Li; Yi Wang; Yongqing You; Yue Cui; Jiayun Liu; Xingbiao Ma; QiuYu Zhu; Qiang Wu; Zanjing Zhai; Zuyan Lu; Kerong Dai; Ye Sun
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Osteoarthritis (OA) involves age‐associated structural and immune changes, yet whether senescence‐associated B‐cell states contribute to cartilage degeneration remains unclear. Integrated single‐cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of healthy, aged, and OA mouse joints identify reduced B‐cell abundance but enrichment of a low‐proliferative, inflammatory state with heightened macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) signaling. Cell–cell communication and spatial ligand–receptor analyses identify enhanced predicted MIF–CD74/CD44 interactions in B‐cell‐associated regions adjacent to cartilage. Constitutive MIF deficiency attenuates senescence‐associated B‐cell changes, MMP13 induction, and cartilage damage in vivo. Joint‐derived B cells from aged and OA mice induce chondrocyte senescence, reduce COL2A1 and HMGB1, and increase FN1 and MMP13 through MIF‐dependent paracrine signaling. These effects are suppressed by MIF neutralization and restored by recombinant MIF in MIF‐deficient co‐cultures. A composite hydrogel carrying quercetin and MIF‐siRNA‐loaded PLGA microspheres for local co‐delivery. The microspheres show gradual siRNA release over 96 h in vitro. In DMM‐induced OA, the formulation reduces MIF, P16, and MMP13 signals, restores HMGB1, and preserves cartilage. These findings support a senescence‐associated B cell–MIF signaling axis associated with joint aging and chondrocyte dysfunction and provide proof of concept for a local biomaterial‐based strategy that attenuates OA‐associated changes.

article.title: Standard treatment against paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma promotes senescence and sensitizes tumours to BCL-xL inhibition
article.authors: Romain Guiho; Hiba Hamdi; Grace Cooksley; Timoty H Chang; Lei Cao; Romain Sigaud; Sophie Bliss; Ashley Vardon; Scott Haston; Florian Selt; Akang Leonard Bassey; Daniela Kocher; Ria Kedia; Daniel Gharai; Jesús Gil; Olaf Witt; Till Milde; Darren Hargrave; Paula Alexandre; Pratiti Bandopadhayay; Juan Pedro Martinez Barbera
article.abstract: Abstract Background Chemo-, radio-, and targeted therapies can induce a stable growth arrest known as therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which may be therapeutically exploited using senolytic compounds that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Children with BRAF-V600E-driven brain tumours are commonly treated with low-dose chemotherapies and MAPK inhibitors, alone or in combination, often with good initial responses. However, a majority of patients experiences tumour regrowth following treatment withdrawal. Here, we investigate the contribution of TIS to treatment response and relapse, and assess the therapeutic potential of senolytics in preclinical models of paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma. Methods Preclinical models of paediatric low-grade glioma were analysed in vitro or following orthotopic transplantation into mice and treated with Dabrafenib, Trametinib, Tovorafenib or Vinblastine. Senescence was assessed using molecular and cytological markers. Sensitivity to senolytic compounds was evaluated using in vitro dose-response assays and in vivo treatment studies. Results Trametinib induced a robust senescent phenotype in BT-40 tumours in vivo, characterised by activation of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype and expansion of IBA-1-positive myeloid cells. In vitro, senescence was induced in BT-40 cells following treatment with MAPK inhibitors and Vinblastine, and was similarly observed in H9-derived human neural stem cells expressing BRAF-V600E. Navitoclax was identified as a potent senolytic against senescent BT-40 cells, primarily through inhibition of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-xL. In vivo, combined Trametinib and Navitoclax treatment ablated senescent tumour cells, significantly reduced tumour regrowth after treatment withdrawal, and improved survival. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that Navitoclax enhances Trametinib's anti-tumour efficacy and limits tumour relapse following treatment cessation.

article.title: Cellular Senescence in Diabetic Kidney Disease: Mechanisms and Treatments
article.authors: Yudian Wang; Yufei Zhang; Di Niu; Yuyan Fan; Yachan Gao; Xinxin Pang; Qi Jin
article.venue: Integrative Medicine in Nephrology and Andrology
article.abstract: Cellular senescence refers to a state of stable and essentially irreversible cell cycle arrest, accompanied by extensive changes in cellular secretory activity. Senescent cells accumulate within tissues during physiological aging and in response to various forms of cellular stress or injury. While transient senescence is essential for processes such as embryonic development, tissue regeneration, and tumor suppression, the persistent retention of senescent cells has been increasingly recognized as a key driver of aging and age-related diseases. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD), a prevalent chronic complication of diabetes, is characterized by accelerated renal cellular senescence and progressive accumulation of senescent cells, both of which contribute to structural damage and functional deterioration of the kidney. These observations have positioned cellular senescence as a promising therapeutic target for slowing the onset and progression of DKD. This review summarizes the fundamental characteristics and major classifications of cellular senescence; discusses its physiological and pathological functions, together with the underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms; examines the role of senescence in renal cell injury during DKD progression, and highlights recent advances in senescence-targeted therapeutic strategies for DKD.

article.title: Trehalose alleviates oxidative stress-induced senescence and is associated with cell-cycle remodeling.
article.authors: Yu Yang; Honghan Chen; Ming Yang; Huan Li; Weitong Xu; Hui Gong; Yang Yang; Yuanliang Mo; Ning Huang; Jin Liu; Xiaoli Huang; Hengyi Xiao
article.abstract: Trehalose has been widely used as a food and drug additive for a long time, and its effects on antioxidant stress, autophagy, and anti-aging have been gradually studied. However, the molecular mechanism by which trehalose exerts anti-oxidative stress and anti-aging effects has not been fully clarified. Our anti-aging cell phenotype study based on trehalose validates its intrinsic mechanisms of anti-oxidative stress and anti-inflammation in cells. We analyzed publicly available transcriptomic data (GSE76643) to identify molecular pathways regulated by trehalose, and then validated the key findings in our own cellular and animal experiments. The results indicate that trehalose alleviates oxidative stress-induced senescence, and that this effect is associated with remodeling of cell cycle progression, including down-regulation of selected cell-cycle regulators. The D-Gal-induced premature aging mouse model demonstrated that trehalose can effectively alleviate aging phenotypes in the hair, liver metabolic abnormalities, lung, and kidney of mice. Trehalose treatment reversed the D‑galactose‑induced upregulation of P16, P21, and P53 proteins in the liver, lung, and kidney, further supporting its anti‑aging effects in vivo. Additionally, the down-regulated expression of BIRC5, CCNE2, and CDK2 mRNA in certain tissues suggests that trehalose regulates or intervenes in the cell cycle. Based on the cell-cycle remodeling phenotype, we hypothesized that trehalose may modulate P65, STAT3, Keap1-Kelch, and CDK2. Molecular docking predicted potential interactions between trehalose and these proteins; these predictions require experimental validation. In conclusion, this study provides evidence that trehalose may alleviate oxidative stress-induced senescence in association with cell-cycle remodeling. These findings lay a foundation for further development of trehalose as an anti-aging intervention, but direct causality remains to be established.

article.title: A Senescence-Associated Transcriptional Signature in PBMC for Molecular Characterization and Diagnosis of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
article.authors: Shangrong Wu; Changqing Yin; Xiaolan He; Lu Xiong; Yuexi Zhou; Yajun Hu; Haiqiang Ke
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a complex metabolic disorder associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) represent an accessible cellular source for investigating systemic molecular alterations in T2DM. This study aimed to characterize senescence-associated transcriptional alterations in PBMCs and to evaluate their potential relevance to the molecular characterization and diagnosis of T2DM. Methods: Publicly available PBMC RNA-sequencing datasets were integrated following normalization and batch-effect correction. Differentially expressed genes were intersected with curated senescence-associated gene sets and subjected to functional enrichment analyses. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis was used to identify T2DM-associated gene modules, and immune deconvolution was performed to characterize alterations in immune-cell composition. LASSO regression, random forest, and support vector machine analyses were integrated to identify candidate diagnostic genes. The resulting gene signature was evaluated in independent cohorts and further validated by RT-qPCR in clinical PBMC samples. Consensus clustering was additionally performed to investigate molecular heterogeneity among patients with T2DM. Results: Senescence-associated transcriptional alterations were enriched in pathways related to RNA processing, cell-cycle regulation, and metabolism. A three-gene signature comprising ICE2, NHLRC2, and RPS24 was identified and showed reproducible diagnostic performance across independent cohorts. A nomogram incorporating these genes achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.882. RT-qPCR analysis of clinical PBMC samples confirmed expression patterns consistent with the transcriptomic analyses. Furthermore, consensus clustering identified distinct T2DM molecular subtypes characterized by differential immune and inflammatory profiles. Conclusions: These findings identify a senescence-associated PBMC transcriptional signature with potential diagnostic relevance in T2DM and reveal molecular heterogeneity associated with distinct immune and inflammatory features. The results provide a transcriptomic framework for further investigation of senescence-related immune–metabolic alterations in T2DM.

article.title: Stemonine Alleviates UVB‐Induced Keratinocyte Senescence by Activating SIRT3
article.authors: Kun Chen; Xudong Yan; Guixiang You; Mingyang Li; Chen Chen; Xiaolan Yu; Jiyi Xia
article.venue: Journal of Biochemical and Molecular Toxicology
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation is the primary environmental factor contributing to skin damage, largely by accelerating cellular senescence, which leads to impaired skin function and premature aging. Recent studies have indicated that Stemonine, a natural alkaloid, has therapeutic potential owing to its documented biological activities. In this study, we investigated the protective effects of Stemonine on immortalized human keratinocyte cell line HaCaT against UVB‐induced cellular senescence and elucidated the underlying mechanisms. Our results demonstrated that Stemonine significantly improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress, and ameliorated mitochondrial dysfunction in UVB‐irradiated HaCaT cells. Furthermore, Stemonine treatment reduced DNA damage signaling, downregulated key senescence executors such as acetylated p53 and p21, and decreased SA‐β‐Gal activity. Importantly, Stemonine upregulated both the expression and activity of SIRT3. Crucially, the protective effects of Stemonine were largely abolished upon SIRT3 knockdown, indicating that its actions are mediated via the SIRT3 pathway. These findings suggest that Stemonine is a promising candidate for mitigating UVB‐induced skin aging.

article.title: Purpurin Alleviates Meniscal Senescence and Osteoarthritis by Blocking the Non‐Metabolic Function of Hexokinase 2
article.authors: Zhencan Lin; Ming Li; Wei Li; Tianfa Xu; Zongrui Jiang; Yanlin Zhong; Aishan He; Xiaoyi Zhao; Dianbo Long; Yan Kang
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Meniscal degeneration, characterised by extracellular matrix (ECM) loss and cellular senescence, plays a critical role in osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Although hexokinase 2 (HK2) is recognised as a key glycolytic enzyme, its potential non‐metabolic functions in the meniscus remain unexplored. In this study, HK2 expression was evaluated in human OA and normal meniscus tissues, and its non‐metabolic effects were investigated in primary meniscal cells using overexpression, knockdown, and site‐directed mutagenesis; protein interactions were analysed by immunoprecipitation‐mass spectrometry (IP‐MS) and co‐immunoprecipitation (Co‐IP). HK2 was significantly upregulated in OA meniscal tissues, and overexpression of catalytically inactive HK2 promoted meniscal ECM degradation and cellular senescence in an MYH10‐dependent manner. Mechanistically, HK2 enhanced the MYH10–PRKN interaction, inducing K48‐linked ubiquitination of MYH10 at lysine 410 and its subsequent proteasomal degradation, thereby reducing COL1A1 mRNA stability. Purpurin, identified through virtual screening, disrupted the HK2–MYH10 interaction in vitro, prevented MYH10 degradation, and attenuated cellular senescence. In the destabilisation of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model, intra‐articular injection of adeno‐associated virus expressing catalytically inactive HK2 exacerbated OA progression, whereas purpurin treatment alleviated meniscal degeneration, ECM loss, and OA‐associated pain. Collectively, HK2 promotes meniscal senescence and OA progression through a non‐metabolic, MYH10‐dependent mechanism, and purpurin represents a promising lead compound for disease‐modifying osteoarthritis drug (DMOAD) development.

article.title: The crosstalk between ferroptosis and cellular senescence in gestational diabetes mellitus: from iron dyshomeostasis to trophoblast dysfunction
article.authors: Min Li; Wendi Zhao; Lei Jiang; Yijing Chu
article.abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) comprises heterogeneous placental phenotypes that include fetal overgrowth, large-for-gestational-age birth, and fetal growth restriction (FGR). We propose a testable endotype model in which maternal hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end products, diabetic dyslipidemia, altered polyunsaturated fatty-acid delivery, gestational iron exposure, and the physiologic fall in hepcidin converge on a redox-stressed trophoblast microenvironment. In proliferative cytotrophoblasts and extravillous trophoblasts, the relative reserve of GPX4 and FSP1/CoQ10, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-phospholipid loading, proliferative status, and insult intensity and duration are predicted to determine whether cells undergo ferroptosis, enter senescence, or occupy an intermediate state. We further propose an asymmetric crosstalk model: senescent trophoblasts are relatively ferroptosis-resistant, retain iron, and act in trans through SASP factors, reactive oxygen species, and oxidized lipids on ferroptosis-susceptible neighboring cells. The model predicts a gestational-age-dependent window in which physiologic senescence accumulates and its paracrine effects become injurious. Ferrostatin-1 or liproxstatin-1 should rescue lipid-peroxidation-driven death in susceptible cells without reversing senescence in iron-retaining cells. The model is GDM-specific in its initiating inputs and gestational context, but the reciprocal links remain hypotheses rather than established facts. It predicts that an injury-dominant placental endotype will show spatially adjacent iron-retaining senescence-like cells and lipid-peroxidation-driven cell death, impaired nutrient transport, and FGR, whereas compensatory transport and villous expansion may produce large-for-gestational-age phenotypes in other GDM placentas. We outline experiments that could support or falsify this model and define pregnancy-specific safety constraints for therapeutic testing.

article.title: Analytical Calculation of the Bending Modulus in a Lipid Membrane: Revisiting Existing Theory
article.authors: Anna A. Drozdova
article.abstract: This work analytically calculates the first moment of lateral pressure in a bent bilayer using a model that treats lipid molecules as flexible elastic chains. The key point is that lateral pressure in a curved lipid membrane influences membrane elastic constants, particularly the bending modulus, which is related to lateral pressure through its first moment. Although the bending modulus is well known, little is known about its theoretical estimate. The microscopic model presented here enables calculation of the bending modulus for the lipid bilayer, the bending modulus for the lipid monolayer, an area-stretching modulus, a bending-stretching modulus, the spontaneous bending moment for the lipid monolayer, and the position of the neutral surface (non-expanded surface). We obtain these theoretical estimates from an analytical expression for the first correction to the lateral pressure profile in the bent lipid membrane, calculated using a well-known condensed-matter-physics method: perturbation theory in the small parameter L0J, where L0 is the unperturbed monolayer thickness, and J is the curvature. The results are compared with available data and fall within the range of experimental values and molecular dynamics data.

article.title: Next-Generation Nanocarrier Systems for Targeted Drug Delivery: Advances in Lipid, Polymeric, Metal-Based, and Green Nanoparticles
article.authors: Isioma Christian Okonta; Micheal Abimbola Oladosu; Moses Adondua Abah; Emmanuel Buchi Onyioha; Judith Osakpamwan Enemudo; Emmanuel C. Ugwuabonyi
article.venue: International Journal of Advanced Pharmaceutical Sciences and Research
article.abstract: Nanocarrier-based drug delivery has evolved from a concept into a clinically proven platform technology, with lipid nanoparticle (LNP)- based messenger RNA vaccine delivery systems and a wide array of polymeric and metallic nanomedicines as just a few examples. The review aims to be a synthesis of recent advances in the four main classes of nanocarriers: lipid-based (liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, nanostructured lipid carriers, and ionizable-lipid LNPs); polymeric (poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid), chitosan, polymeric micelles and dendrimers); metal-based (gold and iron oxide nanoparticles); and green-synthesised nanoparticles (via plants, algae and microbes). For each class, the review discusses synthesis strategies, targeting mechanisms (passive enhanced permeability and retention versus active ligandmediated targeting), and representative preclinical and clinical applications. It compares these approaches with other systems to highlight trade-offs in biocompatibility, payload flexibility, targeting accuracy, and manufacturing scalability. The review discusses key translational obstacles in depth, including interpatient EPR heterogeneity, reproducibility of green-synthesis batches, and gaps in regulatory standardisation, as well as novel solutions such as stimuli-responsive design, microfluidic manufacturing, and image-guided dosing. Based on the overall picture emerging from the review, the future of targeted therapeutics depends on nanocarriers that can adapt to the tumour/tissue microenvironment, with a stronger mechanistic understanding of the tumour/tissue environment.

article.title: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus protects lactating dairy cows from infection.
article.authors: Jefferson J S Santos; Carine K Souza; Giovana C Zanella; Débora B Goulart; Bailey Arruda; Paola Boggiatto; Mitchell V Palmer; Celeste A Snyder; Michaela A Kristula; Charlene Dickens; Terry L Webb; Reilly K Atkinson; Bernadeta Dadonaite; Garima Dwivedi; Mohamad-Gabriel Alameh; Christopher A Hunter; Lisa A Murphy; Jesse D Bloom; Drew Weissman; Gary C Althouse; Amy L Baker; Scott E Hensley
article.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus has recently emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, leading to mastitis and sharp reductions in milk production. The main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract and viral transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk. Here, we generate an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccine encoding the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, representative of circulating bovine H5N1 viruses, and assess its immunogenicity and efficacy in lactating dairy cows. Eight cows were divided into vaccinated and control groups, receiving two intramuscular doses of the vaccine or saline, followed by intramammary viral challenge. Vaccination elicited HA-reactive and neutralizing antibodies in serum and HA-reactive antibodies in milk. Following viral challenge, vaccinated cows had ~1,000-fold lower peak viral RNA in milk and a lower occurrence of mastitis and mammary fibrosis.

article.title: Integrated chemical profiling and lipidomics reveal that Mailuoning oral liquid alleviates diet-induced MASLD via PPARα-mediated lipid homeostasis and COX-2 inhibition, with identification of potential active constituents
article.authors: Sijia Wu; Wangya Jia; Xun Zhou; Linyan Zhu; Keke Wang; Jian Li; Lili Ji; Wei Liu; Hong Xu
article.abstract: Background Mailuoning oral liquid (MLN), a standardized five-herb formula, is used for ischemic vascular diseases and shows potential in ameliorating dyslipidemia. Our previous study showed MLN alleviates metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) via peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) activation, but its comprehensive chemical profile, systemic exposure, and bioactive constituents mediating both PPARα activation and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibition remain unclear. Methods High-fat, high-fructose diet-fed rats received MLN (5.4 or 10.8 mL/kg/day) for 8 weeks. Ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap HRMS) profiled MLN chemicals and identified serum/liver prototypes. Biochemical profiles, glucose tolerance, histopathology, untargeted lipidomics, and targeted polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) analysis were performed. PPARα and COX-2 signaling were examined by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. Key constituents were screened for PPARα activation via dual luciferase reporter assay and molecular docking; COX-2 inhibition was validated by enzyme assays and molecular dynamics. Results A total of 143 compounds were characterized; 48 and 92 prototypes were enriched in serum and liver, respectively. MLN ameliorated dyslipidemia, glucose intolerance, steatosis, and inflammation. Lipidomics revealed bidirectional modulation of hepatic lipids, reversing triglyceride (TAG) accumulation and restoring phosphatidylcholine (PC) and lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) levels. Targeted analysis showed increased eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and normalized COX-2-derived prostaglandins (PGD 2 , PGE 2 ). MLN activated hepatic PPARα and downregulated COX-2. Seven serum-enriched compounds (chlorogenic acid, macranthoidin B, luteoloside, harpagide, angoroside C, oleanolic acid, betaine) were validated as direct PPARα agonists. Secologanoside and chikusetsusaponin IVa were identified as novel COX-2 inhibitors (half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) = 14.61 and 120.9 nM). Discussion MLN alleviates MASLD via dual PPARα activation and COX-2 inhibition, providing a mechanistic foundation for repurposing this herbal formula in early-stage MASLD.

article.title: Electroacupuncture regulates lipid metabolism through PPARγ-associated LXRα signaling: from nuclear receptor signaling to cardiovascular protection
article.authors: Shuyan Zhang; Jihao Yang; Xinhao Yan; Haichun Zhou
article.abstract: Hyperlipidemia is an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and a substantial proportion of patients remain inadequately controlled on statin therapy because single-target interventions cannot fully reverse the systemic inflammation and tissue injury driven by dysregulated lipid metabolism. Electroacupuncture (EA), a modern refinement of traditional acupuncture,has been reported to lower serum total cholesterol, triglycerides, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in clinical trials, yet the molecular basis of these effects has not been systematically synthesized. Here, we review the evidence that EA regulates lipid homeostasis through the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPAR γ )/liver X receptor α (LXR α ) axis. We first outline the structure and function of these nuclear receptors and their transcriptional crosstalk, and then examine how EA modulates their expression, activity, and co-regulators. We next trace the upstream signal transduction from somatic afferent activation through the neuro–endocrine–immune network, and the downstream effector programs, including cholesterol efflux, fatty-acid oxidation, macrophage M2 polarization, and organ-specific cardiovascular protection. Pharmacological antagonism, PPAR γ knockdown, and MerTK deficiency provide causal evidence that the PPAR γ -associated efferocytic program contributes to the lipid-lowering and efferocytic effects of EA, whereas the involvement of LXR α is supported primarily by its coordinated expression with PPAR γ and downstream cholesterol-efflux signaling. We conclude by discussing the heterogeneity of EA parameters, the animal-to-human translational gap, and the limitations of causal inference in the current literature, and outline future directions, including optogenetic dissection of acupuncture neural circuits and PPAR γ /LXR α -guided standardization of EA protocols.

article.title: Hybrid lipid-coated silver nanoparticles as programmable antimicrobial platforms: balancing silver accessibility, efficacy, and toxicity.
article.authors: Megan C Schulte; Priyal D Patel; Genevive L Sheehan; Marilyn R Mackiewicz
article.abstract: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) can deliver reactive silver, but the processes that drive antimicrobial activity can also injure host cells. Lipid interfaces may modify this balance by regulating nanoparticle transformation and interactions with biological targets. This Special Report examines sodium oleate-phosphatidylcholine-alkanethiol hybrid lipid membranes (HLMs) as a case study of interfacial control, with selected alternative coatings providing comparative context. Silver accessibility is defined as a time-, environment-, and target-dependent property that requires separate measurements of silver species, nanoparticle interactions, and coating evolution. Existing HLM studies demonstrate physicochemical control and changes in developmental vertebrate or environmental toxicity under defined conditions; these findings do not establish improved antimicrobial therapeutic benefit. Representative antimicrobial and mammalian-cell studies using other coatings illustrate both the value and limitations of efficacy-toxicity comparisons. Progress requires paired biological measurements, direct assessment of coating and corona evolution, and independent validation in relevant formulations. Dental, wound, device, and intracellular uses are considered as distinct evidence needs rather than established HLM therapies.

article.title: A Deep Learning Framework with Qualitative Post Hoc Explanation for Dry Eye Detection and Tear Film Lipid Layer Pattern Classification Using Anterior-Segment and Tearscope Imaging
article.authors: Sajedeh Talebi; Neda Abdolvand; Mohammad Hassan Emamian; Akbar Fotouhi; Hassan Hashemi; Sara Mazaheri
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: Dry eye disease (DED) is assessed by combining patient-reported symptoms with ocular surface findings. We evaluated a deep learning strategy with qualitative post hoc explanation in two independent ophthalmic imaging tasks: DED-versus-healthy classification from anterior segment slit lamp images; and four-class recognition of tear film lipid layer (TFLL) interference patterns in Tearscope images using the Guillon categories. Methods: ResNet backbones were modified by adding parallel expansion channels while keeping the ImageNet-initialized channels frozen. The added channels were He-normal initialized and trained at 1 × 10−4, with the MLP classification head trained at 1 × 10−3. Latin hypercube sampling was used for hyperparameter selection within the development data. We used Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ only for post hoc interpretation. We evaluated ShECS slit lamp images (n = 434) and VOPTICAL-Is Tearscope images (n = 406). Results: Under the original evaluations, ResNet-101×3 achieved the highest scores among the evaluated configurations on both tasks. On ShECS, accuracy was 74% (95% CI: 0.63–0.82), with precision 0.80, recall 0.90, and F1-score 0.85 for the DED (positive) class, and AUC 0.80. On VOPTICAL-Is, the original image-level evaluation yielded four-class TFLL accuracy of 90% (95% CI: 0.82–0.95), with macro precision 0.89, macro recall 0.90, and macro F14 0.89, and a macro one-versus-rest AUC of 0.98. Conclusions: These preliminary proof-of-concept results support further evaluation of the combined channel-expansion and differential-training strategy, together with qualitative post hoc explanation methods for ophthalmic image classification. Because VOPTICAL-Is contains only healthy-subject images and has no documented subject identifiers in the accessed release (group-code overlap between the development and held-out subsets was observed, and subject overlap cannot be excluded), the second task represents image-level TFLL pattern classification rather than clinical DED-subtype diagnosis. A separate code-grouped sensitivity analysis with a frozen ResNet-50 feature extractor yielded 0.59 held-out accuracy (macro one-versus-rest AUC 0.85). Because this grouped run did not re-run the 0.90 ResNet-101×3 configuration, the numerical difference cannot be attributed solely to partitioning, or interpreted as a direct measurement of subject-level leakage; rather, it demonstrates sensitivity to group-aware partitioning. The original image-level estimates should therefore be treated as exploratory and not as evidence of subject-level generalization. A controlled 2 × 2 factorial ablation (channel width × trainability policy) on the same code-grouped partition, executed as a TensorFlow/Keras ResNet-50 reconstruction with three seeds per cell, indicated descriptively that unfreezing the final convolutional stage was associated with higher accuracy and macro F1 (e.g., standard width: accuracy 0.556 vs. 0.469), whereas the effect of widening was small and inconsistent across metrics and policies. These descriptive summaries involve no significance testing and do not measure subject-level leakage. External clinical validation of identified cohorts is needed before routine use.

article.title: Temporal Changes in Hepatic Fatty Acid Metabolism, Desaturase Expression, and Lipid Peroxidation During Long-Term Sucrose Feeding in Male and Female Rats
article.authors: Sunčica Heštera; Tomislav Mašek; Petra Roginek; Maja Maurić Maljković; Vedran Micek; Kristina Starčević
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic sucrose consumption may contribute to progressive metabolic dysfunction, but the combined influence of long-term exposure, aging, sex, and dietary fiber on hepatic lipid metabolism remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated how time and sex influence hepatic lipid metabolism during chronic sucrose supplementation and characterized responses under different dietary backgrounds. Methods: A total of 120 Wistar Han rats (60 males and 60 females) were allocated to four dietary treatments: control diet (CON), control diet with increased fiber content (CON-fiber), 30% sucrose in drinking water (HS), or 30% sucrose in drinking water with high fiber content (HS-fiber). Five animals of each sex per treatment were euthanized after 1, 12, or 24 months. Glucose homeostasis, hepatic fatty-acid composition, serum malondialdehyde (MDA), and hepatic expression of SCD1, Fads1, Fads2, NRF2, TNFα, and TGFβ were evaluated. Results: Treatment effects became prominent after 12 and 24 months. Chronic sucrose intake increased body mass in HS rats, impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, shifted the hepatic fatty-acid profile toward monounsaturated fatty acids, and reduced several n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids. Increased SCD1 expression accompanied increased relative proportions of palmitoleic and oleic acids, whereas Fads1 and Fads2 showed treatment-associated differences within individual sampling points. Sucrose-exposed groups also developed increased lipid peroxidation and a pro-inflammatory transcriptional response. Conclusions: Metabolic, oxidative, and inflammatory alterations were observed in sucrose-fed groups, with treatment-associated differences depending on sex and sampling time point. These findings emphasize the importance of exposure duration and biological sex in shaping metabolic responses during aging.

article.title: Plasma Lipidomic Features of Adolescent Major Depressive Disorder and Lipid Changes After Fluoxetine Treatment
article.authors: Chenxi Liu; Yao Li; Hanchen Hou; Jiamei Guo; Bingjie Qin; Xiaoxia Xu; Yuqian He; Tingting Lei; Fei Chen; Lige Zhang; Quanbing Liu; Li Gao; Jiaqi Shi; Haoran Xing; Teng Teng; Tian Qiu; Xinyu Zhou
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a major public health concern, yet objective biological markers and treatment‐related metabolic changes remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize plasma lipidomic alterations in adolescent MDD and explore lipid changes associated with fluoxetine treatment. Methods This study enrolled 75 adolescents with MDD and 75 matched healthy controls (HCs). Among the adolescents with MDD, 44 had paired baseline and week‐8 plasma samples available and were included in the longitudinal analysis. Plasma lipidomic profiles were analyzed using ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC–MS/MS). Results A total of 865 lipid species were detected. Compared with HCs, adolescents with MDD showed distinct plasma lipidomic profiles, with 82 differentially abundant lipid species identified, primarily involving triglycerides, lysophospholipids, free fatty acids, membrane phospholipids, and sphingolipids. Among the machine‐learning models, logistic regression showed the highest discriminative performance, with a pooled out‐of‐fold AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79–0.91). Longitudinal analysis identified 21 lipid species meeting the differential criteria following fluoxetine treatment, mainly involving triglycerides and bile acid‐related metabolites. Integrative pathway and target analyses suggested that fluoxetine‐associated lipid changes may involve neurotransmitter signaling, inflammatory lipid metabolism, PI3K–Akt signaling, and nuclear receptor‐related pathways. Conclusion This study characterizes alterations in plasma lipid metabolism in adolescent MDD and the lipidomic changes following fluoxetine treatment, providing new lipidomic evidence for candidate lipid signatures and potential treatment‐associated biological pathways. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov , NCT05814640. Registered 20 February 2023, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05814640

article.title: Maternal HFD and CDAHFD Exposure from Pregnancy to Lactation Differentially Affect Lipid Profiles and Behavior in Offspring Mice
