Mechanistic studies highlight pathways such as short-chain fatty acid production, immune modulation, and gut barrier integrity, which mediate microbial effects on insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, with short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) signaling and gut barrier integrity identified as the most significant pathways driving these effects. Interventional approaches, including probiotics, prebiotics, dietary modifications, fasting, exercise, and bariatric surgery, show preliminary, proof-of-concept potential to reshape the microbiome and improve diabetic outcomes, although none of these interventions has yet been validated in large-scale, adequately powered, multi-center randomized controlled trials with hard clinical endpoints, and none should be regarded as an established treatment. Notably, T1D research emphasizes autoimmune interactions, while T2D focuses on metabolic dysfunction. Despite advances, challenges like establishing causality and addressing inter-individual variability persist. This review underscores the microbiome's therapeutic promise pending confirmation in the larger trials outlined above, and advocates for personalized, multi-omics-driven strategies to enhance diabetes management.

article.title: Highlights of Cardiovascular Disease Prevention Studies Presented at the 2026 European Society of Cardiology Conference.
article.authors: Ali Bin Abdul Jabbar; Kalsoom Zulfiqar; Shahzil Abdur Rehman Malik; Maha Inam; Wahab Fazal; Ali Hyder; Abdul Mannan Khan Minhas; Leandro Slipczuk; Chayakrit Krittanawong; Dinesh K Kalra; Salim S Virani
article.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review summarizes key cardiovascular disease prevention studies presented at the 2026 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress, highlighting new evidence in lipid management, cardiovascular risk assessment, blood pressure control, and vaccination. RECENT FINDINGS: Several studies addressed persistent gaps in lipid management and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease prevention. STAREE showed that atorvastatin reduced major cardiovascular events in adults aged 70 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, although it did not significantly improve disability-free survival. The SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 trials showed that plozasiran produced substantial and sustained triglyceride reductions and reduced acute pancreatitis events in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia. VICTORION-Challenge demonstrated greater LDL-C reduction and target attainment with inclisiran compared with bempedoic acid in high- and very-high-risk patients receiving background statin therapy. In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, VSA003 substantially lowered LDL-C and several other atherogenic lipoproteins by inhibiting ANGPTL3. Two studies examined imaging-based approaches to preventive therapy: RESPECT2 showed that coronary computed tomography angiography-guided lipid management improved adherence compared with conventional risk-score-based treatment, while CorCal found that coronary artery calcium-guided statin recommendations reduced the number of patients selected for treatment and were associated with greater LDL-C lowering and higher reported adherence, although noninferiority for cardiovascular events was not established. Beyond lipid management, long-term follow-up of the China Rural Hypertension Control Project showed that intensive blood pressure management led by non-physician healthcare providers reduced dementia and cognitive impairment. TIMER demonstrated sustained LDL-C lowering with once-monthly ticalicibart in patients with nonfamilial hypercholesterolemia receiving background statin therapy, while TRANQUILITY demonstrated sustained reductions in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein with the interleukin-6 (IL-6) inhibitor pacibekitug in patients with chronic kidney disease. DAN-RSV demonstrated that RSVpreF vaccination reduced RSV-related respiratory and cardiorespiratory hospitalizations across two seasons. Studies presented at ESC 2026 broadened the evidence base for cardiovascular prevention across pharmacologic therapy, imaging-guided risk assessment, blood pressure management, and vaccination.

article.title: Dietary Polysaccharides for Overweight and Obesity Management: Targeting AMPK via the Gut Microbiota and Metabolites-A Review.
article.authors: Zhongxing Chu; Zuomin Hu; Baitong Zhu; Feijun Luo; Yaping Zhou; Qinlu Lin
article.abstract: Obesity arises from dietary energy intake-expenditure imbalance. 5'-Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a core regulator of biological energy metabolism, is a key target for obesity research and can be activated by endogenous stimuli, such as cellular stress and physical exercise. As natural active components with diverse sources and biological functions, dietary polysaccharides have shown potential lipid-lowering and antiobesity effects in preclinical studies. This narrative review systematically summarizes their structural characteristics, sources, absorption-utilization mechanisms and structure-activity relationships, focusing on their regulatory effects on obesity via the AMPK pathway. We searched PubMed and Web of Science for publications (2014-2026) using "dietary polysaccharides,""AMPK,""obesity," and "gut microbiota" as key words, screening original studies and reviews relevant to the core topic. Correlative evidence suggests that dietary polysaccharides are associated with altered expression of lipid metabolism-related factors through potential modulation of gut microbiota and its metabolites, with indirect links to AMPK activation. Such AMPK regulatory effects have tissue/organ specificity, and the causal relationship of each link remains to be rigorously established. Notably, the majority of current evidence derives from in vitro and rodent models, and extrapolation to human obesity management requires caution, as high-quality human clinical trials are urgently needed to validate the translational potential of these preclinical findings. This review clarifies the potential mechanism and existing research gaps of dietary polysaccharides in obesity alleviation, providing a scientific basis for the research and development of lipid-lowering functional foods based on dietary polysaccharides.

article.title: Sexual dimorphism in geriatric periodontology and implant dentistry.
article.authors: Roberto Farina; Yvonne Hernandez-Kapila
article.abstract: Aging is a progressive biological process characterized by accumulating molecular and cellular damage and functional decline. Although some clinical attachment and alveolar bone loss is common in older adults, severe periodontitis is not an inevitable consequence of aging. Sexual dimorphism (SD), encompassing genetic, epigenetic, hormonal, and socio-behavioral differences between sexes, may modify disease susceptibility, progression, and treatment response in geriatric periodontal and implant care. Most available epidemiological evidence generally indicates a higher prevalence and severity of periodontitis in men. Differences in oral hygiene and healthcare utilization partly explain this disparity, but sex-specific biological mechanisms may also contribute. Men may exhibit stronger pro-inflammatory responses and differential regulation of sex steroid-responsive genes, while genome-wide analyses support genotype-sex interactions affecting disease expression. Advanced age is associated with a modestly reduced response to non-surgical periodontal therapy (NSPT), with some evidence of slightly less favorable outcomes in older men, although the clinical relevance appears limited. In implant dentistry, SD may influence bone morphology and density, radiographic interpretability, and preoperative risk assessment. Elderly-specific data, however, do not identify sex as an independent predictor of early implant failure or long-term survival. A possible male disadvantage has been reported for composite implant success in complex rehabilitations, whereas the evidence evaluating the sex effect on peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis in older patients is limited. Sex-related biological factors and gender-related behaviors should therefore be incorporated into individualized risk assessment, but current evidence remains insufficient to support sex-specific therapeutic protocols.

article.title: Probing Optical Response and Surface Conductance in Mixed-Halide Perovskites Using Terahertz Spectroscopy.
article.authors: Sarvani Jowhar Khanam; Naveen Periketi; Sushma Kumari; Arunkumar Meghavath; Srinivasa Rao Konda; Chaudhary Anil Kumar; Banavoth Murali
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry letters
article.abstract: Mixed halide perovskite single crystals (MHPSCs) have attracted considerable attention as promising building blocks for next-generation photovoltaic technologies due to their exceptional optoelectronic properties, low fabrication cost, and facile processability. However, their practical implementation remains limited by phase segregation, which severely undermines the material stability and device scalability. Among the various crystal growth strategies, additive engineering has emerged as an effective approach to address these challenges by facilitating the formation of passivating interfacial layers, enhancing nanoscale crystallinity, and reducing the defect density. In this study, the optical response and surface conductance of MHPSCs were investigated by using terahertz spectroscopy in both reflection and transmission geometries. The influence of choline bromide (CB) and the heterocyclic additive 3-aminopiperidine (API) on the phonon modes and terahertz response were also examined. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed that the suppression of phase segregation, associated with stronger chemical bonding, contributes to an enhanced THz transmission in the modified MHPSCs. In addition, the THz response of the crystals was examined after approximately six months of ambient aging, revealing changes in the reflection response compared with measurements performed shortly after synthesis. Since the fresh and aged samples were characterized by using different THz spectroscopy configurations, the aging-related changes are interpreted qualitatively. Overall, combined time- and frequency-domain imaging provides a comprehensive assessment of spatial and spectral heterogeneity, complementing bulk THz spectroscopy and highlighting the impact of additive-induced microstructural modifications on the THz dielectric response.

article.title: Wavelength-Dependent Photoluminescence Mapping of Depth-Dependent Degradation Under Thermal Stress in Phenethylammonium Tetrafluoroborate Treated Perovskite Solar Cells.
article.authors: Julisa Juarez; Akash Dasgupta; Alan Zhan; Lamtiur P Samosir; David S Ginger
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry letters
article.abstract: Studying real-time degradation in perovskite semiconductors remains an important challenge. Conventional methods often cannot separate interfacial and bulk processes or rely on destructive analysis. Here, we demonstrate multiwavelength excitation photoluminescence (PL) as a nondestructive approach to distinguish interface- and bulk-dominated recombination losses. Using phenethylammonium tetrafluoroborate (PEABF4) treatment as a model, we use PL to show that PEABF4 passivates the electron transport layer (ETL)/perovskite interface, reducing interfacial recombination losses from fullerene deposition. However, upon thermal aging, PEABF4-treated stacks degrade more rapidly, with recombination losses broadening from the ETL/perovskite interface into the absorber. Diffusion-recombination simulations support interpreting excitation-wavelength-dependent PL decay signatures consistent with changes in surface recombination velocity and bulk lifetime, providing a framework for depth-sensitive comparisons during aging. Collectively, these results further establish multiwavelength excitation PL as a platform for studying recombination losses during aging of perovskite films.

article.title: Thymol-phospholipid complex: a promising green natural preservative with improved physicochemical properties and bioactivities.
article.authors: Jianzhuo Du; Pingyu Ge; Tai Gao; Jiapei Wu; Haoyang Du; Jialin Wang; Yu Tong; Chunling Zhou; Xu Zhao
article.abstract: With the growing global demand for safe, green food additives to replace synthetic preservatives, thymol has emerged as a promising candidate owing to its broad-spectrum bioactivities. However, its industrial application is severely hindered by inherent limitations including poor water solubility, high volatility, and environmental instability. Herein, a thymol-phospholipid complex (Thy-PC) was successfully fabricated via optimised anti-solvent precipitation, achieving a complexation efficiency of 81.2 ± 1.3%. Structural characterisation verified that thymol was molecularly dispersed in the phospholipid matrix in an amorphous state, leading to a 2.5-fold improvement in water solubility and a significantly reduced oil-water partition coefficient. Thy-PC exhibited enhanced antioxidant activity (comparable to vitamin C), superior antibacterial efficacy against E. coli and S. aureus, and excellent photostability. Notably, its antioxidant performance in soybean oil matched that of synthetic BHT, providing a practical strategy for developing high-efficiency natural food preservatives.

article.title: Simulating the Permeation of a Therapeutic Peptide through a Phospholipid Membrane.
article.authors: Christopher Kang; Stephen D Stamatis; Huyen Tran; John P Rose; Rui Sun
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
article.abstract: Oral peptide delivery offers a promising route for therapeutic administration but is often hampered by challenges related to the low permeability of peptides across gastrointestinal epithelia. This study employs state-of-the-art molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and enhanced sampling methods (i.e., well-tempered metadynamics extended-system adaptive biasing force, coined WTM-eABF) to investigate the simultaneous folding/unfolding of a linear 39 amino acid peptide with and without a fatty acid modification as it permeates a POPC (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) membrane. The resulting free energy surfaces capture the simultaneous secondary structural changes and the translocation process of the peptides, which are carefully examined against well-established, independent free-energy calculations at key steps in the permeation process. The free-energy surfaces indicate that the peptides assume a more structured configuration upon membrane interaction. The results show that the permeation of neutral peptides, despite their large size, is nearly barrierless. In addition, the simulations show that WTM-eABF is able to qualitatively converge the free energy of the permeation of long, flexible peptides.

article.title: Glycosaminoglycans Recruit IAPP Oligomers on Lipid Bilayers.
article.authors: Suhas Gotla; Meenal Jain; Silvina Matysiak
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
article.abstract: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are anionic polysaccharides that coexist with cell membranes in the extracellular matrix and have been shown to cooperatively enhance the aggregation of islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) at zwitterionic lipid surfaces─a process implicated in β-cell death in type 2 diabetes. However, the molecular mechanisms by which GAGs and lipids concertedly promote IAPP aggregation remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a coarse-grained model for the GAG chondroitin-4-sulfate (CS) and employ molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the aggregation of the IAPP11-29 fragment in environments containing CS, a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) bilayer, or both. By comparing simultaneous and sequential assembly pathways, we show that the order of molecular encounters reshapes the aggregation landscape. CS drives rapid peptide consolidation at the bilayer surface through GAG-chain flexion and peptide crawling on the GAG chain, yielding ternary aggregates in which hydrophobic residues anchor into the bilayer, a globular peptide body extends above the membrane plane, while the CS chain forms a corona. CS further stabilizes helical intermediates through dipole-charge interactions, with helix half-lives four- to five-fold greater than in the bilayer-only system. When introduced to dispersed, bilayer-bound oligomers, CS recruits them into larger, more orientationally ordered aggregates that may serve as superior seeds for downstream fibrillation. Together, these results provide a molecular basis for the experimentally observed cooperative enhancement of IAPP aggregation by GAGs and zwitterionic lipids.

article.title: Molecular Mechanisms of the Cytotoxicity of an Anti-Cancer Peptide.
article.authors: Ehud Neumann; Yang-Sung Sohn; Alfredo E Cardenas; Taylor Hays; Itai Alfoni; Assaf Friedler; Lauren J Webb; Ron Elber; Rachel Nechushtai
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
article.abstract: The molecular mechanisms of anticancer peptides (ACPs) are largely unknown, which makes their rational design challenging. Here, we investigate the action of an ACP, the peptide NAF-144-67, to elucidate a detailed reaction sequence with cancer cells. NAF-144-67 is a 24-amino-acid ACP derived from the human transmembrane protein NAF-1, which resides in mitochondria and the ER. We investigate the specificity, targeting, and induction of cancer cell death by the peptide using imaging experiments, trypsin assays, and atomistic-level computer simulations. We investigate peptide interactions with and permeation into cancer cells, as well as large (LUVs) and giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). The experiments and simulations are conducted on the native peptide and several point mutations. We demonstrate a mechanism with the following sequential steps: 1. The ACPs cross the plasma membrane of cancer cells efficiently without damaging it. 2. Different ACPs target alternate organelles in the cancer cell. The native peptide and two-point mutations (F1W and Q23W) target the mitochondria. Another point mutation (L11W) targets the nucleus. 3. The ACPs initiate apoptosis by damaging the mitochondria. They perturb the mitochondrial membrane and a membrane-embedded protein, NAF-1. We illustrated the critical role of the interaction of the peptide with the protein NAF-1 by examining cells that underexpress or overexpress NAF-1. Overexpressing NAF-1 enhances peptide cytotoxicity, while underexpressing the protein reduces it. The revealed molecular mechanism opens the way for further investigations into ACPs that target different cancer cells and inner organelles and induce apoptosis through multiple pathways.

article.title: Membrane Diffusion Mode of Human Perforin-1 and Its Cholesterol Sensitivity.
article.authors: Yuri Kasubuchi; Ryuhei Harada
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
article.abstract: Perforin-1, a pore-forming protein, is essential for cytotoxic T lymphocyte- and natural killer cell-mediated immune responses. Human perforin-1 (hPRF) exists as a surface-bound monomer that diffuses on the membrane before oligomerizing into a prepore complex. Yet this diffusive stage evades direct experimental observation, and how cholesterol regulates hPRF mobility remains unknown. We therefore performed all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the hPRF monomer on lipid membranes with 0-60 mol % cholesterol to identify which lipid environments support or hinder efficient hPRF diffusion. The lateral diffusion coefficient of hPRF decreased progressively with cholesterol content, tracking reduced area per lipid up to 40 mol %. Beyond this packing-saturation point, the hPRF diffusion continued to slow, suggesting a contribution from direct protein-lipid interactions. Intermolecular contact analysis identified W431 and F432 as persistent cholesterol-binding sites that drive raft-like codiffusion of hPRF with an ordered lipid assembly rather than independent diffusion. These results demonstrate that cholesterol suppresses hPRF lateral dynamics through both indirect membrane ordering and direct, residue-specific protein-lipid local interactions, providing molecular-level insights into the early stages of perforin-mediated cytotoxicity. This dual mechanism suggests that, beyond limiting hPRF binding, cholesterol-rich effector-cell membranes may also suppress its lateral diffusion, providing an additional layer of self-protection from perforin-mediated lysis.

article.title: Two-Dimensional Correlation of Quantum-Mechanical Infrared Spectra Reveals Order of Vibrational-Mode Positions and Predicts Classical RMSD Structural Descriptor.
article.authors: Robert J Allsopp; Curtis W Meuse
article.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
article.abstract: Quantum mechanics (QM) provides the fundamental basis for an in silico (computational) analogue to infrared (IR) spectroscopy. Quantum-chemical vibrational analysis, as used here with the normal-mode approximation, provides an approximate description of molecular vibrations and yields calculated vibrational transition wavenumbers and infrared intensities for the normal modes of a given molecular conformation. One challenge in quantum normal-mode analysis is identifying structural or functional group relationships between modes of two different molecular conformations. Phospholipids, which are of supreme biomedical importance because they form cell membranes, are ideal-sized targets for density functional theory (DFT) scaling in quantum vibrational analysis. Hundreds of QM spectra can be readily simulated by using DFT, enabling comparisons of modes across many lipid conformations. In addition, lipids are long enough in the Z-dimension (perpendicular to the membrane) that the ordering of molecular functional groups based on Z-coordinate centers can help describe the lipid conformation. Snapshots from triplicate bilayer systems in a vacuum were collected in a library of phospholipid quantum-mechanical models. The library illustrates how two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D-COS) can be applied to assign normal modes to local regions and develop a particular order of functional group positions (order-of-positions) of a phospholipid structure. A k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) approach is applied to relate normal-mode wavenumbers and normal-mode Z-dimension positions to find the modes that are most similar in different lipid conformations. This mode-to-mode mapping enables predictions of the atomic position RMSD for pairs of lipids. A separate application of KNN allows for comparisons of many lipids against a fixed reference point. This enables fine-tuning of the reference-point wavenumber and Z-count values to correlate to a given functional group. The reference-point-based KNN reveals a second spectrum-to-structure relationship that shows that quantum normal modes correlate with the actual positions of the functional groups.

article.title: Resensitization of colistin-resistant bacteria by the combination of colistin and L-arginine.
article.authors: Tong Li; Yuan Zhou; Guili Zhang; Weixi Lu; Ji Wu; Jiaqi Chen; Xudong Chen; Lingli He; Yanxian Yang; Min Dai; Qiang Zhang; Lan-Lan Zhong; Guo-Bao Tian
article.abstract: Colistin is the last-resort antibiotic for the clinical treatment of infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. However, the emergence of colistin-resistant bacteria, particularly those harboring the mcr-1 gene, has severely compromised the therapeutic efficacy of colistin. Herein, we demonstrated that L-arginine restores colistin susceptibility in colistin-resistant bacteria, including those with intrinsic or acquired resistance. The combination of colistin and L-arginine effectively treated murine acute peritonitis caused by a colistin-resistant bacterial infection, with no toxicity observed in either in vitro or in vivo assays. Mechanistically, we revealed that the combination enhances the permeability of the cell membrane, thereby promoting the influx of colistin, ATP efflux, and the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS), ultimately leading to the death of colistin-resistant bacteria. Furthermore, the combination downregulates membrane lipid-related genes fabZ and fadL, consequently suppressing fatty acid synthesis. This inhibition resulted in the uneven distribution of membrane lipids and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which further increased membrane permeability. In sum, our findings indicate that the combination of colistin and L-arginine successfully reverses the colistin resistance phenotype, providing a potential therapeutic strategy to combat infections caused by colistin-resistant bacteria.IMPORTANCEThe global spread of colistin-resistant bacteria has eroded one of the last lines of defense against life-threatening infections that no longer respond to conventional antibiotics. Here we show that L-arginine, a natural and safe amino acid, is an agent that can restore colistin susceptibility in strains with intrinsic or acquired resistance, and is effective in a murine peritonitis model without observable toxicity. Mechanistically, the combination increases membrane permeability and compromises the integrity of the membrane, leading to altered membrane lipid and LPS distribution that further amplifies membrane disruption. These findings establish that colistin combined with L-arginine constitutes a readily translatable therapeutic strategy to overcome colistin resistance and preserve the clinical utility of this critical last-resort antibiotic.

article.title: Research progress on cereal-derived bioactive factors for improving muscle function and counteracting sarcopenia.
article.authors: Chen Cheng; Jiayan Zhang; Yansheng Zhao; Juan Bai; Yufeng He; Xiang Xiao
article.abstract: Sarcopenia is an age-related syndrome characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical performance, closely associated with anabolic resistance, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, neuromuscular degeneration, and gut microbiota imbalance. Cereal grains and their by-products (e.g., bran, germ, and whole grains) are rich sources of bioactive components, including dietary fiber, polysaccharides, proteins, peptides, and polyphenols, which represent promising functional food resources for improving muscle health. This review systematically summarizes the structural characteristics, processing-induced transformations, and mechanisms by which cereal-derived functional factors may improve muscle health. Key bioactive components such as proteins, peptides, and polyphenols may enhance muscle function by activating mTORC1-mediated protein synthesis, suppressing the PI3K/Akt/FoxO ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, and modulating oxidative stress and inflammation via Nrf2/ARE and NF-κB signaling. Cereal polysaccharides (e.g., β-glucan, arabinoxylan, resistant starch) exert effects primarily through the gut microbiota-short-chain fatty acid axis, improving mitochondrial function, insulin sensitivity, intestinal barrier integrity, and systemic metabolic homeostasis. Although preclinical evidence is promising, human intervention studies remain limited. Future research should integrate mechanistic and clinical evidence to develop cereal-based functional foods for sarcopenia prevention and management.

article.title: Loss of LKB1 protects against acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in mice through sex-specific mechanisms.
article.authors: Debasree Bhadra; Jenna S Caswell; Kathryn L Smith; Natalie Porat-Shliom; Mitchell R McGill
article.venue: Toxicological sciences : an official journal of the Society of Toxicology
article.abstract: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF). We previously observed activation of liver kinase B1 (LKB1) in non-surviving patients with APAP-induced ALF. Thus, we hypothesized LKB1 is detrimental in APAP hepatotoxicity. To test our hypothesis, we overdosed hepatocyte-specific LKB1 knockout (KO) mice and wildtype (WT) littermates with APAP and measured liver injury 2, 6, and 24 h later. Consistent with our hypothesis, LKB1 KO protected against APAP hepatotoxicity. However, the mechanisms of protection were sex-specific. Male KOs had lower NAPQI formation due to lower mitochondrial CYP2E1. In contrast, NAPQI formation was similar between female KO and WT mice, but female KOs still had reduced oxidative stress. The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is a major source of NADPH to counter oxidative stress, so we hypothesized that female KO mice have increased PPP enzymes. To test that, we measured hepatic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the rate-limiting enzyme in the oxidative PPP. Importantly, G6PD was increased in female WT mice compared to male WT animals and even further increased in the female KO mice. Furthermore, 1.5 h post-treatment with the G6PD activator AG1 protected against APAP and increased hepatic NADPH in WT animals. Finally, re-analysis of our prior proteomics data revealed LKB1 activation occurred in both male and female ALF non-survivors, though it was greater in males. We conclude LKB1 regulates CYP2E1 and the PPP, that mitochondrial CYP2E1 is critical in APAP toxicity, and PPP activation is a potential therapeutic approach in liver injury in men and women.

article.title: A new validated UHPLC method for the simultaneous determination of diclofenac sodium and oxacillin sodium monohydrate for their combined dosage form for dermal delivery.
article.authors: A Thomas; D H Pink; A Buanz; T Chalati; A M Totea
article.venue: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
article.abstract: The rising prevalence of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among biofilm-forming pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), has intensified the need for therapeutic strategies capable of improving antibacterial efficacy against resistant infections. Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) exhibit limited intrinsic antimicrobial activity, growing evidence suggests that certain NSAIDs can potentiate conventional antibiotics, producing synergistic antibacterial and antibiofilm effects. Accordingly, the combined delivery of an NSAID and an antibiotic represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting infection-associated inflammation and bacterial persistence while potentially enhancing antibacterial activity. Incorporation of such drug combinations into nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) may further support topical delivery; however, reliable simultaneous quantification of both drugs within this complex lipid-based system remains analytically challenging. An ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography method with diode array detection (UHPLC-DAD) was developed and validated for the simultaneous quantification of oxacillin sodium monohydrate and diclofenac sodium in nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) intended for dermal delivery. Chromatographic separation was achieved on an XTerra MS C18 column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) using gradient elution with 0.05 M orthophosphoric acid in water and acetonitrile at a flow rate of 1.0 mL min-1, with detection at 210 nm. Oxacillin and diclofenac were baseline separated with retention times of 8.74 and 13.73 min, respectively. The method was validated in accordance with International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidelines and demonstrated linearity over the concentration range of 5-100 µg mL-1 for both analytes (R2 ≥ 0.9996). The limits of detection and quantification were 1.38 and 4.18 µg mL-1 for oxacillin, and 2.69 and 8.15 µg mL-1 for diclofenac, respectively. Precision was satisfactory, with intra-day and inter-day relative standard deviation values below 3%. Specificity was confirmed by the absence of matrix interference, while recovery studies demonstrated acceptable accuracy for both analytes in the formulation matrix. Under thermal (65 °C) and photolytic (405 nm) stress conditions, oxacillin showed recoveries of 81.16-97.77%, while diclofenac showed recoveries of 84.92-93.50%, indicating reduced recovery following stress exposure. The proposed method is reliable for the routine quantification of both drugs in dual-drug lipid-based formulations and is applicable to quality control, formulation development, and permeation studies.

article.title: Fibroproliferative Remodeling of Immune-Vascular Co-Culture Spheroid Models in Response to Atherogenic Stimulation.
article.authors: Ibukunoluwa Naiyeju; Stephanie Lehoux; Maryam Tabrizian
article.abstract: Cell-based models are highly valuable platforms for preclinical studies of atherosclerosis, offering controllable environments to investigate disease mechanisms. Three-dimensional (3D) spheroids, a class of cell-based models, enable the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena under physiologically relevant yet controlled conditions. In this study, we examined the lipid-induced changes in a co-culture spheroid model comprising THP-1-derived macrophages and primary human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs) following treatment with 20 or 40 µg/mL oxidized LDL (ox-LDL), a known atherogenic agent. Over a 10-day period, we assessed changes in spheroid morphology (size and compactness), cell viability, metabolic activity, intracellular composition, gene expression, pro-inflammatory cytokine release and extracellular matrix deposition, relative to the untreated control. Lipid exposure increased the abundance of macrophages in ox-LDL-treated spheroids (LS20-3 h: 35.5 ± 21.9%; LS40-3 h: 38.3 ± 8.7%) compared with controls (21.8 ± 0.7%) as early as day 3. Upregulation of fibronectin (LS20-3 h: ~1.8-fold; LS40-3 h: ~2.1-fold), CD36 (~1.8-fold), and ABCA-1 (~1.9-fold) was also observed. Moreover, spheroids exposed to 40 µg/mL ox-LDL exhibited reduced viability and compactness compared with those treated with 20 µg/mL by day 10. While lipid-treated spheroids showed non-statistically significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory IL-1β cytokine expression at day 0 which declined (> 85% decrease) by day 3, all spheroid groups showed comparable global fibronectin ECM secretion indices. Collectively, these findings reveal lipid-induced proliferative changes to spheroid composition & functionality and show their potential as biomimetic models for the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena.

article.title: Fructose as a systemic metabolic signal orchestrating metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease pathogenesis.
article.authors: Chunlin Li; Meng Li; Bing Wang; Guang Ji
article.venue: Critical reviews in food science and nutrition
article.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of the global population, yet the specific role of dietary fructose in disease progression remains inadequately defined. This review delineates the "Fructose-ectopic lipid accumulation (ELA)-MASLD" axis, identifying refined fructose (e.g., from sugar-sweetened beverages) not merely as a substrate but as a systemic signal that coordinates a pathological metabolic network. Hepatic fructose metabolism via the ketohexokinase-C (KHK-C) pathway bypasses the rate-limiting phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) checkpoint, promotes unregulated de novo lipogenesis (DNL), ATP depletion, and organellar stress. We identify the functional decline of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) plasticity as an important driver of this lipotoxic cascade. This tends to result in systemic lipid spillover, promoting an inflammatory cascade that impairs the intestinal barrier and induces insulin resistance (IR) in skeletal muscle and bystander organs. Furthermore, we discuss how genetic variants amplify this toxicity and critically evaluate emerging preclinical hypotheses regarding epigenetic remodeling and transgenerational inheritance. Finally, we propose stratified management strategies that integrate evidence-based nutritional modifications with targeted pharmacotherapy, distinguishing between hepatic-dominant and adipose-derived lipid excess to optimize clinical outcomes.

article.title: The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis.
article.authors: Peter K Smith; Nicholas P West; Stanley Du Preez; Hugh A Sampson; Peter W Hellings; David Price; Liam O'Mahony; Carina Venter; Cezmi A Akdis; Gil Yosipovitch
article.abstract: Allergic disease has risen too rapidly for inherited susceptibility to explain it, and the risk variants so far reported lie in the epithelial barrier and in type-2 immunity. We propose a five-layer model in which epithelial barrier and bioenergetic dysfunction may precede and promote type-2 immune deviation rather than arise solely as its consequence, progressing from (1) barrier and bioenergetic dysfunction, with mitochondrial DNA escaping into the cytosol, through (2) danger sensing and (3) epithelial-immune communication, to (4) type-2 immune amplification and (5) a systemic layer of circulating IgE, neurogenic amplification and the atopic march, with reciprocal inflammatory feedback. Layer 1 is also the least measured: standard immune panels carry almost none of these genes, and no genome-wide association study has implicated the mitochondrial genome or its nuclear regulators. From 1856 catalogued transcriptomic series, 985 of them expression series, we drew 116 case-control cohorts from 110 series, 3776 patients and 2164 controls, with Layer 1 prespecified as 350 genes across 19 domains. Of 212 module estimates nine survived false-discovery correction: two type-2 positive controls, two cytosolic sensing and inflammasome modules, raised in oesophageal tissue (Hedges' g +1.70) and atopic skin (+1.27), and five bioenergetic modules in oesophageal tissue. In eosinophilic oesophagitis the mitochondrial clearance limb was reduced in every one of thirteen cohorts (HIF1A -1.94, BNIP3-1.98). STING1 increased in all thirteen skin cohorts that measured it while MAVS fell in ten of thirteen oesophageal cohorts, and a STING1 minus MAVS contrast separated the allergic epithelia from psoriasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma without exception (exact p 0.029). In one series of clinically uninvolved atopic skin KEAP1 increased while NFE2L2, claudin-1 and filaggrin decreased (p < 0.001), in tissue that is not inflamed; pooled across nine series the directions largely hold without reaching significance. Broad suppression of mitochondrial programmes across allergic tissues was not supported: the phenotype is tissue-dependent, present in eosinophilic oesophagitis and atopic dermatitis, absent in nasal polyposis and established asthma and conditional in allergic rhinitis. Prospective and experimental studies must establish temporal and causal relationships.

article.title: Antiviral nanoparticles: mechanisms, biomedical applications and clinical translation toward next-generation therapies.
article.authors: Ravi Perugu; Siddavatam Sivajyothi; Young Jung Wee; Suresh V Chinni; Subash C B Gopinath; Veeranjaneya Reddy Lebaka
article.abstract: Viral infections represent a major global health challenge due to the rapid emergence of new pathogens, increasing antiviral drug resistance and limited efficacy of traditional treatments against evolving viruses. Nanotechnology is a promising interdisciplinary approach to fighting viral diseases, which can perform direct viral inactivation, targeted drug delivery, immune modulation, vaccine development, rapid diagnostics, and prevention of infection. This review offers an in-depth and critical overview of the major antiviral nanoparticle platforms, including metallic, metal oxide, carbon-based, polymeric, lipid-based, and bio-inspired nanoparticles. In this article, we employ a comparative framework to systematically analyze classes of nanoparticles based on their physicochemical properties, molecular mechanisms of antiviral action, biomedical applications, and translational potential. Antiviral mechanisms are discussed within the framework of the viral life cycle, including the inhibition of viral attachment and entry, destruction of viral envelope and capsid integrity, suppression of intracellular viral replication, reactive oxygen species-mediated viral inactivation, immune-modulation, and nanoparticle-assisted therapeutic delivery. Moreover, the review critically discusses the increasing biomedical applications of antiviral nanoparticles in therapeutics, vaccine delivery, diagnostics, antiviral coatings, gene therapy and precision nanomedicine, while highlighting the clinically successful technologies such as lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA vaccines. Special attention is paid to the main obstacles in clinical translation, such as nanotoxicity, biodistribution, manufacturing scalability, regulatory challenges, and the lack of standard evaluation protocols. Finally, major knowledge gaps and future research priorities are highlighted, focusing on the design of multifunctional, clinically translatable and regulatory-compliant nanoplatforms. This review offers insights on antiviral nanomedicines and practical insights for the rational design and successful clinical translation of next-generation antiviral nanoparticle.

article.title: Efficacy and Safety of Recaticimab in Patients With Dyslipidemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials With GRADE Assessment.
article.authors: Ahmed Talkhan; Amr M Abou Elezz; Nermin Ezzat Borham; Ahmed Noureldeen Abbas; Habiba Tariq Saeed; Lamees Taman; Mazen Momtaz Shehata; Muhammad M Elsharkawy; Mohamed Hamouda Elkasaby; William H Frishman; Wilbert S Aronow
article.abstract: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the principal target for preventing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, yet many patients do not reach treatment goals with statins, and established proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) antibodies require injections every 2-4 weeks. Recaticimab is a humanized anti-PCSK9 monoclonal antibody designed for dosing intervals of up to 12 weeks. We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library up to March 3, 2026, for randomized controlled trials comparing recaticimab with placebo in adults with dyslipidemia. Four double-blind trials (1657 randomized participants) were included. At week 12, recaticimab reduced LDL-C by 47.31 percentage points relative to placebo (95% confidence interval [CI], -49.87 to -44.75; I2 = 0%), with similar reductions for 150 mg every 4 weeks (-49.63), 300 mg every 8 weeks (-49.43), and 450 mg every 12 weeks (-45.50) (P for subgroup difference = 0.29). Recaticimab also reduced non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-45.17), apolipoprotein B (-42.31), lipoprotein(a) (-31.06), the total cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (-36.94), and the apolipoprotein B/apolipoprotein A1 ratio (-45.28), whereas the change in triglycerides was not significant (-10.05; 95% CI, -20.18 to 0.08).

article.title: Molecular drivers of intercellular communication in physical exercise: insights from omics approaches.
article.authors: Ana Carolina Pinto; Fernando Corrales; Maria do Rosário Domingues; Helena Beatriz Ferreira; Daniel Moreira Gonçalves; Rui Vitorino; Tânia Melo; Rita Ferreira
article.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Physical activity enhances overall health by promoting coordinated communication among organs. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) play a key role in this process by transporting proteins, RNAs, lipids and other molecules that reflect how different tissues respond to physiological stress. Proteomics has been instrumental in clarifying how exercise reshapes EVs, providing insights into their role in mediating intercellular communication and systemic adaptations. AREAS COVERED: Current proteomics of exercise-induced EV remodeling are overviewed and integrated with complementary transcriptomic and lipidomic findings. We highlight modality-dependent changes in EV abundance and cargo, including antioxidant enzymes, metabolic regulators and muscle-associated markers, such as α-sarcoglycan. Methodological challenges in EV isolation, molecular profiling, data normalization, and functional validation are critically examined, along with the potential of EVs as minimally invasive sources of biomarkers and therapeutic vectors. EXPERT OPINION: Circulating EVs transmit information between tissues to support the body's adaptation to exercise. Proteomics has identified important molecular signatures in EVs, but significant gaps remain regarding their cellular origin, the influence of exercise modalities on cargo selection, and the functional roles of these vesicles. Progress will require standardized workflows and integrated multi-omics approaches, combined with functional assays and physiological parameters of exercise adaptation.

article.title: Toxic Concentrations of Glutamate Induce Ferroptosis without Affecting Mitochondrial Respiration in Rodent Brain Slice Cultures.
article.authors: Annette Vaglio-Garro; Marco Theuermann; Katharina E Sweis; Sergejs Zavadskis; Márton Kokas; Zsuzsanna Környei; Miriam Karas; Laszlo Tretter; Tímea Komlódi; Adelheid Weidinger; Andrey V Kozlov
article.abstract: Many neuronal disorders are characterized by glutamate toxicity, which is closely associated with mitochondrial and neuronal dysfunction. The aim of this study was to investigate the link between mitochondrial function and mechanisms of cell death induced by glutamate. The study was carried out on male (C57BL/6) mice and male Sprague Dawley rat acute brain slices (ABSs), as well as male and female organotypic brain slice cultures (BSCs). Mitochondrial respiration, activities of tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, and the cell death rate [assessed by lactate dehydrogenase release and histological analyses] were determined. Memantine was used to inhibit excitotoxicity, while ferrostatin-1, rosiglitazone, and deferoxamine were used as inhibitors of the ferroptotic pathway. In astrocytes, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (OGDHC) showed <1% of the enzymatic activity observed in the whole-brain tissue. In BSCs, glutamate exposure induced a marked increase in oxidative phosphorylation-linked mitochondrial respiration, which was independent of OGDHC activity and disappeared when BSC homogenates were analyzed. Glutamate-induced cell death was not alleviated by memantine but was significantly reduced by ferrostatin-1. The activation of ferroptosis by glutamate was also observed in ABSs, as well as the inhibition of lipid peroxidation induced by ferrostatin-1, rosiglitazone, and deferoxamine. Ferrostatin-1 and rosiglitazone additionally inhibited cell death, while deferoxamine did not. The unusual response to deferoxamine requires further elucidation. In summary, our data suggest that elevated glutamate levels enhance neuronal energy metabolism in brain slices, compensating glutamate-mediated Ca2+ influx and reduce excitotoxicity. In contrast, persistently elevated levels of extracellular glutamate impair the cystine/glutamate antiporter, leading to ferroptosis.

article.title: Transcriptomic signatures of lipids in blood provide hypotheses of functional mechanisms linked to lipid metabolism and immune-cell regulation.
article.authors: Jessica I Lundin; Mariaelisa Graff; Jeff Haessler; Xinruo Zhang; Yanwei Cai; Harriett Fuller; Nancy Heard-Costa; Tianxiao Huan; Roby Joehanes; Joshua M Landman; Gina Marie Peloso; Yuxuan Wang; Zhe Wang; Jennifer E Below; Daniel Levy; Kari E North; Alex P Reiner; Ryan Zukowski; Ulrike Peters; Charles Kooperberg
article.abstract: Blood lipids are well-established risk factors for cardiovascular and other chronic diseases, yet the underlying functional mechanisms remain unclear. We conducted a large-scale, genome-wide transcriptome analysis of serum lipid levels using whole blood RNA-sequencing data from 6898 individuals of diverse races and ethnicities (17% Black or African American, 15% Hispanic Latino/a, 68% White). We utilized mixed-effects linear regression and meta-analyzed four discovery datasets (n = 4398 participants), identifying significant associations for 27 genes with low-density lipoproteins (LDL), 974 with high-density lipoproteins (HDL), 1229 with triglycerides (TRIG), and 276 with total cholesterol (TCHO). Two replication datasets (n = 2500 participants) confirmed 3, 55, 380, and 31 genes, respectively. Enrichment analysis revealed lipid metabolic processes for LDL, HDL, and TCHO associated genes, including LDLR, NPC2, and SQLE for LDL and TCHO, while TRIG associated genes highlighted immune and allergic response, cancer, and molecular signaling gene enrichment pathways. To infer causality, we performed bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and colocalization analyses. MR identified the expression of 8 genes as possibly causal for lipid levels; notable EEPD1 expression, linked with cellular cholesterol homeostasis, was inversely linked with TRIG levels. We also identified novel variants shared with LDL levels and gene expression of DDAH2, associated with cardiovascular disease, and TRIG level and expression of FCGRT, linked with maintaining triglyceride homeostasis. Phenome-wide enrichment analyses reported TRIG associated genes were enriched in secondary malignancy of bone suggesting broader systemic health implications of modified lipid levels. These findings highlight novel associations and genetic regulatory mechanisms as potential therapeutic targets for lipid dysregulation.

article.title: Effects of Prebiotics, Probiotics, or Synbiotics on Health Outcomes, Sex Hormones, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammatory Biomarkers in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A GRADE Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials, and Umbrella Review.
article.authors: Qiaozhi Dong; Hang Chen; Nia Liu; Mia Wang; Yangjie He
article.abstract: Numerous individual studies have examined the effects of biotics on isolated health outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). However, a comprehensive evaluation of their impact on the full metabolic panel and sex hormone profiles is lacking. Accordingly, this meta-analysis of RCTs and umbrella review attempted to form a complete picture of the overall efficacy of biotics on human metabolism and endocrine function. The PubMed, Scopus, Cochran, Web of Science, and Embase databases were used for conducting a comprehensive systematic search. Twenty RCTs were included in the meta-analysis and 11 meta-analyses were included for umbrella review. The pooled estimates of the studies evaluating the effects of biotics on anthropometric measurements indicated that biotics are associated with an improvement in weight (SMD: -1.21, 95%CI: -2.06, -0.36) and body mass index (BMI) (SMD: -0.77, 95%CI: -1.45, -0.10), waist circumference (WC) (SMD: -0.67, 95%CI: -1.18, -0.16), waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) (SMD: -0.84, 95%CI: -1.52, -0.15), glycemic control fasting plasma glucose (FPG) (SMD: -0.71, 95%CI: -1.19, -0.24), insulin (SMD: -0.64, 95%CI: -1.07, -0.21), and HOMA-IR (SMD: -0.78, 95%CI: -1.24, -0.32), total cholesterol (TC) (SMD: -0.69, 95%CI: -1.25, -0.13), low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL) (SMD: -0.71, 95%CI: -1.21, -0.20), high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL) (SMD: 0.39, 95%CI: 0.19, 0.60), triglyceride (TG) (SMD: -0.53, 95%CI: -0.95, -0.10), oxidative stress biomarkers such as malondialdehyde (MDA) (SMD: -0.96, 95%CI: -1.29, -0.63), total antioxidant capacity (TAC) (SMD: 0.59, 95% CI: 0.29, 0.89), testosterone (TT) (SMD: -1.29, 95%CI: -1.98, -0.68) level. However, umbrella review showed that biotics may contribute to an improvement in weight, BMI, WC, FPG, insulin, HOMA-IR, QUICKI, lipid profile, CRP, oxidative stress markers (MDA, TAC), TT and LH/FSH ratio too. In conclusion, this meta-analysis and umbrella review provide evidence that prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics may confer beneficial effects on a range of health outcomes among patients with PCOS.

article.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction as a Convergent Mechanism of α-Synuclein Toxicity: A Systematic Review of In Vitro Fibrillar Models.
article.authors: Hanadi Al Tbeishat; Douglas G Ward; Ilse S Pienaar; Richard J Elsworthy
article.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy bodies, and Multiple System Atrophy, are characterised by intracellular accumulation of misfolded α-synuclein (αSyn). Although αSyn aggregation is central to disease pathogenesis, the mechanisms linking αSyn to progressive neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood. Mitochondrial dysfunction is recognised as a key pathological process, particularly in experimental models using exogenously applied αSyn species, including preformed fibrils (PFFs). This systematic review synthesises evidence from mammalian in vitro studies that examined the effects of disease-associated αSyn conformations, including monomers, oligomers and PFFs, on mitochondrial structure and function. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycInfo were searched to identify eligible peer-reviewed studies published up to March 2026, yielding 33 included studies. Models encompassed neuronal, astrocytic, microglial, endothelial, fibroblast, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived systems, enabling comparison across cell types, αSyn conformations, and genetic backgrounds. Across included studies, oligomeric and fibrillar αSyn consistently induced mitochondrial depolarisation, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, reduced ATP production, complex-I dysfunction and increased reactive oxygen species generation. Additional mitochondrial pathological changes included fragmentation, cristae disruption, impaired TOM20-mediated protein import, calcium dysregulation, defective mitophagy and increased heteroplasmy i.e. accumulation of damaged mitochondria. These alterations frequently preceded cell death and were amplified in dopaminergic and genetically vulnerable models, including αSyn A53T, SNCA triplication, and PARK2-associated transgenic systems. Our review highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as a mechanism underlying αSyn toxicity, whilst suggesting methodological heterogeneity can limit cross-study translation. Priorities for future research using 'in vitro' models of PFF synucleinopathies include standardised fibril preparation protocols, improved mitochondrial phenotyping, and use of human multicellular and organoid models.

article.title: Mitochondrial Lactate Signaling and Protein Lactylation in Neurological Diseases.
article.authors: Yu Gu; Potao Zhang; Chunyan Lei; Wenyan Xu; Yunyu Cui
article.abstract: The brain, as a highly metabolically active organ, depends on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to sustain energy demands. When mitochondrial function is impaired, cells undergo metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis, leading to lactate accumulation. Beyond its traditional role as a metabolic byproduct, lactate is now recognized as a signaling molecule that links metabolism to epigenetic regulation through protein lactylation, a post-translational modification identified by Zhang et al. in 2019. Research on lactylation has progressed through three stages: initial discovery in histone lactylation as an epigenetic mark, expansion to non-histone proteins revealing roles in metabolic and structural regulation, and recent identification of mitochondrial protein lactylation influencing OXPHOS, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. This review summarizes the mitochondrial-lactate-lactylation axis in the nervous system, including brain lactate metabolism, the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle, and regulatory mechanisms of lactylation (writers, erasers, and readers). We further discuss its roles in histone and non-histone modification, its bidirectional relationship with mitochondrial dysfunction, and its involvement in neurodegenerative, cerebrovascular, and neuropsychiatric disorders. Finally, we highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting lactylation pathways. Collectively, mitochondrial lactate signaling and protein lactylation emerge as a central link between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic dysregulation in neurological diseases, providing new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

article.title: Medicarpin Alleviates Isoflurane-Induced Cognitive Dysfunction in Mice by Regulating the BDNF/TrkB Pathway.
article.authors: Tu Shen; Qiaoling Wu; Zifeng Xie; Shuai Yang; Siqi Dai; Zhichao Zhang
article.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) seriously threatens elderly surgical patients and has garnered substantial attention in recent years. Anesthesia and/or surgery-induced POCD remains a major issue. This study aimed to evaluate the potential protective effect of medicarpin, a bioactive pterocarpan, against isoflurane-induced cognitive dysfunction. The isoflurane exposure-induced cognitive dysfunction model was established using aged mice. We found that medicarpin reduced isoflurane exposure-induced neuroapoptosis, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial damage in hippocampal tissues and isoflurane-exposed HT22 cells. We also found that medicarpin prevented the inactivation of BDNF/TrkB pathway in cognitive dysfunction mice and isoflurane-exposed HT22 cells, implying that the neuroprotective effect of medicarpin might be mediated by the BDNF/TrkB signaling. Inhibition of TrkB signaling by K252a attenuated the beneficial effects of medicarpin against isoflurane‑induced neuronal damage in HT22 cells. These findings suggest that medicarpin improves cognitive dysfunction by suppressing neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction via activation of the BDNF/TrkB pathway. The results of this study provide important evidence for developing medicarpin into a potential therapeutic agent for POCD in elderly surgical patients.

article.title: Molecular detection of Rickettsia spp. in ticks (Ixodida: Argasidae and Ixodidae) and mites (Trombiculoidae) from a Brazilian taxonomic collection.
article.authors: Almir R Pepato; Nikolay V Anisimov; Jefferson C Carvalho Farias da Silva; Teofania H D Amorim Vidigal; Marcelo B Labruna; Brenda K Gomes-Almeida
article.abstract: Rickettsia species are arthropod-hosted endosymbionts classified into phylogenetic and serological groups, heterogeneous concerning their ecologies. This study aims to screen ticks and mites deposited in the Acarological Collection at Center of Taxonomical Collections at Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Brazil, for rickettsial occurrences, making available genetic data on hosts and bacteria. Endogenous mitochondrial markers for ticks and mitochondrial and nuclear genes for chiggers were sequenced for sample quality control and species identification. A total of 38 soft ticks belonging to the genus Ornithodoros (at least six putative species), 18 hard ticks belonging to the genus Amblyomma (7 spp), and 52 chiggers belonging to genus Whartonia (2 spp) led to sequences. Polymerase Chain reactions for a Citrate Synthase gene fragment led to 21 sequences grouped in the phylogroups Bellii, Spotted Fever, and Transitional, with one sequence of Rickettsia obtained from Amblyomma dubitatum (identified as R. bellii), eight sequences from Ornithodoros (classified in six gltA genotypes associated to the phylogroups Bellii, Spotted Fever and Transitional) and twelve associate to Whartonia pachywhartoni (three likely in the Spotted Fever and nine in the Transitional phylogroup). Considering the diversity of rickettsial occurrences in Ornithodoros, with four of the nine gltA genotypes detected only in O. fonsecai, a species known to bite humans, the medical relevance of Rickettsia associated with caves and bats needs to be further investigated.

article.title: The Skin Barrier as an Integrated System: Physical, Chemical, Microbial, and Immunological Components and Their Key Interactions.
article.authors: Omar Lupi; Ted Lain; Jerry Tan; Latanya T Benjamin
article.abstract: The skin barrier is a dynamic and multicomponent system that serves as the first line of protection for the body against pathogens, allergens, and transepidermal water loss. This narrative review, based on key insights from an international meeting on skin barrier function, provides a summary of the structural, chemical, microbial, and immunological components that form the skin barrier. The interplay between physical and chemical architecture of the stratum corneum in regulating barrier permeability and balancing immune responses is also discussed, particularly the roles of the acid mantle and ceramides in the extracellular lipid matrix. The interactions between the exposome, the skin and gut microbiomes, and the genome that influence skin barrier function are also considered. Finally, we review developmental and ethnic differences in skin barrier properties, which underscore the need for personalized approaches to skin care and disease management. Overall, the topics discussed in this narrative review highlight the importance of maintaining skin barrier integrity as a cornerstone of skin health, and present recent advances in our understanding of the complex interactions among skin barrier components, immune cells, and environmental factors. However, further research using innovative tools, such as the skin interactome, is essential for advancing targeted therapies and patient-centered care.

article.title: Red Light Therapy and Mitochondrial Rejuvenation in Age-Related Disorders.
article.authors: Maria Iglewska; Kinga Agata Flis; Maja Kołakowska; Witold Wit Hryniewicz; Agnieszka Pluto-Prądzyńska
article.abstract: Aging is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired ATP production, and a decline in tissue regenerative capacity, leading to the development of age-related diseases. This review summarizes current evidence regarding the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) on mitochondrial function and age-related disorders. PBM using red and near-infrared light may enhance proper mitochondrial function by acting on cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) and other signaling pathways, including the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel, leading to increased ATP production, modulation of ROS signaling, and improved cellular homeostasis. We review in vitro, animal, and clinical studies investigating PBM in metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, cardiovascular, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and skeletal muscle disorders associated with aging, as well as its application in the management of cancer therapy-related oral mucositis. Current studies demonstrate beneficial effects on glucose metabolism, cardiovascular function, neuronal function, lipid metabolism, liver function, muscle regeneration, and visual function in AMD, as well as the safety and efficacy of PBM in the management of cancer therapy-induced oral mucositis. The therapeutic effects of PBM appear to be dose-dependent and influenced by treatment parameters including wavelength, fluence, irradiance, and exposure protocol. Although photobiomodulation still lacks standardized treatment protocols and differences exist in the wavelengths used, dosage, and frequency among studies, it represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of age-related diseases.

article.title: Cubosome integrated with polymeric carbon nitride and cisplatin: in vivo biodistribution and in vitro photodynamic therapy studies.
article.authors: Sk Jahir Abbas; Shiraz Mehmood; Yen-Hsien Li; Sabina Yesmin; Cheng-Kuan Su; Nayim Sepay; Chih-Sheng Chiang; Wei-Chun Chang; Yao-Ching Hung; Wen-Lung Ma
article.abstract: Cubosome based lipid nanoparticles have emerged as a premier system for drug loading and delivery. Their outstanding preclinical results underscore the importance of precision medicine for developing next generation nanomedicines. We have reported a novel engineered route for insitu formation and hybridization of cubosome based nanomaterial (lipid-g-C3N4-cisplatin nanoparticle), integrated with polymeric carbon nitride and cisplatin. Using an interfacial aqueous organic phase drive, we have successfully achieved cubic architecture with particle diameters of 150-200 nm. Cryogenic electron microscopy confirmed about structural integrity, while zeta potential measurements indicated to the stability with a near positive surface charge. Electron paramagnetic resonance spin trapping experiments demonstrated to the capacity of generating reactive oxygen species, specifically peroxide and superoxide. C57BL/6 mice intravenously injected with the nanoparticle which have shown preferential biodistribution in the lungs (0.09 ug Pt/g), liver (0.03 ug Pt/g), kidneys (0.06 ug Pt/g), and plasma (0.012 ug Pt/ml). The nanoparticle accumulation have exhibited a minimum in the thymus, heart, spleen, and intestines. Under dark conditions, IC50 was 176.2 µg/mL for A549 cells, 139.1 µg/mL for Tong cells, and 279.3 µg/mL for HEK-293T cells. The efficacy of photodynamic therapy observed at concentrations of 50-200 µg/mL for A549 cells and 100-200 µg/mL for Tong and HEK-293T cells, highlighting that the efficiency of nanoplatform towards oncological applications in the organs of lungs, liver, and kidneys.

article.title: Metabolomic profiling unveils differential modulation of tomato fruit quality by microbial interventions.
article.authors: Deepti Varsha; Sourabh Shukla; Radha Prasanna
article.abstract: The potential of bio inputs to enhance the organoleptic attributes of tomato, particularly, their nutraceutical benefits and export potential motivated us to develop stimulatory microbial formulations. Towards this endeavour, untargeted metabolic profiling and fruit volatile analysis in 'Pusa Cherry 1' tomatoes were undertaken, to analyse the differential elicitation of metabolites by microbial interventions. Treatment with cyanobacterium Anabaena laxa enhanced the fruit lycopene content by 1.13-fold while, a mesocarpic bacterium- Enterobacter cloacae enhanced the fruit lycopene, phenolics and flavonoids by 1.07, 1.5 and 2.54-fold respectively; combined inoculation led to 1.25 and 1.68-fold increase in phenolics and flavonoids, compared to control fruits. Untargeted metabolome analyses of fruits revealed A. laxa mediated enrichment of spermidine and benzoquinone and likely, induction of plant's antioxidant defense system and hormonal modulation, towards enhanced lycopene content and accumulation of benzenoid derived floral volatiles. High lycopene, flavonoid and ascorbic acid content along with carotenoid and lipoxygenase derived fruity volatiles in the fruits of E. cloacae treatment can possibly be associated with the stimulation of sphingolipid metabolism, lipoxygenase mediated oxylipin synthesis and the accumulation of S-adenosyl methionine, both suggesting jasmonate/ethylene mediated induced systemic resistance. Enrichment of α-ketoglutarate, amines, purines and pyrimidines besides S-adenosyl methionine, sphingolipid and rutin accumulation in the fruits due to co-inoculation of A. laxa and E. cloacae was also supported by 20.4% increase in fruit yield. It is noteworthy that both the microbes elicited distinct modes of defense system activation and co-ordinated hormonal responses which influenced fruit overall ripeness, nutritional and sensory quality, along with increased fruit yield.

article.title: Pseudodominant inheritance in paraplegin (SPG7)-associated CPEO-ataxia syndrome.
article.authors: Weber Liu; Serge Geara; Simon Rowe; Carolyn Mary Sue
article.abstract: SPG7 encodes paraplegin, a mitochondrial AAA-metalloprotease critical for inner mitochondrial membrane protein quality control. Pathogenic variants most commonly cause autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) but its phenotypic spectrum includes cerebellar ataxia, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myopathy and parkinsonism.We report a 47 year old man presenting with a progressive external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, progressive gait disturbance, and spasticity. Ten-year follow-up of this individual showed slowly progressive spastic ataxia with ocular motor involvement and neurogenic bladder. His mother and maternal aunt both had marked spasticity, ataxia, ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia. Genetic testing demonstrated compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in paraplegin in this individual. Genetic testing in his mother and aunt revealed homozygous canonical splice-site variants (c.2182-2 A > G). Cascade testing of his asymptomatic father showed a common pathogenic missense variant p.(Ala510Val) in the same gene.This family demonstrates a pseudodominant inheritance pattern, instead of the expected autosomal recessive trait that applies to paraplegin. We highlight diagnostic pitfalls in relying on family history and assumed inheritance traits. We emphasise the importance of segregation analysis and comprehensive genomic testing. Recognition of pseudodominance inheritance has important implications for genetic counselling, family planning and cascade testing.

article.title: The Molecular Logic of Platelet-Activating Factor (PAF).
article.authors: Xiao Corey Ma; Jon Clardy
article.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
article.abstract: Platelet-activating factor (PAF) is a well-known if enigmatic lipid signal with important roles in inflammatory responses, allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases, and thrombotic cascades. Several lines of evidence suggest that our current model of PAF's molecular mechanism is inadequate. This report describes a recontextualized model for PAF. The revised model embeds PAF in a plasmalogen-based molecular mechanism in which activation is a spontaneous chemical reaction triggered by environmental conditions that liberates a PAF receptor (PAF-R) agonist from a membrane-bound phospholipid. The active ligand subsequently undergoes a thermodynamically driven spontaneous rearrangement into an inactive isomer, a feature that controls response lifetime. The revised model is a molecule-autonomous set of transformations that create a response with spatial and temporal control. More generally the revised model's congruence with a similar model for RORγt supports a picture in which plasmalogens form a part of the immune system that is separate from the cell-based innate and adaptive immune systems.

article.title: Preclinical Studies of MVT-100, A Novel Ultrasound Enhancing Agent.
article.authors: Emmanuelle J Meuillet; Joel Lusk; Holly Tadevich; Jonathan R Lindner; Soheb Anwar Mohammed; Benay Ozbay; Muhammad Wahab Amjad; John J Pacella; Xucai Chen; Leyla E Sade; Flordeliza S Villanueva; Evan C Unger
article.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Over the past decades, many investigations have used perfluorocarbon (PFC)-based contrast products to enhance ultrasound (US) imaging. Currently octafluoropropane (OFP), decafluorobutane, and sulfur hexafluoride or a combination of those gases is used for the preparation of ultrasound enhancing agents (UEA). This study reports the development of MVT-100, a novel microbubble ultrasound enhancing agent (UEA) designed for improved stability, safety, and imaging performance. The objective of these studies was to fully characterize and compare the biophysical, chemical and in vivo properties of the new UEA (herein referred to as MVT-100) as compared with the well-known and widely utilized UEA known as perflutren lipid microspheres (Perflutren) (commercialized under the name of Definity®). METHODS: Analytical methods were used to characterize the MBs. Low mechanical index (MI) contrast-enhanced ultrasound was performed in mice and pigs. RESULTS: Comparison of Perflutren MB with MVT-100 MB showed similarities of the products in their overall particle numbers, gas content, osmolality, pH and phospholipid concentrations. However, MVT-100 exhibited a zeta potential that was essentially neutral (+0.5 ± 0.1 mV), compared with the negative zeta potential of Perflutren (-4.2 ± 2.0 mV), a tighter size distribution and lower polydispersity index (0.114 ± 0.012 vs. 0.159 ± 0.036, p = 0.048). Under accelerated storage conditions (40°C for 4 weeks), MVT-100 demonstrated markedly greater lipid stability, with only 2.05% loss of total phospholipid content compared with 13.10% for Perflutren. Murine renal retention studies showed that MVT-100 MB exhibited significantly lower (∼2.5 fold) renal retention in the kidney as compared with Perflutren. In porcine studies, MVT-100 hemodynamic parameters were identical to those of Perflutren. Echocardiographic porcine studies showed that ventricular opacification and endocardial border delineation following MVT-100 administration were comparable between agents at early time points, with higher and more sustained opacification with MVT-100 at later time points (generalized linear mixed model: main effect of agent p 0.99). CONCLUSIONS: MVT-100 is a novel UEA that exhibits promising properties as a new imaging agent for contrast echocardiography with appealing storage conditions.

article.title: Discovery and pharmacological profiling of quinoline- and quinoxaline-based phenoxypropanoic acid derivatives as multitarget modulators of PPARα, FXR, and LXRα receptors.
article.authors: Iuliia Melnikova; Galina Karabanovich; Jan Dušek; Martin Ambrož; Hana Laštůvková; Tomaš Smutný; Mária Bajnoková; Rajamanikkam Kamaraj; Rudy Salam; Adam Reguli; Petra Štěrbová-Kovaříková; Otto Kučera; Stanislav Mičuda; Jaroslav Roh; Petr Pavek
article.abstract: Fibrates, derivatives of phenoxypropanoic acid, have long been used in the therapy of dyslipidemia, targeting the nuclear receptor Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) in the liver and other organs. To discover novel modulators of metabolism-regulating nuclear receptors, we synthesized and evaluated libraries of novel fibrate derivatives based on 2-(4-(quinolin-2-yloxy)phenoxy)propanoic and 2-(4-(quinoxalin-2-yloxy)phenoxy)propanoic acid. We found that some of the prepared compounds exhibit unique properties activating PPARα and the Farnesoid X receptor (FXR) while simultaneously inhibiting Liver X receptor α (LXRα) in cellular in vitro assays. Pilot experiments demonstrate that quinoline derivatives 6d and 6e have suitable pharmacokinetic properties and a significant metabolic effect on selected lipid metabolism genes in vivo in mice and human hepatocyte spheroids. Peroral administration of compound 6d to mice fed a high-fat diet decreased the levels of plasma triglycerides and promoted the expression of critical genes of β-oxidation in the liver. We thus propose that we have discovered and pharmacologically profiled new quinoline/quinoxaline phenoxypropanoic acid compounds with combined PPARα/FXR activation and LXRα antagonistic activity, supported by preliminary hepatic target-engagement and in vivo metabolic data. In particular, halogen-substituted 2-(4-(quinolin-2-yloxy)phenoxy)propanoic acid derivatives could be promising multitarget ligands for orchestrating distinct metabolic programs of individual nuclear receptors, supporting their further optimization.

article.title: The NAP transcription factor: An integrative node for environmental and developmental signals in plant senescence.
article.authors: Ziyu Guo; Yueying Ding; Min Yuan; Ruiju Wang
article.abstract: Organ senescence is a pivotal developmental transition that is finely tuned by developmental age and environmental cues. The NAC transcription factor NAP acts as a central integrator of these signals, translating them into the coordinated execution of senescence across reproductive and vegetative organs. This review focuses on its upstream regulation and downstream regulatory network in leaf senescence. We first summarize how developmental, hormonal, and environmental signals converge on NAP through specific transcriptional, epigenetic, post-transcriptional, and post-translational mechanisms. We then describe how NAP executes the leaf senescence program by directly activating a suite of effector genes, forming self-reinforcing loops with abscisic acid, ethylene, and salicylic acid biosynthesis, promoting cytokinin degradation, and accelerating water loss through stomatal regulation. Beyond leaves, NAP also governs senescence in ovules, siliques, and petals. Comparative analyses across monocots and eudicots reveal deep conservation of NAP function in senescence regulation but lineage-specific divergence in stress responses. Finally, we highlight key bottlenecks and emerging opportunities for translating NAP research into crop improvement. Together, these insights position NAP as a conserved regulatory hub for organ senescence and provide a framework for fine-tuning senescence timing to improve crop yield and resilience.

article.title: Attenuating NKG2D stimulation reshapes intratumoral NK cell functional state to enhance persistence and anti-tumor efficacy.
article.authors: Sizhe Liu; Ryan J Brown; Payal Dhar; Geetha Priyanka Yerradoddi; Tyler A Smith; Bin Zhang; Deyu Fang; Congcong He; David J VanderWeele; Masha Kocherginsky; Arabela Grigorescu; Seth M Pollack; Qingshu Meng; Qi Cao; Karla Guerra; Weiguo Cui; Jennifer D Wu
article.abstract: NK cell-based therapies for solid tumors are limited by poor persistence and progressive functional impairment. Here, we investigated how the strength of NKG2D stimulation shapes NK cell fate and therapeutic efficacy. Using B10G5, a MICA/B-targeting partial agonist antibody that attenuates NKG2D stimulation, we show that reduced NKG2D stimulation reshapes the intratumoral NK cell compartment by enriching EOMEShiTCF1hi stem-like NK (stemNK) cell pool, preserving functional diversity, and limiting mitochondrial oxidative stress and exhaustion induced by chronic sMIC/MIC exposure. Mechanistically, we identified the H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B as a conserved regulator of NK cell stemness whose enzymatic activity is required to maintain the intratumoral stemNK cell pool. Conversely, strong NKG2D stimulation induced mitochondrial ROS accumulation and upregulated the inhibitory receptor LAG3 on NK cells. Attenuated NKG2D stimulation on human NK cells increased KDM6B expression and reduced repressive H3K27me3 mark at the TCF7 locus. Importantly, attenuated NKG2D stimulation during ex vivo expansion enhanced human NK cell in vivo persistence and antitumor efficacy following adoptive transfer. Together, these findings establish NKG2D stimulation strength as a key determinant of NK cell fate and function in solid tumors and identify a translatable concept to improve NK cell-based immunotherapy for solid tumors.

article.title: Investigating the efficacy and toxicity of partial in vivo reprogramming as a rejuvenation intervention.
article.authors: Franziska Meiners; Daniel Palmer; Roberto A Avelar; Israel Barrantes; Georg Fuellen
article.abstract: Partial reprogramming by cyclic expression of Yamanaka factors has been proposed as a rejuvenation strategy, yet evaluating tissue-specific responses and potential risks remains challenging. Here, we reanalyzed RNA-seq data from the liver, kidney, and spleen of aged mice subjected to seven months of partial reprogramming. We used the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) framework to estimate adverse and beneficial signatures, assessed functional changes via gene set enrichment analysis and deconvoluted bulk RNA-seq data to estimate differences in cell type proportion. In the liver and kidney, partial reprogramming suppressed age-activated immune and inflammatory processes, while activating age-suppressed metabolic and catabolic pathways.
